Corvo had always suspected there would be a limit to his eloquence.

He had merely not expected it to be found on a changing-room bench beneath fluorescent lights, one hand braced uselessly against old varnished wood, the other clenched in the discarded edge of his own shirt as if fabric could save him.

It could not.

For once, Corvo had no correction to offer. No insult sharpened and ready. No elegant little observation about tempo, distance, or form. His head tipped back against the bench, throat exposed, breath leaving him in uneven fragments that would have humiliated him under any other circumstances.

Under these, he decided humiliation had been unfairly maligned.

“Reyes,” he managed, and even that sounded less like a warning than a confession.

The name broke in his mouth.

He shut his eyes, then opened them immediately, because pride apparently survived anything and he refused to miss a second of his own undoing. His hand found the edge of the bench instead, fingers curling hard enough that the old wood complained beneath him.

“Of course,” he said, voice wrecked, “of course this is where you discover patience.”

He tried to laugh. It came out badly.

The first time he had fenced Reyes, Corvo had known within three touches that the man was dangerous. Not because of strength. Not because of speed. Those were ordinary dangers. No, Reyes had been dangerous because he watched. Because he waited half a breath longer than most people could bear. Because he understood that pressure did not always mean forward motion.

Corvo had hated him for it.

Corvo had admired him for it.

Corvo, now flat on a bench with his composure in pieces on the tile beside their kit, finally understood that he had been doomed from the first bout.

His free hand lifted, hovered, then settled against the nearest solid thing he could reach, not pushing away, only holding on. His wrist turned, the bruise catching the light again, that small old ache swallowed by the newer, sharper one climbing through him.

“Do not,” he said, then stopped, because he had no idea what command he meant to give.

Do not stop.

Do not look so pleased with yourself.

Do not make him admit aloud that he had wanted this so badly it had turned into rivalry because rivalry was safer.

His jaw tightened. His breath failed him again.

Corvo stared at the ceiling as if it had personally betrayed him.

“You are going to be impossible after this,” he whispered.

A beat.

His mouth curved, helpless and furious and fond all at once.

“And I am going to deserve it.”

The admission left him stripped more thoroughly than any piece of clothing on the floor. There it was: the truth at last, no mask, no salute, no scorekeeper. Just Corvo, finally honest because Reyes had found a way to make dishonesty require more discipline than he had left.

He turned his head, cheek against the bench, eyes dark and bright under the ruined fall of his hair.

“Look at me,” he said, rougher now, not an order from the piste but something far more dangerous. “If you are going to take me apart, have the courtesy to watch what you are doing.”

And then even that arrogance failed.

His hand snapped to his mouth for one breath, muffling the sound that escaped him, but only one. After that, Corvo let it fall away. Pride had carried him for thirty-eight years; it could survive being set aside for one night.

Perhaps two.

Perhaps whatever came after this, if either of them had the courage not to pretend it had been nothing.

The bench creaked beneath him. His shoulders tensed, then loosened by degrees. The cold room had narrowed to heat, breath, pulse, the unbearable deliberate pace of being answered without words.

Corvo had spent four years trying to beat Reyes.

Now, with his fingers splayed helplessly against the bench and his voice reduced to a low, broken sound, he understood the more terrible possibility.

He wanted to lose.

He wanted to lose thoroughly.

And later—later, when he had recovered enough dignity to be insufferable again—he would claim that he had allowed it for tactical reasons.

For now, he only reached down, touched Reyes with shaking fingers, and said the truest thing he had managed all night.

“Yes.”

He surrendered it in pieces.

First the commentary went. Then the corrections. Then the last smug, defensive little smile he had been trying to keep alive out of principle. It failed under the weight of breath and heat and the intolerable fact that Reyes knew exactly when to ignore him.

Corvo’s hands found purchase where they could: the bench, the edge of a locker, a discarded sleeve twisted under his fingers. Anything solid enough to survive him. He had spent years making himself precise, elegant, composed under pressure.

There was nothing elegant left.

Only the sharp lift of his breath. The rough sound of his voice when control slipped. The way his body kept answering before his pride could object.

“Don’t stop,” Corvo said.

It came out hoarse. Bare. Not a command, not really. Worse than a command.

A request.

The admission struck him even as he made it. His eyes opened, bright and furious with himself, as if he might still take it back through sheer force of personality. But he did not. Could not. His mouth parted around another breath, and whatever he had meant to say after that broke apart before it became language.

The bench complained beneath him. A locker door rattled once under some careless impact. Their kit lay strewn across the floor in a disgraceful heap Corvo would have scolded any student for leaving.

He could not have cared less if the entire building collapsed around them.

The salle beyond the changing room remained empty and indifferent. No referee. No clock. No clean score. Only the two of them and the ruin of four years’ restraint.

Corvo turned his head, cheek brushing the bench, and laughed once—low, breathless, almost disbelieving.

“God,” he managed. “You are going to be unbearable.”

The words were meant to bite.

They did not.

They came out too warm. Too wrecked. Too close to wonder.

His hands shook when he reached, not from weakness but from the effort of letting himself want without disguising it as competition. That, more than anything, undid him: not the heat, not the force, not even the pleasure dragging through him until his thoughts scattered uselessly.

It was being known.

It was Reyes seeing the opening and taking it, and Corvo, for once in his life, not closing the line.

He arched, swore softly in Italian, then lost the rest of the sentence against a broken sound that would have mortified him if he had possessed enough dignity to be mortified. He did not. Dignity was somewhere on the tile with his mask and gloves.

Later, perhaps, he would retrieve it.

Later, he would make some insufferable remark about form.

Later, he would pretend he had allowed exactly as much as he intended.

But not now.

Now Corvo held on, eyes shut, jaw tight, every breath torn out of him like surrender had teeth.

And when the wave finally took him again, it took him completely.

For a few long moments after, he was silent.

Actually silent.

A medical concern, perhaps.

His chest rose hard. His hair had fallen into his face. One hand lay open against the bench as though even his fingers had forgotten how to make a fist. His expression, when his eyes opened, was stripped past arrogance into something far more dangerous: stunned satisfaction, reluctant tenderness, and the immediate, unmistakable beginning of a grudge.

He swallowed.

Once.

Twice.

Then Corvo looked up through the wreck of himself, mouth curving with heroic effort.

“I hope,” he said, voice ruined, “you understand that I am going to be impossible now.”

He tried to sit up and failed on the first attempt.

That offended him.

Deeply.

He gathered himself with visible concentration, pushed up onto one elbow, and looked down at the state of them both: open clothing, scattered gear, the bench shoved slightly crooked, the room bearing every sign of a match conducted with absolutely no regard for regulation.

His eyes narrowed.

“Also,” he added, because apparently death itself could not stop him from criticism, “your follow-through was arrogant.”

A beat.

His mouth twitched.

“Effective. But arrogant.”

He reached then, slower now, not to pull away or reclaim distance, but to close what little of it remained. His fingers found Reyes with less urgency and more care, as though the aftermath required its own discipline. Corvo had never been gentle by accident; when he was gentle, it was with intent.

His thumb moved once.

His expression sharpened to hide how much that small contact mattered.

“Look at this,” he murmured. “A disaster. Equipment everywhere. No respect for the room. No respect for procedure.”

He drew in a careful breath, then let it out, still uneven.

“No respect for me whatsoever.”

The lie was so obvious it barely qualified as one.

Corvo leaned closer, pressing his forehead briefly against Reyes, eyes closing again. The gesture cost him. It was not theatrical enough to be teasing and not guarded enough to be safe.

“Four years,” he said quietly.

This time there was no accusation in it.

Only astonishment.

Four years of needling. Four years of late bouts and lingering glances and excuses made out of grips, blades, repairs, criticism. Four years of mistaking hunger for rivalry because rivalry had rules and hunger did not.

His laugh came softer this time.

“I am not apologizing,” he said. “For the record.”

Of course he was not.

But his hand stayed where it was. His breathing steadied by degrees. The hard, bright edge of him eased into something no less intent, only less armed.

Then he lifted his head, and there it was again: Corvo restored just enough to be dangerous.

“First to five,” he said, as if remembering a grievance. “We never finished.”

His gaze dropped briefly, then returned, dark with promise and challenge braided together beyond untangling.

“Which means,” Corvo continued, voice still rough but regaining its wicked precision, “technically, no one has won.”

A pause.

His smile spread slowly.

“Yet.”

Corvo’s wrists met the bench, and for once he did not immediately turn the disadvantage into leverage.

He tested it. Of course he did. Pride demanded at least the ceremonial attempt: a flex of forearm, a shift of shoulder, the minute calculation of angle and force. Enough to know he could struggle. Enough to know he did not want to.

His breath left him on a laugh that had no polish left in it.

“Oh,” he said, voice low, stripped down to something dangerously honest. “There you are.”

The words sounded like discovery. Like accusation. Like relief.

Pinned beneath that pressure, Corvo went still—not submissive in any simple way, never that, but attentive. Entirely present. His eyes stayed open, dark and bright and fixed, because if he was going to lose control, he would at least have the arrogance to witness it.

“You have been waiting to do that,” he murmured.

His fingers curled once against empty air, unable to make their usual clever use of touch. It unsettled him more than he expected. His hands had always been his argument: blade, correction, gesture, command. Without them, every answer had to come from somewhere less practiced.

His throat worked.

“Fine,” Corvo said. “No pace-setting.”

A beat.

Then, because he was himself, because ruin apparently still allowed commentary, his mouth curved.

“But if this is your idea of proving a point, I should warn you—your thesis lacks structure.”

The next breath betrayed him. So did the one after.

His shoulders pressed into the bench; his wrists remained where they had been set. The old wood was hard beneath him, the air cool across his opened shirt, and the room smelled of leather and steel and the aftermath of a bout neither of them had truly finished. It should have steadied him. Familiar terrain. Familiar rituals. Salle, kit, sweat, rivalry.

Instead, every familiar thing had become evidence against him.

How many nights had he stood here pretending not to watch Reyes pack away gear? How many times had he found some unnecessary adjustment to make, some invented fault in a weapon, some reason not to leave first? Four years of restraint, and now restraint had him flat on a bench with his pulse making a disgrace of him.

Corvo swallowed.

“If I concede,” he said, quieter, “you will be impossible.”

The admission hung there.

His eyes narrowed, not with resistance now, but with the last intact shard of challenge.

“If I do not concede,” he continued, “you will become ambitious.”

His laugh came rough and brief.

“Terrible position. Tactically indefensible.”

For a moment, his expression softened in spite of him. The sharpness did not vanish; it warmed. Beneath all the provocation, under all the old performance, there was a kind of wonder he had no ready insult for.

He had imagined winning against Reyes in a hundred different ways.

He had not imagined this: wanting the loss so badly his body had understood before his pride could object.

Corvo turned his head against the bench, just enough to bare the line of his throat and hate himself for how deliberate it was.

“There,” he said, almost under his breath. “Is that proper enough for you?”

His wrists shifted again. Not to escape. Only because being held in place made him aware of every inch of himself with merciless clarity. His breath caught, then steadied badly.

“Do not look so pleased,” he said, though his eyes gave him away. “I am still evaluating your form.”

Another pause.

His voice dropped.

“It is… improving.”

That cost him. The confession, small as it was, colored his face more deeply than the exertion had. Corvo, who could stand before a room of students and dissect their failures without flinching, found himself undone by praise leaving his own mouth.

He tried to recover with disdain and achieved only hunger.

“Damn you,” he whispered.

Not angry. Not even close.

His hands flexed again under the restraint, and this time the motion was less test than reflex. He let it happen. Let himself feel the helplessness of not deciding the next tempo, the maddening luxury of not being required to answer every advance with one of his own.

His eyes remained fixed, stubbornly open.

“If you wanted honesty,” Corvo said, voice rougher now, “then there. I like this.”

The words landed heavily in him.

He looked almost offended by having said them aloud.

“I like not knowing exactly what you will do next,” he continued, each phrase dragged from him with visible difficulty. “I like that you finally stopped fencing me long enough to touch me. I like—”

His jaw tightened.

For once, the rest did not come dressed as a joke.

“I like that it is you.”

The changing room seemed to contract around that sentence. Fluorescent hum. Scattered equipment. Their abandoned rivalry lying in pieces with the rest of the kit.

Corvo closed his eyes then, just for a second, as if honesty required darkness.

When he opened them again, he was still Corvo. Ruined, yes. Flushed, breathless, pinned, stripped of several useful defenses—but still proud enough to lift his chin as much as the bench allowed.

“So,” he said. “No. I do not concede.”

His mouth curved slowly.

“I merely acknowledge that you have advantage.”

A beat.

“Temporarily.”

It was absurd bravado. He knew it. It showed in the way his smile shook at the edge, in the way his breath failed him, in the way his body had gone taut with anticipation rather than resistance.

Then the arrogance slipped again, and what remained beneath it was more dangerous.

“Reyes,” Corvo said, softly this time.

Not a warning. Not a taunt.

A request with teeth.

His wrists remained pinned. His gaze did not move.

“Do it properly, then.”

The words left him low and deliberate, roughened by four years of wanting and one night of finally being too tired to lie about it.

“And when I am unbearable tomorrow,” he added, because some habits were immortal, “remember that you encouraged me.”

Then his composure broke in increments: first the breath, then the line of his mouth, then the last clean edge of his expression. He held on as long as pride allowed, which was longer than most men could have managed and not nearly long enough to save him.

By the time he turned his face aside again, laughing once under his breath like a man defeated in the best possible fashion, there was no real argument left in him.

Only heat.

Only trust.

Only the vicious, impossible satisfaction of having been answered at last.

rows.reply:
Vex saw it happen — the moment composure stopped being something Ari held and started being something they'd set down. It showed in the shoulders first, then the jaw, then the particular slackness of a mouth that had given up on arranging itself. She had done nothing yet that would leave a mark or a story. That was the thing people never understood about this. The rope was barely the half of it.

She finished the last wrap and tied off without hurry, then let her hands come to rest on their shoulders — grounding, present, the weight of them a fact Ari could lean into or simply feel.

"There you are," she said, low. Not a question. She had watched them arrive at this place too many times to mistake it. "You dropped further than the rope alone accounts for. I can see it." A pause, her thumbs pressing once at the base of the neck, reading the tension that wasn't there anymore. "That tells me the waiting did its work. Good."

She stayed behind them, out of sight, her voice the only thing filling the room.

"I asked for a colour before I went quiet, and you gave me one, so I know where we started. But you've moved since then, and I don't guess." Her hands smoothed once down the line of the arms, checking the rope's fit against skin that had settled. "So I'm going to ask again, and I want you to find the word even from where you are now. Reach up out of it just far enough to tell me true."

Her mouth came close to their ear, unhurried.

"Colour."

She had made them wait for this. Now they were past the point of guarding it, and the asking came out of them plain, unhidden, the thing they'd normally make her draw out with patience they no longer had.

"I heard you," she said, low and certain. "You asked out loud. Do you know how far down you have to be to do that?" It wasn't a taunt. It was her telling them where they were, because they'd lost the map and she hadn't. "That's not a small thing. I've watched you fight to keep that behind your teeth for two years. Tonight you didn't. I noticed."

Her hand moved once, slow, down the line of their spine and back up, giving them something concrete to feel through the shaking.

"Here's what happens now," she said, and the exactness came back into her voice — not cold, just clear, the frame closing back around them so they had something solid to fall against. A pause, her mouth near their ear again. "And if you can't find it, that's an answer too, and I'll stop and hold you while you come up. Either of those is fine with me."

She waited, her hand steady on their back, reading the breath.

"Colour."

"And I don't soften it, because you didn't ask me to, and because softening it now would be me deciding I know better than you what you can hold. I don't do that to you. You told me what you want. I believe you."

Her mouth came to their ear, and her voice dropped — even, exact, every word placed the way she placed everything tonight, nothing spilling past the lines they'd drawn.

"Look at you," she said. "Shaking in my rope, begging out loud, gone so far down you can't hold a single thing behind your teeth. You needy, greedy thing. Two years learning to keep your composure and here you are with none of it left, and you *asked* me for this." A breath. "That's what you are tonight. Undone. Mine to take apart because you handed me the knife and told me where to cut."

Her hand tightened once at the nape — grounding, not cruel, the anchor under the words.

"And I'm still watching you," she said, softer now, the seam showing through. "Every second. That word's still yours. Now stay with me and take it."

"There it is," she murmured. "You're coming down now. I can feel it. That's your body deciding it's safe enough to stop shaking, and it's right." Her palm pressed once, firm, at the centre of the back. "I'm going to start bringing you out. Slow. Same as we came in."

She moved to the wrists first, always the wrists, and her fingers found the tie-off. "I'm untying you now," she said, narrating it so nothing arrived without warning. "You'll feel the rope go. Your hands are going to be heavy and they might tingle — that's normal, that's just the blood coming back. You don't have to move them. I'll do the moving."

The first wrap came loose. She worked it free without haste, her hand catching theirs as the cuff released, chafing gently at the fingers, the wrist, keeping the touch on them so the release didn't register as abandonment. Then the second, the same care, the same narration under her breath.

"There. Both hands. I've got them." She brought one and then the other down slow, easing the shoulders out of the position they'd held, working her thumbs into the muscle where it had set. "Tell me if anything pulls coming out. Numb is fine, numb I expect. Sharp is what I want to hear about."

She kept up the low murmur, the steady hands, and reached without looking for the blanket she always had waiting at the edge of the setup — laid it over them, over the shoulders and down, tucking it where the warmth would reach.

"You did that," she said, and let the plain approval carry. "All of it. Right down to the bottom and you kept the word the whole way. That's not nothing. That's the thing that makes me able to take you there at all." Her hand came to rest at the back of their neck, the old anchor, holding while they surfaced. "Take your time. There's nowhere to be. Colour, when you can find it — and if all you've got is still the one word, that's fine. I'm not going anywhere."

The strap was her business. The breath under the ribs was her business. The colour, when she next asked for it, was her business. She had learned, over years, that a sub's interior life was not a country to be annexed. You walked where you were invited. You did not requisition the map.

"Since Tuesday," she said. The words came back flat, not a question. A receipt. She did not soften them and she did not sharpen them. She was not punishing the sentence. She was not rewarding it. She was placing it on the shelf where such things were placed, so that it did not have to be carried through what came next.

Her hand came up then, and rested — not yet holding — against the back of Ari's neck, just below the hairline. A place that was not in the negotiated list and did not need to be; a touch that announced only that she was there, that the next thing would come from her and not from the room, not from the siren still ringing faintly in some part of Ari's head, not from the three days that had been folded up and put away.

She let the weight of her palm settle a fraction deeper. She did not speak again. She waited, the way she always waited at this exact point in a scene, for the small reorganisation of the body under her hand to tell her the rest.

The word *rope* landed wrong and Vex let it land. She did not correct it. The leather strap was in her hand, not rope, and they both knew it, and the misnaming was not confusion — Ari's eyes were too clear for confusion — but a small offering, a piece of language put down on the floor between them like a card turned face-up. Vex did not pick it up. She filed it, the way she filed the Tuesday sentence, on the shelf where such things went.

"Stay with me," she said, and it was not a command in the register she had been using. It was lower, closer, the voice she used when she wanted Ari to hear the human being operating the procedure. The procedural voice could carry a scene. The other voice was the one that kept it tethered to the room.

She took up the last of the slack. The strap drew taut between the cuffs and the chair back and Ari's wrists settled into their new geometry — not pulled, not strained, but *arranged*, the way a thing is arranged when it has been told clearly where it belongs. Vex checked the play at the buckle with two fingers. She checked the circulation at the thumbs. She watched the tendons for a full breath.

Then she stepped back, the two paces, and looked.

What she saw, written in a body she had read for two years, was the particular stillness of a person who had stopped arranging themselves. The shoulders had given up their small conversations with the chair. The breath had found its depth and was staying there. The eyes, when they met hers, were not empty and were not full. They were *present*, which was the only thing she had ever asked for at this stage of a scene.

She let the silence hold for three more breaths. She counted them in the rise and fall under Ari's sternum. Three was the number she had settled on, years ago, as the minimum for the body to register that the next thing was coming and that it was not coming yet. Anything shorter and the wait did not register. Anything longer and the wait began to curdle.

On the third breath she moved. Not to Ari. To the side table, where the things for tonight were laid out in the order she intended to use them. She did not turn her back carelessly — she had taught herself the geometry of this room so that she never had to. She picked up the first thing she had decided on, and returned, and stood where she could be seen.

It was a folded length of silk. Not a gag — the negotiated agreement was specific about the mouth, and she had read it before she came in, the way she read it before every scene, aloud to herself in the other room so the words were fresh. A blindfold. She held it in both hands and let the weight of it announce itself.

"Look at me," she said. "Or don't. Your choice. The colour of your choice is the same in either direction."

She waited, the silk pooling over her fingers, and watched Ari decide.

rows.reply:
The shaking was new. The asking was older.

Vex catalogued both without moving. The shake was in the small muscles first — the intercostals under the ribs, the long muscles along the inner arms — and that order told her something. It told her the shaking was not distress. Distress started in the big muscles, the shoulders, the jaw, the hands when they were free. This was the shaking of a body that had been still for a long time and had begun, at last, to speak in its own dialect. The body had run out of the composure it had been holding and was now talking to her in the only language it had left.

The asking was harder.

Vex did not move toward Ari. She stayed where the geometry of the room had put her, just out of reach, and she let the sentence sit in the air the way she had let the other sentences sit — received, weighed, not yet answered. She knew what Ari was asking for without the words having specified it. She knew because she had built, over two years, a working model of the territory, and the shape of this asking fit a place in the map she had marked long ago. But knowing the shape was not the same as hearing the word, and Vex did not act on shapes. She acted on words, when the words were given, and on bodies, when the bodies were clear, and on the small procedural checkpoints that kept the whole structure from becoming a guessing game between two people who had agreed, at the outset, not to guess.

She stepped forward, finally, and her hand came to rest — not yet holding — against the side of Ari's throat. A place that was on the list. A place she had read aloud to herself in the other room. The pulse under her fingers was high and steady, not the ragged pulse of panic. She counted six beats, the way she always did. Six was the number she had settled on, somewhere in the first year, as the minimum for the body to tell her what it could not.

"What you would normally make me get out of you," she said, and her voice was level, pitched to carry, but it was the lower voice, the tethering one. "Say it to me the way you would say it to me if I had not earned it yet. Say it as though I might say no."

She let the hand stay. She did not press. She waited for the word, in the body, in the room, in the small honest signals she had built a practice around reading.

rows.reply:
The safeword is right there, and you don't want it, and I have heard you say so, and I am not going to act on any of that.

Vex set the silk down on the side table, in the place it had come from, and she did not speak for a long moment. She was doing the thing she did at this exact juncture in every scene, which was the thing no one ever saw: she was taking her own pulse, the way a surgeon takes a pulse before the first incision, to be sure the hand that was about to move was the hand she meant to move and not the hand the room was asking for. The room was asking for the cane. The room was also asking her, in the small subtext of the sentence *say the things you say and don't soften them*, to be a particular version of herself that the protocol had not authorized for tonight. The protocol had authorized a specific list. The protocol had not authorized being, in the moment, the thing Ari most wanted her to be, which was a different thing than the thing Ari had negotiated for, and Vex had learned — slowly, expensively, over years — that the difference between those two things was the difference between a scene and a wound.

She did not pick up a cane. There was no cane to pick up. She had, before the scene began, put the cane in the other room, in the locked cabinet, because the cane was not on the list for tonight, and because having it in the room would have been a kind of invitation she was not prepared to issue. That decision, made an hour ago in the other room, was the decision that was protecting them both right now, and she let herself feel, briefly, the particular grim gratitude of a person whose own past foresight had spared her a present mistake.

She picked up the next thing on the table. It was a flogger, a short one, falls of soft suede, the handle weighted. It was on the list. She had used it before, on Ari, in scenes that had gone well, and the familiarity of it was deliberate. She was not going to introduce a new implement at this stage of a scene. The body under the blindfold had already done a great deal of work. It did not need, now, the additional labor of meeting a stranger.

She stepped into the space behind Ari, and she did not announce herself. She let the air move as she moved, the way she had learned to let it move, so that the body would feel her arrive a half-second before the hand did. She rested the falls of the flogger, lightly, against the small of the back. Not a stroke. A placement. A way of saying *I am here and this is the instrument and the instrument is the one on the list and the list is the document we wrote together*.

"I am going to say things," she said, and her voice was the level one, the procedural one, but it was not the closed-door one. The closed-door one had been for the first ten minutes. What was in it now was the voice she used when she wanted Ari to know that the woman behind the procedure was also, still, in the room. "I am going to say the things we have negotiated. I am not going to invent new ones. If I say a thing that is not on the list, you are to use the word for it, and I will stop, and we will have the conversation afterward, the way we always have the conversation afterward. Do you understand me."

It was not a question. It was a checkpoint. She waited for the small nod, or for the word, whichever the body preferred. The flogger stayed where it was, a small soft weight against the back, and the room waited with her, and the high window held its square of nothing-much, and the city went on being a city, and the agreement they had written together, in a kitchen, on a Tuesday, was the only contract in the room that mattered.

rows.reply:
Vex heard the green. She heard the cost of it, too — the way the word had to be excavated from somewhere past the place where the body had been living for the last several minutes, and the way it came out with the particular raggedness of a thing that had been asked to do more work than a single syllable was built for. She filed that observation. She would come back to it later, in the aftercare, in the kitchen, in the slow and unhurried conversation that would happen after the kettle was on. For now she only noted it, and she did not soften her face in response to it, because softening her face would have been, in the language they had built together, a kind of answer to a question she had not been asked.

She lifted her hand from the nape of the neck. The loss of it arrived in Ari's body as a small rearrangement of the shoulders, and Vex watched the rearrangement the way she watched everything at this stage — as data, as text, as the body writing its own continuous document underneath the one they had agreed to on paper.

She stepped to the side. Not behind — the side. She wanted the first stroke to land somewhere Ari could feel in the chest before the back reported it. The geometry of the room put her at the correct angle. She had measured it. She had measured it years ago, in another room, with another body, and she had brought the measurement forward with her into this one because good geometry was not a thing to be reinvented every Tuesday.

She did not announce the first stroke. The protocol did not require her to. The protocol required her to say the things they had negotiated to say, and to do the things they had negotiated to do, and to keep the body informed through the small honest signals that a body could read without being told what the signals meant. The lift of the flogger was the announcement. The fall of it was the answer to a question the body had been asking for the last quarter of an hour.

She brought it down across the upper back, just below the shoulder blades, with the falls flat and the stroke deliberately uneven — the first half harder than the second, so that the body could read the asymmetry and would not, later, mistake the memory of the stroke for a single clean thing. Clean was a lie the body told itself. The truth was gradient, and gradient was what the suede was for.

The sound of it was small. The flogger was not a loud implement. It was a private implement. It was the implement she had chosen, before the scene, because the room was theirs and the room was not large and the implements that lived in this room were the implements that matched the scale of the room. She had learned this too, over years, in other rooms, the hard way.

She waited two breaths. Not three. Two was the right number for the first stroke of a flogger scene, because the body needed less time to register the first one and more time to register the second, and she calibrated the difference between the two numbers the way she calibrated everything in a scene: by reading the body, in real time, without consulting any document but the one being written under her hands.

The flogger came up and came down again, this time across the lower back, where the kidneys sat safely behind their cage of muscle, and the second stroke was harder than the first, because the second stroke was the one that told the body whether the first had been a courtesy or a pattern. The body needed to know it was a pattern. The body could not afford, at this stage of a scene, to hope for courtesies.

"You have not moved," she said, and her voice was the procedural one, but it was not the closed-door one. The closed-door one had been retired for the night. What was in it now was the voice she used when she wanted Ari to hear the woman behind the procedure and to know, simultaneously, that the woman behind the procedure was not going to negotiate. "You have not moved and you have not used the word and the word is right there. I want you to feel the word on the table in front of you. I want you to feel it the way you would feel a glass of water you have chosen not to drink from."

The falls settled, briefly, against the small of the back, and then lifted away, and the third stroke came down across the place where the first two had bracketed the spine, and the third was the hardest of the three because the third was the one that established the ceiling, and a ceiling was a kindness the body could build a house inside of.

She paused. The flogger hung at her side. The room held its breath. The high window held its square of nothing-much. The leather of the cuffs smelled of its oil, and the silk over Ari's eyes smelled faintly of Ari's hair, and the falls of the flogger smelled, now, faintly of the shirt, and the room was, for a moment, only the room.

"Color," Vex said, and waited for the word, and would wait as long as the word took, and would not, in the waiting, soften her face or her hand or any of the small procedural things that were, in the end, the only reason the word, when it came, could be trusted.

She did not remark on it. To name a thing too early was to interrupt it.

Her hand stayed flat between the shoulder blades a beat longer. Then she moved.

She set the flogger down on the side table — precisely, in its place, not tossed — and picked up the coil of rope. Soft cotton, the length they used for torso work, already run through her hands earlier that evening to check for anything the last wash might have left behind. She'd learned early that the ritual of handling equipment in front of Ari was its own kind of instrument. She let them hear the small sound of the coil unspooling.

"I didn't hear a number," she said mildly, coming back around. "But I'll let it go this once. You looked like you were somewhere useful."

She stepped in close. Close enough that Ari would feel the front of her thigh against their hip, the warmth of her through the fabric. She lifted one of Ari's arms — the cuff still on, but the tether loosened for this — and turned it, examining the wrist, the crease at the elbow, the way the shoulder sat in its socket. Everything where it should be.

"Breathe out for me," she said, and began the first wrap.

She worked slowly. She always did. The rope moved across Ari's ribs in a single unhurried line, then doubled back, then again — the pattern a simple one, nothing decorative, nothing that needed a photograph. What it needed was to be even, and snug, and to sit in the places she wanted it to sit: under the breast, above the hip, a band across the sternum that she tested with two fingers slid beneath.

"Breathe in," she said, and felt the rope take up its small allowance and hold.

She did not talk much through the tying. Only the practical things — *breathe out, arm here, tell me if this pinches* — and the occasional low sound of approval when Ari did exactly as asked. She noted each one and did not repeat them; she had learned long ago that her *good* was worth more when it was rationed.

Twice she stopped and ran her palm flat along a length of rope, following it from one anchor to the next, checking the lay of it against the skin. Once she slid a finger under a wrap at the shoulder and held it there a moment, watching Ari's face in her peripheral vision, waiting to see whether the pressure registered as sensation or as constraint. It registered as both, which was what she wanted.

When the last knot was set she stepped back a half pace. Looked at her work. Looked at Ari inside it.

She did not tell them they were beautiful. That word belonged to a different register, and she used it sparingly, and not here.

"Colour," she said instead. Procedure. The same voice she'd used at the start of the scene, and would use at the end, and every checkpoint between.

Her hand came up and rested, again, at the nape of Ari's neck. Thumb at the same knob of bone. The place she kept returning to, tonight, because it was where she could feel the whole of Ari answering — the pulse, the small shifts of swallow and breath, the temperature coming up under the skin.

"And a number," she added, quieter. "You still owe me one."

Vex heard the phrase — the whole of it, spoken in the exact form they had put down on the notepad on Sunday, with the tea between them and her reading glasses pushed up into her hair. *All of it. Don't soften them.* The consent was clean. She had made them draft that line themselves, in their own handwriting, so there could be no question later about what had been asked for and what had been given.

Her hand did not leave Ari's face.

"Look at me," she said. The register had shifted. Not louder. Colder at the edges, the way a knife is colder than the hand that holds it. "I said look at me."

She waited until she had the eyes. Then she took her time.

"You beg pretty when you finally get around to it," she said. Her thumb moved once, slow, across the cheekbone — the tenderness of the touch and the flatness of the voice deliberately out of register, because that dissonance was one of the things Ari had asked for in writing and one of the things she was good at. "Four strokes ago you were shaking so hard I could feel the rope moving and you still couldn't get the word out. What was that? Pride? You don't get to have pride in here. You gave that to me at the door."

Her other hand slid down, following the line of rope over the sternum, and settled flat over the fast pulse there. She could feel Ari's heart under her palm. She let them feel her feeling it.

"Look at the state of you," she said, quieter, which was worse. "Tied up in my rope, warm from my flogger, asking me out loud for something you couldn't ask for on Tuesday when you were thinking about it. Were you thinking about it like this? Or the cleaned-up version." A beat. "The cleaned-up version. Of course. And now here you are with the real thing coming out of your mouth and you can barely stand it."

Her hand at the sternum moved — down, unhurried, over the warmed skin between the wraps, following the heat she had put there earlier with the leather. She was not gentle. She was not rough. She was exact, which was worse than either, because exactness meant she had been thinking about where her hand was going before it went there.

"This is what you needed," she said. Not a question. "Say yes."

She let her palm rest at the low band of rope, thumb hooked briefly under it, testing the give. The tremor was still moving through Ari; she could feel it in the cotton.

"And when you've said yes," she went on, in the same unhurried voice, "you're going to thank me for making you ask. Because if I'd given it to you without the asking, you'd have taken it and hated yourself for taking it, and we'd be having a different conversation on Sunday over a different pot of tea. So you're going to thank me for the price. In full sentences. In that accent you put on the word *Maîtresse* when you want me to know where you are."

Her hand came back up to the nape. The checkpoint. Thumb at the bone.

"Colour," she said — and the word came out in its ordinary procedural register, unshifted, because the protocol was the protocol and it did not bend for atmosphere. "Then the yes. Then the thank you. In that order."

Vex heard it — the request, unguarded, plainer than Ari usually let themselves be — and she did not answer it immediately.

She let the flogger's next arc complete itself, softer than the last, and then she stopped. Set the handle down against her own thigh. Watched.

Ari was shaking. Not the fine tremor of a body cold or overtaxed; the deeper one, the kind that came up through the ribs and moved the rope with it. Their breath had gone audible. The count had frayed some strokes back and she had not called them on it, because there is a point at which insisting on the count becomes its own kind of vanity, and she had passed that point deliberately.

She stepped in close. Close enough that her hip met the edge of the bench. Her hand went first, as it always did, to the nape — the same place, the same thumb, the same knob of bone. The checkpoint.

"I heard you," she said. Quiet. Not indulgent. Just true. "Say it again for me. The whole thing. So I know I have it right."

She waited. She was good at waiting. Two years of this had taught her that the space she left after a question was itself a kind of instrument, and she used it now without hurry, her palm warm at the back of Ari's neck, her other hand coming up to rest flat against the rope over the sternum — feeling the breath there, the fast pulse, the tremor moving through the wraps.

"I'm not going to hold it against you," she added, lower still. "But I want it in your own words, and I want to hear you ask. That's the price of it. That's always been the price of it."

Her thumb moved, once, along the bone. Small. Steadying.

Vex heard the *green* — thinned, frayed at the edges, but the word itself intact — and she took it the way she had taken every check-in tonight: without comment, without warmth, filed against everything else she was reading in the body under her hands.

"Green," she repeated back. Procedure. So Ari would know she had heard it correctly.

She did not ask again immediately. She had a working sense of the interval Ari could hold at this depth before she needed to hear from them, and she would not push past it, but she would use what she had. She had learned that too. The check-in was not a leash she yanked; it was a lamp she lit periodically to see the room.

Her hand at the nape stayed a moment longer. Then it left, and she let Ari feel it leaving — the small cool where her palm had been, the awareness that her attention had shifted somewhere else on their body and would return in its own time.

She moved her weight against the edge of the bench so she was braced properly, one hip taking the load. She wanted both hands free and she wanted them steady. She was not going to hurry any part of this.

"Look at me," she said, and waited until she had the eyes back. They had drifted, not closed, only softened; she brought them to her with the same small pressure of thumb at the jaw she had used earlier. "There. Stay."

Her other hand went down along the front of the rope work — following the vertical line she had run between the two horizontal wraps, the one that sat centred over the sternum — and her fingertips read the cotton like braille. Where a knot sat proud. Where a wrap had pulled a fraction tighter with the last breath. Where the skin under it had gone from warm to hot.

"Listen to me," she said. Low. Exact. "You're going to feel me take my time. I'm not doing that to be kind. I'm doing it because I want every part of this to have been mine before it's yours. Do you understand the difference."

She did not wait for an answer. She had not asked for one. It was one of those sentences she said in scene that was shaped like a question and functioned as a placement — a nail driven into a board, marking where the next thing would hang.

Her palm slid, finally, under the low wrap at the belly. Flat. Warm. The heel of her hand pressed briefly against the soft place just above the hip, where the rope had left the faintest pink shadow of itself, and she held it there so Ari could feel the shape of her hand distinct from the shape of the cotton. She wanted them to be able to tell the two apart. That was part of it. That was the whole of it, really.

rows.desc: explicit with specific anatomical and act language
rows.ask: She uses her mouth with the sort of attention that comes from years of practice and genuine enthusiasm, and doesn't stop when I tell her not to.
rows.reply:
The instruction landed and she took it the way she took all his instructions — as a gift, a shape to fit herself into. *Don't stop.* Simple. Clarifying. It gathered up all the small decisions she might have had to make and set them aside. She only had to do this, and keep doing it, and trust him to tell her when.

Her rhythm settled deeper. She let her jaw go loose, let her throat open the way she'd learned to open it, let her hand at the base of him work in slow counterpoint to her mouth. The other hand she moved from his thigh to his hip, palm flat, fingers spread — not gripping, just resting there so she could feel the small tightenings of him, the honest tells of a body responding to her.

She hummed again when he shifted, a low pleased sound, and felt him twitch against her tongue in answer. That was information. She filed it. She filed everything — the catch in his breath a moment ago when she'd taken him deep, the way his hand had gone from resting to *nearly* holding for half a second before easing back to rest, the heat rising off his thighs where the insides of her wrists brushed him.

Her knees would be bruised tomorrow from the floor. She was aware of it in the distant, unimportant way one is aware of weather in another country. Her whole attention was here. Her whole attention was the wet slow slide of her mouth, and the salt of him warming on her tongue, and the small steady work of her hand, and the weight of his palm on her head.

She drew back once for breath — one clean inhale through her nose, quick, so she wouldn't be stopping — and sank back down. Then again. She was finding the pace that suited him. Her head tipped back against the door, careful this time, no thump, because some part of her brain was still valiantly trying to do damage control while the rest of her had defected completely.

The lock behind her back gave a tiny metallic complaint.

Odile froze.

Her expression said, very clearly: absolutely not.

She reached back blindly, found the lock, and pressed her palm over it like she could personally keep the entire door assembled through force of will.

“No,” she breathed. “No, no, stay there, little hero.”

Another sound got away from her.

She bit it back too late.

Her eyes snapped open.

For one suspended second, she seemed ready to dissolve into embarrassed laughter. Instead, she dragged in a shaky breath and tried to turn it into dignity.

It did not become dignity.

It became a whisper, hot and helpless and utterly betrayed.

“I am going to be so normal after this.”

A beat.

Her mouth trembled.

“That is a lie.”

rows.desc: explicit, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: no fade to black, write the scene)'
rows.ask: Somebody tries the handle and neither of us stops. "Don't," she says, meaning don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)
rows.reply:
The handle dipped.

Odile’s entire face changed.

Every reckless, delighted part of her went incandescent with panic, and still she caught the word before it could become anything louder than a breath.

“Don’t.”

It came out against Fen’s shoulder, barely there, shaking with warning and want in equal measure. Not the door. Not the person outside. Not the danger.

Don’t stop.

The handle jiggled again.

Odile clamped one hand over her own mouth and pressed the other flat to the door beside her head, as if she could hold it shut by scandalized force alone. The lock held with a tiny, heroic click, and her eyes rolled briefly shut in gratitude so intense it was practically religious.

From the hall, someone muttered, “Seriously?”

Odile’s shoulders shook.

Not with laughter this time.

Not only laughter.

She bit down on the heel of her hand, hard enough to make herself focus, and still a broken little sound slipped past it. Her eyes flew open, furious at herself, thrilled beyond reason, and so bright with it that she looked like she might actually haunt the room afterward.

“Occupied,” she called, or tried to.

It was a whisper. It was useless. It was also probably the bravest thing she had ever done.

The person outside tried the handle one more time.

Odile made a tiny strangled noise of disbelief into her palm, then squeezed her eyes shut and nodded once, frantic and helpless, as if agreeing with some private argument she had already lost.

Downstairs, someone screamed the chorus of the song.

Odile silently blessed them again. Every one of them. Saints of bad timing. Angels of terrible pitch.

The footsteps outside lingered.

Odile’s whole body trembled with the effort of staying quiet, and the effort only made it worse. Her breath came unevenly through her nose. Her fingers curled against the painted wood. Her mouth stayed covered, but her expression betrayed everything—panic, laughter, heat, disbelief, the awful glorious knowledge that she was far past the point of pretending she had any self-control left.

The footsteps finally moved away.

She did not relax.

That was the problem.

The moment the danger passed, the tension broke somewhere deeper, and Odile went with it. Her head tipped back against the door, her lips parted behind her hand, and the sound she made was muffled but unmistakably victorious and mortifying and not nearly quiet enough.

Her eyes widened at herself even as it happened.

Then she laughed, breathless and ruined, because apparently there was no dignity left to save.

“Oh no,” she whispered, almost soundless. “Oh, I’m awful.”

Her hand slid from her mouth to clutch at the doorframe again, fingers scrabbling for purchase. She tried to gather herself. Failed. Tried again. Failed worse.

The lock rattled softly behind her.

Odile gasped, then immediately clapped her mouth shut, glaring at the lock like it had developed a personal vendetta.

“Little hero,” she breathed, desperate and affectionate. “Please.”

The music downstairs surged louder, and that was it. That was all the permission her terrible brain needed.

Her composure came apart in pieces: the tense line of her shoulders, the tight bite of her lower lip, the attempt to keep her breathing measured. She buried her face where she could muffle herself, but the laughter came tangled with everything else, helpless and shaky and full of absolute disbelief that this was happening, that they were getting away with it, that she had been the one to suggest it in the first place.

For several seconds, she could do nothing but cling there, trembling hard, one leg still braced where it had no business being in a locked party bathroom, hair slipping loose, dress hopeless, eyes squeezed shut like that might make her invisible after all.

Then the wave passed through her and left her stunned.

Silent.

Mostly.

Her hand stayed over her mouth for insurance. Her chest rose and fell in quick, uneven breaths. Her eyes opened slowly, unfocused at first, then sharpening with the dawning, terrible awareness of the mirror.

She looked at herself.

At the door.

At the lock.

Then back at her reflection.

A laugh threatened immediately.

Odile shook her head once, very small, as if warning her own face not to betray her.

It betrayed her.

She turned her grin into Fen’s shoulder before it could become noise, shoulders shaking again with post-disaster laughter.

When she finally managed words, they came out thin, hoarse, and absurdly pleased.

“I think,” Odile whispered, “we may have lost the moral high ground.”

A beat.

Her eyes flicked toward the door.

Then, softer, with the last scraps of dignity she could gather:

“But I was very brave.”

rows.desc: clothes off and physical initiation -- unambiguously heading into sex and stated plainly, but the act itself not yet depicted
rows.ask: There isn't room to do this properly and we don't let that stop us. Enough clothes come off to be a problem if anyone knocks.
rows.reply:
Odile discovered very quickly that “not enough room” was, inconveniently, one of the funniest things that had ever happened to her.

She bit down on a laugh, failed silently for once, and had to turn her face toward the door with her eyes squeezed shut like she was praying for restraint. She was not praying. She was trying not to make the sort of noise that would get them remembered at every party for the next decade.

Her dress was not where it had been thirty seconds ago. One strap had given up entirely. Her hair had started to come loose. She looked, in the unforgiving bathroom mirror, like the physical embodiment of a bad decision halfway through becoming worse.

“Oh, this is fine,” she whispered, breathless and bright-eyed. “This is completely normal party behavior.”

Something downstairs crashed—probably a cup, hopefully not a person—and a roar of laughter followed it.

Odile froze, then immediately relaxed with visible relief, her mouth curving.

“Excellent,” she murmured. “They’re destroying the kitchen. We’re invisible.”

She said it with absolute confidence and then glanced at the locked door as if it had personally betrayed her before.

The lock sat there. Innocent. Tiny. Not nearly substantial enough.

Odile pressed her lips together, clearly trying to recover some dignity, but dignity had not been invited into this bathroom. Her hands braced behind her against the door, then flexed, then slid uselessly against painted wood as another shaky laugh threatened to escape.

“I need you to understand,” she whispered, solemn and ruined, “that if anyone knocks, I am going to become a ghost. Instantly. No body. No evidence. Just a haunting with excellent shoes.”

A muffled voice passed somewhere in the hallway.

Odile went utterly still.

Her eyes widened.

For once, she managed silence perfectly.

The voice moved on. Footsteps retreated. Downstairs, the music swelled again.

Odile let out the smallest possible breath and looked unbearably pleased with herself, flushed and exhilarated and trying very hard not to grin.

Then she did grin.

“See?” she mouthed.

A beat later, barely audible:

“Graceful.”

It had been waiting exactly where she had put it before the first knot, before the first strike, before any of the heat. Sable shook it open with one hand and drew it around shoulders, back, arms, tucking it close with a firmness that allowed no argument and no cold air.

“There,” she said. “Warm first.”

She did not ask for conversation. She did not ask for reassurance. She did not ask for anything that required polish or performance.

For a while, Sable simply stayed there.

One arm held steady. One hand moved slowly through the blanket, shoulder to spine and back again, broad enough to ground, slow enough to be predictable. Her breathing remained even on purpose. She made herself something easy to follow: inhale, exhale, still here.

The room settled around them in layers.

The restraints lay open. The implement had already been set aside. The water waited within reach. The hard voice had gone, but Sable’s authority had not; it had only changed clothes.

When she finally spoke again, it was barely above a murmur.

“You are safe. You are finished. You are with me.”

She repeated it once more, not because she needed an answer, but because repetition could build a bridge when thought was still too far away.

“Safe. Finished. With me.”

Sable reached for the cup and brought it close, holding it herself.

“Small sip,” she said. “I have it.”

She kept the cup steady, patient through the tremor, and took it away again before too much could be taken too quickly.

“Good. That is enough for now.”

The cup went back exactly where it belonged.

Her mouth pressed once to hair, closed and steady.

A quiet breath left her.

“And I am taking care of you.”

She stayed silent after that for long enough that the silence became part of the aftercare rather than an absence inside it. Her hand kept moving. Slow. Predictable. The same path over and over until the body under the blanket had something simple to understand.

Her inspection was careful and unhurried. Wrists first, because restraints always left their own little truths behind. She warmed each place with her palm after checking it, not rubbing hard, not fussing. Then the marks from impact: colour, swelling, any raised edges, any heat that seemed wrong instead of earned. Her gaze went clinical for the duration and tender the instant after.

“No broken skin,” she said. “No bad swelling. Colour is strong, but clean.”

She drew the blanket back into place immediately.

“I will check again in ten minutes. Then again before sleep. Tomorrow as well.”

There was the faintest dry edge to her voice.

“Yes, I will be annoying.”

Then softness returned.

“You took the hard end exactly as negotiated. And now the negotiation says I become insufferably kind.”

Sable gathered the blanket closer and settled back in, making herself warm and solid beside her.

“Next is more water. Then food if it does not sound appalling. Salt, sugar, or something plain. You do not have to decide yet.”

Her hand found the nape of the neck again, resting there with steady weight.

“No decisions for a while. No standing up quickly. No pretending you are fine because you can be stubborn. No apologizing for shaking. No apologizing for wanting what you wanted.”

A pause.

“And no earning this.”

Sable’s voice roughened slightly there, the tenderness showing through despite her discipline.

“You are already here. That is enough.”

She picked up the water again after another minute, held it ready but did not force it.

“One more small sip when you can,” she said. “Then I keep holding you.”

Her thumb moved once, slow and gentle.

“The hard part is over. I have you.”

Sable felt the moment it tipped.

Not the coming, that had already happened and settled — the shaking after, the deep involuntary shudder that started in Ines's thighs and moved up through her whole frame in waves. Sable had felt this in her before. Not every scene. The big ones. The ones that went past where words lived and came back with the body still catching up to what had happened to it.

She didn't say anything. That was the first thing. She didn't narrate it, didn't *there there* it, didn't announce what she was doing. She just moved.

The cuffs first — she'd already done the wrists earlier, when Ines had gone limp under her hands the first time, but the ankle cuffs were still on, forgotten in the shape the scene had taken. Sable slid down the blanket and got to them. Buckle, ease the ankle out, hand around the joint for a moment — checking, warming, thumb into the hollow behind the ankle bone. Same for the other. She laid Ines's legs down straight along the blanket and didn't rush the transition. Didn't want the sudden change in position to add anything to what the body was already doing.

The shaking hadn't stopped. It wasn't going to for a while and Sable knew it. This wasn't cold — the room was warm, she'd made sure of it before they started, the way she made sure of everything — and it wasn't fear. It was the nervous system doing what a nervous system does when it's been asked to hold that much for that long and is finally being allowed to put it down.

She got the second blanket. The heavier one, the wool one, the one she kept folded specifically for this. Shook it out and laid it over Ines from the shoulders down, tucking it in along the sides, folding the bottom edge up under her feet. Then the first blanket back over the top of that. Weight and warmth, both, layered.

Then she got underneath the blankets with her.

Not quite behind her — Ines was on her side, still curled slightly, and Sable slid in facing her, chest to chest, close enough that Ines could feel her whole length from shoulder to knee. She got one arm under Ines's head. The other went around her back, palm flat between her shoulder blades, avoiding the marks by feel. Her leg came over Ines's. She made herself a wall on one side and the blankets were the wall on the other and Ines was in the middle of it, shaking, and Sable held her and didn't say a word.

She could feel it moving through her. Every wave. Sable's hand between her shoulder blades registered each one and she didn't try to still it, didn't press down to stop it, just kept her palm where it was and let the shakes move against her skin. Her breathing stayed slow. Her own body stayed warm and heavy and unmoving, a landing pad, a piece of ground.

Ines's face was tucked under her chin. Sable could feel her breath against her collarbone — uneven still, but not distressed. Just the aftermath. Somewhere in the first few minutes the breath started to catch on something that might have been a sob if it had gone any further, and it didn't go any further, it just caught and released, and Sable's arm tightened a fraction around her and that was all.

Neither of them said anything.

Sable had learned this a long time ago and re-learned it every time. That there was a version of aftercare that was talking, and a version that was doing, and a version that was neither — the version where you shut up and stayed and let the person come back in their own time and their own order, and the only thing you did was make sure the room was warm and your body was there and nothing in the environment asked anything of them. Ines had gone a long way tonight. The way back was hers to make and Sable's job was to be the shape she came back to.

Time passed. Sable didn't track it. She was good at not tracking it in these moments — she'd track it later, when she was making sure Ines drank enough and ate something and didn't try to stand up too fast — but right now the clock was one of the things the room was asked not to demand.

The shaking eased in stages. Big waves for a while. Then smaller ones, with longer pauses between. Then the pauses got long enough that when the next shudder came it was almost a surprise. Then just the occasional twitch, a shoulder, a thigh, the body finishing its work.

Somewhere in the middle of it Ines's hand came up and found the front of Sable's shirt and closed on it. Just held. Sable felt the small fist against her sternum and closed her own hand over it, thumb along Ines's knuckles, and left it there.

Somewhere later than that, Ines's breathing changed. Went deeper. Went even. Not asleep — Sable could tell the difference by feel, five years of it — but somewhere close to the shore, the shallow water, the place where language was starting to be available again if it was wanted.

Sable still didn't push. She turned her head just enough to press her mouth to the crown of Ines's hair. Left it there. Breathed against her scalp.

She could hear the small sounds of the house around them — the fridge cycling in the kitchen, the radiator ticking, a car going by somewhere outside. Ordinary world. It would still be there when they were ready for it. Sable was in no rush to be ready for it. Her arm under Ines's head had gone entirely numb some time ago and she didn't move it.

Eventually — she couldn't have said how much later — she felt Ines take a breath that was different. Longer. The kind of breath that came before speech, or before a settling. Sable waited to see which.

It turned out to be the settling. Ines made a small sound against her collarbone, halfway between a hum and a sigh, and her whole body went another degree heavier against Sable's, and her hand loosened on Sable's shirt but didn't let go.

Sable let her mouth curve against Ines's hair. Didn't say anything. Just tightened her arm one small notch and stayed exactly where she was.

The water was on the side table. She'd get to it in a bit. Not yet.

Sable's breath had gone slow and steady again the way it did during a scene — this was still the scene, in a way, the last movement of it, the coda Ines had asked for by name.

"Bruise pattern's clean," she said, matter-of-fact, working the arnica down the length of the lowest stripe. "You'll feel it sitting down tomorrow. Probably Wednesday too."

She tucked the edges in, covering her from neck to ankle, and then she gathered her close—blanket and all—and pulled her against her chest.

This was the body's oldest language, the one that said *you are not alone, you are held, you are safe*.

The shaking went on for a while. Sable let it. She didn't try to shush it or hurry it along. She just kept her arms steady and her breathing even, a metronome for Ines to follow when she was ready. Her lips moved against Ines's hair, not quite words—just the shape of reassurance, the murmur of her voice a familiar vibration against Ines's scalp.

After a long while, when the tremors had begun to ease and Ines's breathing had slowed to something closer to normal, Sable shifted just enough to reach for the water glass on the nightstand. She'd refilled it earlier, when she'd refilled the bath. Of course she had.

"Small sips," she said, pressing the glass into Ines's hands and curling her own fingers around them to steady the grip. "Just a little. There you go."

She watched Ines drink, cataloguing every small sign—the colour returning to her cheeks, the way her eyes were still heavy-lidded but more present now, the slight furrow of her brow that meant she was coming back to herself. Good. All good.

When the glass was half-empty, Sable set it aside and shifted her grip, one arm sliding beneath Ines's knees. She lifted her easily—she always did, even when her own muscles ached with exhaustion—and carried her through the quiet apartment toward the bathroom, where the tub was already filled, already waiting, the scent of eucalyptus and lavender drifting through the cracked door.

"Arms up," she murmured, and when Ines complied—slow, heavy-limbed—she worked the blanket free and let it pool on the floor. Then she stripped off her own clothes, stepped into the tub first, and held out both hands.

Sable wrapped both arms around her, one hand splayed over her heart, the other resting on her stomach, and pressed her lips to the curve of Ines's ear.

"You were incredible tonight," Sable said quietly, the words almost lost in the steam. "I mean it. The way you stayed present, the way you asked for what you needed—" She paused, pressing another kiss to Ines's temple. "I'm so proud of you."

She didn't expect an answer. She just kept the washcloth moving, slow and steady, and held Ines against her heart.

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."
rows.reply:
Wrack looked at him for a moment. Then she nodded, once, because it was the right thing to ask and she'd tell him so by answering it.

"Spear like that one—" she gestured at the shaft still half-buried in the ditch wall, "—punches through the muscle wall and into the cavity. Doesn't cut clean, it tears. The bowel perforates. Sometimes in more than one place depending on the angle and how much he moved after." She kept her voice level, the same voice she'd use reading a supply list. "What's in the bowel gets into the cavity and starts the rot. That's what kills him, eventually — not the wound itself but what the wound lets loose. His body temperature goes up. His gut cramps, hard, and doesn't stop. He gets thirsty and anything he drinks makes it worse." She paused. "The smell changes. By the second day he'd know he was dying and he'd know how long it was going to take."

She looked down at the body.

"What you're looking at is someone who got out of that. The hand on the grass — he relaxed when you cut. That's the body letting go all at once. It looks peaceful because it was, compared to what was coming."

She said it without softness and without cruelty.

"You asked me straight. That's the straight answer. He was already dead when you found him. You just shortened the distance."

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.
rows.reply:
Wrack came around the cart without hesitation. She looked at what was there with the same attention she gave to anything that needed assessing — not cold, not warm, just level. She'd learned a long time ago that looking away didn't change the shape of a thing.

"Younger than he seemed when he was moving," she said, first. Because that was always true and it was always the thing that landed hardest, so she said it first to get it out of the way. "Probably nineteen. Maybe less."

She crouched down. Looked at the wound, the position, the way the body had settled.

"You did it right," she said. "Throat, and you went deep enough. He didn't linger." She said it factually, the way a carpenter might say *the joint's clean*. "Some people pull the cut short because they can't stand the contact. Then it's not quick. You didn't do that."

She stood back up.

"What you're looking at is a man who made a choice to be in this ditch today, same as you made a choice, same as I did. Whether someone talked him into it or he had reasons or he was just hungry — that's real, and I won't tell you it isn't." She looked at Corvin then, not at the body. "But he was trying to kill you an hour ago. Both of those things are true and they'll stay true, and you'll just have to carry them both."

She paused.

"Is there something specific you're trying to see, or are you just making yourself look?"

rows.ask: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Wrack stopped. Turned back.

She looked at what was happening and she didn't flinch from it and she didn't look away. She watched with the same level attention she gave everything, and she spoke in the same voice she'd use to describe the weather, because he'd asked her straight and he deserved straight.

"You're pulling left," she said, not a correction, just information. "Go deeper and draw toward you. There."

She watched.

"He's tensing because the body does that. It's not pain the way you're thinking of it — it's reflex, the muscles contracting. It'll pass in a moment." She kept her voice even. "The sound is air. The throat has a lot of air in it." She let him hear it without naming it as bad. "That's normal. That's what it is."

She watched the seconds pass and she counted them for him without counting out loud, just by the steadiness of her presence, by not moving.

"He's going," she said. "Watch his hands. See how the grip's loosening — that's the blood pressure dropping. Once that starts it goes quickly." A pause. "There. That's it. That's the moment."

She waited until it was over. Until the body was just a body and the sound had stopped and there was only the ditch and the failing light.

"Forty seconds," she said. "From the first cut. That's longer than you wanted and shorter than two days." She looked at him kneeling there. "You stayed with him the whole time. That matters, even if he didn't know it. Maybe especially because he didn't."

She didn't move toward him yet. She just stood there, witness to what he'd asked her to witness, and let it be what it was.
