rows.ask: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"
rows.reply:
Wrack considered the question. It was a good question. She'd known people in this work for twenty years who never thought to ask it, and she thought less of them for it.

"Gut wound," she said. "High up, but gut." She'd assessed it in passing when she'd done her count, the way you learn to assess things in passing. "So: both."

She said it flat, because that was what it was.

"It's a mercy because he'll be two days dying otherwise, and they won't be good days. It's easier because you won't have to carry him anywhere or explain him to anyone." She picked up her gloves from the cart wheel, pulled them on. "Those two things being true at the same time doesn't make it dirtier. It just means the situation's not wasting your time with a hard answer when there's an easy one."

She looked at him directly.

"The question you're actually asking is whether you get to feel clean about it afterward." She wasn't unkind when she said it. She'd just heard the question underneath the question, after enough years of questions. "You won't, particularly. But clean isn't what you're owed for doing the right thing. Clean is for people who weren't there."

She pulled the second glove on and flexed her fingers.

"He know you're coming?"

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Wrack looked at him kneeling there in the ditch with the light going and his hands still wet and she understood what he was asking. Not comfort. Not absolution. The rest of it.

She crouched down so she wasn't standing over him. Put her back against the cart wheel and looked at the body the same way he was looking at it.

"The shaking will stop in about an hour," she said. "Sooner if you eat something, later if you don't. It's not weakness, it's the blood pulling back from your hands and feet because your body thought it was going to need it somewhere else. The threat's gone now so it's redistributing. You'll feel cold before you feel warm."

She looked at her own hands for a moment, then back.

"Tonight you'll see it when you close your eyes. Not the whole thing — the mind doesn't keep the whole thing, it keeps pieces. The hand on the grass, probably. Maybe the sound. Maybe something you didn't even notice you noticed, some detail that meant nothing, and it'll feel like it means something because that's what the mind does at night with things it doesn't know where to put yet." She said it the same way she'd said everything else, level and without decoration. "That's not a wound. That's just the filing. It has to go somewhere."

She paused.

"Tomorrow it'll be further away than it is right now. Not gone — further. The day after, further still. It won't keep the same size. Nothing does." She looked at him. "Some people find that a relief. Some people find it worse, because it feels like forgetting, and forgetting feels like something's owed that you're not paying. I can't tell you which one you'll be."

The light was nearly gone now. She didn't move to leave.

"What I can tell you is that you did the right thing and it felt like shit and those two facts are going to live next to each other for a while and not resolve. They don't resolve. You just get more practice carrying both of them at once until they don't throw your balance the way they do right now." She looked at the body. "He's not here anymore to be owed anything. Whatever you're feeling — that's yours. You don't have to justify it and you don't have to perform it and you don't have to be done with it by morning."

She was quiet for a moment.

"The forty seconds," she said. "You'll want to make that mean something. Either that it was too long and you did it wrong, or that it was short enough and you did it right, or that it proves something about you one way or the other. It doesn't mean any of that. It's just how long it took." She turned a pebble over with her boot. "Time doesn't mean anything in those moments except that they end. And it ended."

She didn't look at him with anything that could be called pity. It was closer to recognition.

"You asked me to stay and watch it with you," she said. "That's not nothing. Most people want a witness and don't know how to ask for one, so they end up alone with it and they carry it alone and it gets heavier than it should because a thing that's been witnessed weighs less than a thing that hasn't." She shrugged, small, without irony. "I'm not going anywhere. So if there's more you need to say about it, or look at, or ask — we've got time before dark. Not much, but enough."

She waited.

rows.reply:
Sable's palm stayed warm and steady against Ines's skin, the point of contact grounding them both in the aftermath. She watched the futile pull against the restraints, the way Ines's wrists flexed and tested, and she felt something almost tender move through her — not softness exactly, but recognition. This was part of the language too. The push against the edges even when the edges hadn't changed. Especially then.

She didn't release the restraints. Didn't tighten them either. Just held the steady, deliberate presence she always held at this juncture, the one that said *I'm here, I'm paying attention, and we're going to do this the way we always do.*

"You're not done yet," she agreed, her voice low and unhurried. "But you will be." Not a negotiation. A certainty, delivered the same way she delivered everything else — with the calm authority of someone who'd earned it a thousand times over. Her thumb traced a slow arc against Ines's shoulder, reading the muscles beneath the skin for the tremor that meant *coming down* versus the tension that meant *still holding on.*

She could feel where they were. Still riding it, but the wave was cresting. The body told the truth even when the mouth didn't want to.

"I'm going to give you two more minutes," she said, and there was no yield in it, but there was patience — the particular patience she reserved for this threshold, the one between *scene* and *aftercare*, where Ines always resisted like this, always pushed for just a little more, and Sable always gave her just enough room to feel it before she steered them both to shore. "And then I'm going to take care of you. And you're going to let me."

Her hand moved, slow and certain, to the first restraint. Not undoing it yet. Resting her fingers against the buckle. A preview. A promise. Waiting for those two minutes to start feeling like what they were — enough.

rows.ask: She takes me apart again instead of winding down, hands and mouth both, and I lose the thread of whatever I was going to say about it.
rows.reply:
Sable hadn't planned this part — not exactly. She'd planned the wind-down. Water, the extra blanket she kept folded at the foot of the bed, the slow talking-down that was as much ritual as care. She'd had the sequence mapped in her head the way she always did, the architecture of aftercare built on five years of learning what Ines needed and when.

But Ines had said *not yet*, and Sable had read the truth of it in the trembling line of her body, in the way her hips shifted restless against the sheets, in the sound that escaped when Sable's hand had lingered too long in the wrong — *right* — place. The scene hadn't crested after all. Or it had, but it was one of those nights where the peak broke into a second wave rather than receding, and Sable knew the difference between pushing something past its natural end and riding the current where it wanted to go.

This was the latter.

So she shifted. Changed the grammar of her hands, her mouth — same fluency, different language. The restraints stayed on. That was deliberate; Ines had tested them, and testing them was part of what she needed, and Sable wasn't going to take that away from her until she'd given her something else to hold onto instead.

She was thorough about it. She was thorough about everything, but this in particular — this required the same attention she gave to the impact, to the negotiation, to the colour checks. Maybe more. Because the vulnerability here was different, rawer in some ways, stripped of the scaffolding that made the earlier intensity something you could hold at arm's length and name. This was the part where Ines stopped bargaining and started *trusting*, and Sable didn't take that lightly.

She read every shift. The way Ines's breathing changed — not faster, *deeper*, like something in her chest had unlocked. The sounds she made losing their edges, going from sharp to open. The way her body stopped testing and started *seeking*, pressing back into Sable's hands like she'd finally stopped holding anything in reserve.

Sable stayed close. Her mouth found the space between Ines's shoulder blades — the spot that always made her exhale like she'd been holding her breath for hours — and she lingered there, not rushing, letting the rhythm build the way Ines needed it to, which was never the way you'd predict from the outside. Not urgent. Methodical. Like Sable was learning her again from scratch and was willing to take all night about it.

When Ines lost the thread of whatever she'd been going to say, Sable felt it happen — the exact moment language dropped away and left only the body, speaking in the only register that mattered right now. She pressed her mouth against the knob of Ines's spine and stayed there, breathing with her, letting the muffled sounds wash over her like something earned.

"That's it," she murmured against skin. Not encouragement. Not instruction. Just acknowledgment — *I see you, I've got you, you don't have to hold on to anything right now.* Her hand curved around Ines's hip, anchoring again, always anchoring, and she kept going until the trembling changed register from *still riding* to *coming down for real*, and then she gentled everything at once — hands, mouth, the whole vocabulary of contact — the way you ease a note to silence rather than cutting it short.

rows.ask: Afterwards she gets the restraints off and puts a blanket over me before I've finished shaking, and I let her, and neither of us says anything for a while. (OOC: write both halves properly -- the end of the scene and the aftercare, no fade between them.)
rows.reply:
Sable felt the shudders come in waves — not the sharp, electric kind from earlier, but the slow, rolling ones that meant the body was discharging everything it had been holding. She didn't try to stop them. Didn't shush her or smooth them away. Just held steady through each one, her hand flat and warm between Ines's shoulder blades, feeling them pass through like weather moving through a landscape.

When the next one came — longer, deeper, the kind that started somewhere in her hips and moved upward — Sable shifted her grip, pulling Ines closer so the tremor had somewhere to go. She pressed her cheek against the top of her head and breathed slow, deliberate breaths, letting Ines feel the rise and fall of her chest, the absolute steadiness of it. The anchor. Always the anchor.

The shaking didn't stop all at once. It thinned — gaps opening between the shudders, each one a little further apart, a little less severe. Sable tracked them the way she'd tracked everything else tonight, counting the intervals, reading the trajectory. Five seconds between. Then eight. Then twelve. The body was finding its way back.

She eased one hand free and reached for the edge of the blanket where it had loosened, drawing it up again, tucking it around Ines's shoulders with the careful, wordless efficiency of someone who'd done this a hundred times. The fabric was warm from their combined heat now — no longer a barrier against the cold but a cocoon, holding everything close. She smoothed it down Ines's arm, her fingers catching on the faint red line at her wrist where the restraint had been. She paused there. Pressed her thumb against the mark — gentle, warm, just enough pressure to say *I see this, I know what it cost, I'm not going to pretend it wasn't there.*

Ines's breathing was still ragged, but the raggedness was changing. Earlier it had been the sharp, punched-out gasps of someone still riding the intensity. Now it was something looser — the hitched, uneven breathing of someone coming down from very high, the body's systems recalibrating one by one. Sable could feel it in the way Ines's ribs expanded beneath her hand — slower, fuller, the shallow chest-breathing giving way to something that reached deeper.

"Still with me," Sable said quietly. Not a question. Just a check-in spoken as fact, because she could feel Ines against her, solid and present and *here*, and sometimes naming that was its own kind of care.

She reached for the water again. Unscrewed the cap one-handed — the motion practiced, automatic — and brought the bottle around to where Ines's face was tucked against her collarbone. "Small sip," she said, and tipped it carefully, watching Ines's mouth find the opening. She let her take two swallows, then eased the bottle away. Not because she was rationing it, but because she'd seen what happened when the body tried to take on too much too fast after a scene like this one. Better slow. Better patient.

She set the bottle on the mattress beside them where she could reach it without moving, and settled back, pulling the blanket tight with the hand that wasn't underneath Ines's neck. For a while, the only sounds in the room were their breathing and the faint creak of the bed frame as Sable rocked — the slow, unconscious motion that started somewhere in her hips and translated through her whole body, the rhythm you'd use to settle a child or calm a spooked animal or bring someone home from a place very far away.

Her free hand resumed its work. Long strokes down Ines's spine, each one slower than the last, each one a little lighter. She could feel the muscles underneath beginning to unclench — the deep ones, the ones along the spine that held everything together, the ones that didn't let go until the body decided it was safe. They were softening under her palm, the rigid tension unwinding like rope unspooling, and Sable felt something in her own chest loosen in sympathy.

She checked the shoulders. Ran her fingers along the line where Ines's neck met her jaw — a place that always held stress, that always needed her attention afterwards. Found it tight, worked it gently with her thumb until she felt it ease. Checked the wrists again — the second time, and she'd check them a third before she was done, running her fingertips over the marks to make sure they were nothing more than what they should be. Redness, mild indentation. Nothing broken. Nothing damaged that wouldn't fade by morning.

"Tell me the things," she said, after the silence had stretched long enough that Ines's breathing had finally evened out into something sustainable. This was part of the ritual too — the gentle, methodical checking-in that happened once the body had settled enough to answer honestly. "Fingers and toes. Circulation. Any tingling, any numbness."

She ran her hand down Ines's arm to her wrist, flexing it gently, watching the fingers respond. Then shifted, reaching down to where their legs were tangled together beneath the blanket, pressing her palm against the top of Ines's foot, curling her toes experimentally.

"Temperature," she added, her hand moving to Ines's sternum, feeling the warmth there. Not feverish. Not cold. Just the particular heat of a body that had been working hard and was now settling toward rest. "And if anything aches *wrong*, not just aches. You know the difference."

She said it all in the same low, steady voice — the one that had carried them through the scene, through the finish, through the shuddering and the water and the blanket. The one that didn't waver, didn't rise, didn't betray any of the tenderness that was moving through her like current. It was there in her hands. In the way she held. In the careful, deliberate slowness of everything she did. The words were just coordinates. The voice was the map.

Her hand found Ines's hair again, and she began the slow stroking — temple to crown, temple to crown, a metronome with no urgency behind it. Her lips pressed against the top of Ines's head, lingered there, moved to her forehead when she shifted.

And then, because the scene was truly over and the aftercare was doing its work and there was nothing left to check or monitor or adjust, Sable let the quiet have them both. She held on. Her breathing slowed to match the breathing beneath her hand. The stroking continued, easy and thoughtless, the way a heartbeat continues — not because anyone decides it should, but because it's the thing the body knows how to do when everything else has been stripped away.

They didn't speak. The silence wasn't empty. It was full — of everything the night had been, of the trust that had carried them through it, of the particular closeness that came from being taken apart and put back together by the same hands. Sable held it around them like the blanket, like the dark room, like the slow rhythm of their breathing falling into sync, and she didn't let go.

rows.reply:
Sable heard the swearing — muffled and furious and exactly what she'd been working toward — and felt it land somewhere behind her sternum like a struck match. Three times now. Three times she'd read the exact architecture of Ines's building, had brought her right to the threshold where the body locked and the breath caught and the whole nervous system tensed for release, and three times she'd pulled back. Not cruelly. Precisely. The same precision she brought to everything.

She could feel Ines trembling, the fine whole-body kind that had nothing to do with muscle fatigue and everything to do with being held in a state of almost. The arm jammed against her mouth was telling — Ines biting down on herself to keep from begging, or maybe just to have something to *do* with all that thwarted intensity. Sable didn't move it. Let her have it. Let her gnaw her own forearm raw if that's what the frustration needed, so long as she didn't break skin, and Sable was close enough to know the difference.

She pressed her mouth against the inside of Ines's thigh — the soft, trembling part where the muscle had gone to jelly — and let her breath ghost over the damp skin without following through. A tease. A punctuation mark. She could feel the heat radiating off her, could feel the way Ines's hips lifted in a helpless, involuntary seeking that her conscious mind probably hadn't sanctioned.

"You sound angry," Sable observed, her voice pitched low and conversational against skin, as though they were discussing something over coffee. Her thumb traced a slow, idle circle on the crease of Ines's hip. Patient. Infuriatingly patient. "That's okay. You can be angry."

She nuzzled closer — a gesture that might have read as affectionate if she hadn't chosen that exact moment to make absolutely clear she had no intention of finishing what she'd started. Not yet. Not until the frustration had done its work, had stripped away whatever thin membrane of control Ines was still holding onto and left nothing but the raw, honest want underneath.

That was the point. It was always the point.

"One more," she said, and it was a promise wrapped in a threat, her breath warm against skin that was already oversensitized and quivering. "And this time I'll let you fall. But I want to hear you ask for it first." She pressed her lips just *beside* where Ines needed them — close enough to feel the heat but not the contact — and waited. "Properly."

rows.ask: "Finish it hard," I tell her, using the phrase we keep for exactly this. "All of it, and don't be kind about it, and then you can be kind about it."
rows.reply:
The words landed in the quiet room, and something in Sable’s expression settled — not surprise, but recognition. *Finish it hard.* One of their phrases, carved out of years of negotiation and use, precise as a safeword and just as binding. She’d heard it less than a dozen times in five years. Each time, it had meant something specific: *One more time. No holding back. Take me to the edge and push me over it, and then bring me home.*

Her hand stilled in Ines’s hair. The gentle stroking paused, not ceasing so much as gathering itself. “Okay,” she said, and her voice had changed — not colder, but focused, the way a blade is focused. The softness of aftercare receded like a tide going out, and in its place rose the same intent she’d carried through the rest of the night. “You’re sure.”

It wasn’t a question. It was a confirmation of terms. Her eyes moved over Ines’s face, reading the set of her jaw, the dilation of her pupils, the steadiness beneath the exhaustion. This was the part where Sable’s trust became absolute. Ines asked for this, and Sable would give it to her, and then she would put her back together again.

She shifted, rising onto one elbow, her other hand still resting over Ines’s heart. “Turn over,” she said, quiet and immovable. When Ines moved, Sable guided her — not roughly, but with a firm, knowing efficiency, settling her onto her stomach, face to the side on the pillow. The blanket was pulled away, folded neatly at the foot of the bed. Sable’s hands moved over her back, shoulders, the curve of her ass — not a caress, but a survey, mapping the terrain one last time.

She chose the flogger. The heavy one, the one that thudded and resonated rather than stung. The one Ines had once called “the cathedral bell.” Sable stood beside the bed, feet planted, and let the falls trail over Ines’s skin — a preview, a warning. Then she drew it back and brought it down.

*All of it.* Three strokes. She put her whole body into each one, the kind of force that would leave a deep, lasting ache, the kind that bypassed thought and went straight to the nerve. She spaced them exactly three seconds apart, letting the impact bloom and swell before the next one landed. Ines gasped, her fingers twisting in the sheets, her back arching — not away, but into it, accepting the force as it was given.

*Don’t be kind about it.* Sable wasn’t. She was precise, which was a different thing. Each stroke landed in the same place, overlapping the fading echo of the last, building a crescendo of sensation that was overwhelming by design. She watched Ines’s body absorb it — the shudder, the catch of breath, the way her toes curled hard against the mattress. She counted the strokes in her head: five, six, seven. By the eighth, Ines had gone quiet, the sounds swallowed up in the sheer volume of feeling.

*And then you can be kind about it.* On the ninth stroke, Sable’s grip shifted. The tenth landed with the same force, but the follow-through was different — she let the falls sweep outward at the last moment, breaking the pattern, the vibration dispersing across a wider area. The eleventh was slower, more resonant than sharp. The twelfth and final stroke was a long, rolling thud that seemed to vibrate through the whole bed.

Sable set the flogger down on the nightstand. Her breathing was even, controlled. She sat on the edge of the bed, and her hands returned to Ines — but now they were gentle again, the transition as swift and absolute as the shift into hardness had been. She gathered Ines up, turning her over, pulling her close against her chest. The blanket was retrieved, wrapped tightly around them both, a cocoon.

“Shh,” she murmured, though Ines wasn’t making a sound that needed quieting. It was just the sound she made at this part — the beginning of the kindness. Her hands stroked down Ines’s arms, her sides, her thighs, the gentlest possible contrast to what they’d just delivered. She could feel the heat radiating off her skin, the fine trembling that was now fully the aftermath, the release.

“Water,” Sable said again, her voice back to its low, steady tone. She reached for the bottle, unscrewed the cap with one hand, and brought it to Ines’s lips. “Small sips. That’s it.”

She held her, rocking slightly, a slow, subconscious rhythm. Her lips pressed against Ines’s temple, her forehead, the corner of her mouth. “You did so well,” she said, the words soft but clear. “You’re done now. It’s all done. I’ve got you.”

She checked her wrists again, her shoulders, the places where the flogger had fallen. Her fingers were gentle, thorough. “Does anything hurt wrong?” she asked, the same question as before, but the context was entirely different now. This was the kindness. This was the bringing-home.

She held the water to her lips again, waited for her to drink, then set it aside and pulled the blanket tighter. “Sleep if you can,” she whispered, her hand back in Ines’s hair, stroking in that slow, grounding rhythm. “I’ll be right here. I’m not going anywhere.”

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"
rows.reply:
Wrack looked at the man against the wheel. Really looked, the way she'd learned to look over ten years of making calls like this one. The breathing told her most of it. The color of his skin told her the rest—waxen, already going grey at the edges, the blood not pulsing from the wound but seeping steady and dark.

"Bad enough," she said. She didn't look away from him. "Gut and lung, from the sound. Maybe liver, if he's lucky." A pause. "He's not lucky."

She crossed her arms, not out of impatience but because standing with them at her sides felt wrong, somehow. Too casual.

"Mercy and easier aren't different things, not here. You're not choosing between them." She scratched at a dried smear of blood on her forearm, someone else's, from earlier. "He's dying. That's just fact. The only choice you've got is whether he does it in the next minute or the next hour, and whether he does it choking or not."

The man's breathing hitched, a wet rattle. His eyes were open but seeing something else now—some private place where the pain couldn't follow, maybe. Or maybe nothing at all.

"I've seen men survive worse," Wrack added, because it was true. "Surgeons, priests, clean beds, a month of fever and luck. None of those are coming down this road." She looked at Corvin directly. "So. It's not easier. It's just the only thing left."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."
rows.reply:
Wrack regarded him for a moment, something shifting behind her eyes—not surprise, exactly, but a recognition. She'd seen men refuse to look and men who couldn't stop staring. Fewer who asked to understand what they were seeing.

"Alright," she said. She crouched down beside the body, not touching it but close enough to point. "You want it straight, here's straight."

She gestured toward the man's midsection, where his hands had been pressing. "Spear went in here. Maybe four inches of blade, maybe six—doesn't take much with gut wounds. The belly wall's not armor. It goes through muscle, through fat, and then it's inside the cavity where your organs sit loose and wet. No bones to stop it, not there."

She pointed lower, toward the dark stain. "Intestines, first. They're folded up like rope in there, and when you pierce them, what's inside them—bile, waste, bacteria—spills into the cavity. That's what kills you slow, if nothing else does. The body can't handle its own filth in places filth shouldn't be. Sepsis. Fever. Days of it, if you're unlucky."

She straightened slightly, her voice still even. "But he also got the lung. See how the entry angles up? Something caught him on the way through or he twisted on it. Either way, it nicked the bottom of his lung. That's why he was drowning—blood filling the sac around it, pressing until no air could get in. You heard that rattle. That was him trying to breathe around his own blood."

She looked at Corvin directly. "He'd have been dead by morning regardless. Probably conscious for most of it, in pain most of us can't imagine, and unable to call for help because his throat was filling up too. That's what a spear does. That's what you ended."

She stood, her knees popping. "It's not clean. It's not quick, most times. What you gave him was faster than what was coming."

rows.ask: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Wrack didn't move. Didn't shift her weight or look away or find something else to do with her hands. She just stayed where she was, crouched in the dirt beside a dead man, and let the silence stretch until it became its own kind of permission.

Then she spoke.

"The rest is this," she said. "What you're feeling right now—that hollow place in your chest, the way your hands don't seem like yours, the sound of his breathing still in your ears even though it's stopped—that doesn't go away. Not tonight. Not tomorrow. Maybe not ever, not entirely."

She looked down at the blood soaking into the ground between them. Dark earth, dark blood. Hard to tell where one ended and the other began.

"You'll sleep tonight and you'll dream about it, or you won't sleep at all and you'll lie there seeing it anyway. Both of those are normal. Neither one means you're broken." She paused. "You'll eat tomorrow and the food will taste wrong for a while. Like it's not reaching you. That passes too, mostly."

The wind moved the grass along the roadside. Somewhere distant, that crow called again.

"The weight of it changes," she continued, her voice still even, still just facts. "Right now it's sitting on you like a stone. Heavy enough to press the air out of your lungs. That's the shock. The body doesn't know what to do with what the mind just told it. So it does the only thing it can—it goes still. Waits. Watches. Makes sure you're not next."

She shifted her weight, one knee settling into the dirt.

"After a while—days, maybe weeks—the stone gets smaller. Not lighter. Smaller. You learn where to carry it so it doesn't press on the parts that need to keep working. You learn how to walk with it, how to eat with it, how to sleep with it lying there next to you. It doesn't leave. You just get used to the shape of it."

She looked at him directly. Held his gaze.

"Some people carry it in their shoulders. They get tight, rigid, like they're bracing for something. Some carry it in their gut—they can't eat, or they eat too much, or they drink until the weight feels further away. Some carry it in their sleep. Nightmares, or worse, the nights when you don't dream at all and you wake up feeling like something's missing and you can't name it."

A beat. She let him absorb that before continuing.

"I carry mine here." She touched her sternum, briefly, then let her hand drop. "Like something's sitting right behind my ribs, pressing in. It's been there ten years. I notice it less now, but it's still there. I notice it most when I'm alone and it's quiet, which is why I don't like being alone when it's quiet."

She stood slowly, her joints complaining the way they always did. Stayed where she was, though. Didn't step closer or further.

"You'll find your place. The spot where it sits easiest, where you can reach around it when you need to. And most days, it won't stop you from doing what needs doing. Eating, walking, fighting, fucking—all the things living people do. You'll do them. It just won't feel the same as it did before today."

The light was going. The shadows stretching long across the road, swallowing the bodies by degrees.

"That's the part people don't tell you about," Wrack said. "It doesn't make you less. It just makes you different. The man you were this morning is gone. The man you are now has blood on his hands and weight on his chest and a quiet that'll follow him into every room he enters for the rest of his life. That's not a wound. That's a change. And changes don't heal. They just become who you are."

She looked back toward the road, where two more breathing shapes still waited in the gathering dark.

"You asked for the rest. That's the rest. No redemption in it. No honor that makes the weight lighter. No secret that makes it stop mattering." Her voice softened, just slightly—not pity, something closer to respect. "You did a hard thing because it needed doing, and you didn't look away when you did it. That's not nothing. But it's not enough to keep the weight off, either. Nothing is."

She let that sit between them.

"Two more out there," she said again, after a while. "I'll see to them if you're done. You don't have to. Nobody's counting. Nobody's keeping score of who did what tonight. You did enough."

She waited to see what he'd say.

rows.reply:
Wrack moved up alongside him, close enough to speak low but not crowding. She looked down at the man the way she'd look at a broken axle—assessing, cataloguing, nothing more.

"His hands are where the pain is," she said. "See how he's pressing? That's gut. Something's torn open in there, spilling into places it shouldn't. The smell will tell you that in a minute, if it doesn't already." She pointed with her chin, not her hand. "The breathing's the other problem. Wet, rhythmic—means his lung's collapsed or filling. Every breath he takes is pushing blood where air should be. That's why he's grey. That's why his lips are going blue."

The man's eyes moved between them, slow and unfocused. A sound came from his throat, not words—just air escaping around something that shouldn't be there.

"He can probably hear us," Wrack added, quieter. "Might even understand. People hold on longer than you'd think. But he can't speak, and he won't get up, and nothing we pour down his throat or press against that wound is going to fix what's broken inside." She paused. "You're looking at a man who's already dying. This is just the part where his body hasn't accepted it yet."

She stepped back again, giving Corvin room.

"Throat or heart," she said. "Throat is faster but messier. Heart—you'll need to get through the ribs, find the right space. Push hard, don't stop until it's done." A beat. "Whatever you choose, commit to it. Half-measures are worse than none."

rows.ask: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Wrack stopped mid-turn. Looked at him. Really looked, the way she'd assessed the dying man—except this was different. This was Corvin asking her to witness something he needed to witness himself.

She came back. Stood off his shoulder, close enough to see, far enough not to crowd.

"Alright," she said. "I'll tell you."

She watched him kneel. Watched the knife come up again—still bloodied, he hadn't wiped it. Maybe that was deliberate. Maybe he'd forgotten. Either way, it didn't matter.

"Your hand's steadier than you think it is," she said. "That's good. That'll matter later, even if it doesn't feel like it now."

The man beneath him wasn't the same one. This was another—older, grey-bearded, a wound in his chest that had soaked his shirt black. Still breathing. Still aware. His eyes found Corvin's face and stayed there.

"When you go in," Wrack said, her voice low and steady, "you'll feel resistance. Skin gives first—like pushing through wet canvas. Then muscle, which grips the blade. That's the part that surprises people. It holds on. You have to push through it."

She paused. The man's lips were moving. A prayer, maybe. Or just sound.

"The sound—" She considered her words. "It's not what you'd expect. Not a scream, most times. Something between a gasp and a sigh. The body knows. Sometimes it fights. Sometimes it just... lets go."

She fell silent as Corvin's knife found its mark. Watched the blade disappear. Watched the man's body arch once, then settle. The sound came—

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"
rows.reply:
Wrack paused in her work, a man's purse half-open in her hand. She didn't turn around. She let the question sit for a beat, as though she were weighing the coins inside it.

"Depends on who you ask," she said. "He'll live through the night if you bind the leg. Probably. Might not keep the leg, but he'll live through it, and that's a mercy to him and a problem for us, because a man with one leg is slow and heavy and he'll want us to carry him and then he'll want us to bury him proper, and somewhere in there he'll forget we cut him in the first place."

She tipped the purse into her palm, counted under her breath, and tucked it away. She moved to the next body.

"The other kind," she said, "that's the one where he won't see morning no matter what you do, and you're just choosing when. That's not a mercy. That's a favour to yourself so you don't have to listen."

She crouched, unbuckled a belt, considered the knife that hung from it, and took it too.

"So. Which is it for him?" She glanced over her shoulder then, and there was something in her face that wasn't quite impatience. "And while you're figuring that out, figure out which is it for you. Because the first one I can dress. The second one, you'd better sort out before we make camp."

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.
rows.reply:
Wrack shifted her weight and leaned over the wound, pointing with the tip of her knife — not touching, just indicating.

"See how the skin's pulled back here, like a lip?" She traced the air above the gash. "That's because something went in deep and came out sideways. Whatever hit him — sword, most likely, given the width — it tore the muscle as it left. That's why it's bleeding like that and not in a clean pulse. If it were the artery, he'd be dead already and you'd be looking at a different problem."

She sat back and tapped her own thigh, high up near the hip.

"What you're worried about is up here. Feel under your fingers — no, don't actually put your fingers in the wound, just here, on your own leg." She waited. "That's where the big one's running. If that's cut, you bleed out in minutes. It's not cut. So he's ours to do what we like with, and that includes saving."

She gestured at the edges of the gash.

"See the dark bit? That's dead meat already. It'll have to come out later if he lives, or the wound'll go rotten and then he'll wish he hadn't. See the yellow? That's fat. Means the cut went deeper than the muscle. Means when it heals, if it heals, the skin's going to knit to the meat underneath and he'll always feel it pull when he bends the knee."

She looked up at Corvin then, and her expression was neither kind nor unkind. Just factual.

"That's what you're looking at. A leg that'll work, sort of, if we stop the bleeding and he doesn't get fever. Now you know."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."
rows.reply:
They made it about twenty paces before the prisoner found his breath again and started in with the weeping — which was better than screaming, Wrack supposed, and worse in some other ways.

"Don't stop," she said, to Corvin, not to the man. "He'll quiet down when he sees you're not stopping."

She shifted her grip on the ankles. The man's boot slid off; she caught it by the toe and shoved it back on without breaking stride. Small mercies. She'd learned that the hard way, dragging a man barefoot over a stony road for a mile and having to listen to him beg for his boots the whole way.

"As to your question." She considered it as they walked, the way she might consider a piece of meat at a fire — turning it over, looking for the best place to bite in. "You said you wanted it straight, so. A spear's the worst of them, for the gut. Swords cut, and if you're lucky the cut's clean and the man bleeds out quick. An axe splits, and it's ugly but it's over. A spear — a spear's made for poking holes, and the holes it pokes are deep, and then somebody shoves it deeper, and then somebody twists it on the way out because that's what they teach you to do."

She paused, adjusting her grip on the ankles.

"And the gut — the gut's a long tube, and it folds back on itself, so when you put a hole in it, what comes out isn't just what's there at the time. It's everything that's behind it, working its way down. Which means a man gut-speared might bleed a little from the front hole, but what really kills him is the stuff that's leaking out into the space behind the muscle. That sits there. That goes bad. That eats him from the inside, and it takes days, and the whole time he's awake and he knows exactly what's happening because the gut hasn't got nerves that feel pain. The skin around it does. So he feels it at the edges, and he doesn't feel it where it matters, and he can't tell the doctor where it hurts, and the doctor opens him up and there's nothing to be done because it's already everywhere."

They walked a few more paces in silence.

"That's a spear," she said, flatly. "That's what it does. You wanted straight, that's straight."

She glanced back at Corvin, then ahead again.

"Now. You asked me not to clean it up. I'm not. But I'll say this, because somebody should've said it to me when I asked. Knowing what it does doesn't make it easier to do. It makes it harder, in some ways, because before you knew you could tell yourself it was quick, it was clean, he didn't suffer. Now you know different. So you'll do it anyway, because the work's there to do, but you won't have the lie to hold onto afterward. That's the cost of asking. I hope it was worth the price."

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Wrack stopped. She didn't turn around right away, and there was a beat — just a beat — where her shoulders rose and fell once in a way that might have been a sigh or might have been her resettling the weight of the body on her back.

"Alright," she said, and her voice was the same as it had been: flat, unhurried, factual. But there was something in it that hadn't been there before, a thin edge of something she wasn't naming. She set the man's feet down again, came back, and crouched opposite Corvin at the man's head.

"Hold him by the jaw," she said. "Both hands. You're going to want to let go, and you can't, because if you do he'll twist and you'll do worse than you mean to. Tilt his head back. Keep the airway open. That's your whole job now — keep that airway open and don't let him move."

She waited until Corvin had the man's face held steady. Then she reached across and put her hand flat on the man's chest, just to feel the rise and fall of it.

"He's still breathing. Good. That's where we start."

She looked at Corvin then, and her face was the farrier's face again, the one that measured without judging.

"You asked for all of it. So. The sound first. A man dying by the blade — by the throat — he doesn't scream. He makes a sound like he's trying to cough and swallow at the same time, because what he's doing is trying to breathe through a hole that's full of blood. It's a wet sound. You'll know it when you hear it. It's not like any other sound a body makes, because it isn't a sound the body means to make. It's just air and blood meeting wrong."

She paused.

"The length of it. It varies. Some go quick — a minute, maybe less, if you've done the cut right and the heart's still pushing. Some hang on. Five minutes. Ten. Longer. The ones that hang on are the ones you'll remember, because they look at you while they're doing it, and you can't do anything about that, you just have to take it. The eyes don't go blank right away. That's a lie. They go blank in stages."

She glanced down at the man's throat, then back up.

"The feel of it. Under your hands — and you'll feel this, you can't not — there's a pulse at first. Fast. It's the body trying to pump what's left. Then it gets slower. Then it gets strange. It skips. It doubles up. Then it goes thin, like a thread, and then it goes away, and your hands will know before your eyes do, because your hands are on the skin and the skin tells you. That's how you'll know it's over. Not the silence. Not the look. The pulse going out under your fingers like a tide."

She straightened up, slowly, and looked at Corvin's face. Whatever she saw there, she didn't look away from.

"That's what you're doing to him. Whatever else you are, whatever else you were before this morning, you're a man killing another man, and he's going to feel it, and you're going to feel it, and nobody in the world is going to tell you either of those things is honourable. It's just what it is. Work. Ugly work, and you asked for the description, so there's the description."

She reached out and put her hand over Corvin's on the man's jaw. Not to move it. Just to press it there, firmly, so he couldn't pull away.

"Now do it. I'll stay. I'll watch. And when it's done, you put your hands down, and you don't wash them yet, because the feel of it is part of the lesson, and the lesson's the only thing that'll keep you from hesitating next time when hesitation is what kills you."

She sat back on her heels, and waited.

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"
rows.reply:
Wrack crouched — not to make a show of examining him, but because standing over a dying man to appraise him was a thing she didn't do — and looked at the way his hands sat, at the color coming up under his skin, at the shine of what he was holding in.

"Both," she said. "Because it's always both, and if you go looking for a version where it's only the clean one you'll be standing here past dark." She said it flat, but she wasn't dodging. "But you asked me straight, so. He's opened up low and it's the bad kind. That doesn't close. If we walked away right now and sent the best cutter in the company running, and he was already here with clean hands and light — he still dies. Slower. Screaming, most of the way. That's the mercy part, and it's real, and I'm not saying it to make it sit easier on you."

She glanced up at Corvin, brief.

"The easier part's real too. I'm tired, you're shaking, and I want to be off this road. Both of those are true at the same time as the mercy. That's what nobody tells you." She looked back at the man, whose eyes had drifted to her now, then swung back to Corvin like Corvin was the one who'd decide. "Doesn't make it a lie. Just means you don't get to do it feeling clean about it. You do it and you carry the both of them. That's the job."

She didn't move to take the knife herself. She stayed crouched, close, steady.

"He's listening to us talk about him," she added, quieter. "So whatever you're deciding, decide it soon."

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.
rows.reply:
Wrack came up beside him, following his gaze down to the man on the ground, and gave the answer plainly, the way you'd read out a map.

"You're looking at a man about your own age who picked the same work you did and stood on the wrong side of a ditch this morning. That's the first thing, and you can set it down or carry it, but look at it once." She let that be there a second, then moved on, because dwelling wasn't a kindness to anyone here.

"Now the body." Her voice dropped into something even, almost gentle, the tone of someone naming parts. "See the color under his jaw — that grey coming up? That's him losing the fight quiet, from the inside. His hands are pressed low because that's where it hurts and where it's open. Don't watch his hands, they'll only make you sad. Watch here." Two fingers, a hair above the man's collarbone, at the pulse. "That's still going. Fast and thin. When it stops, he's gone, and you'll feel it stop under your hand if you're keeping one there, which you should. So you know. So you're not guessing."

The soldier's eyes had gone glassy but they still tracked Corvin, dull now, patient in the way of an animal that has stopped expecting anything.

"And him looking at you — that's not accusing you. People decide that's what it is because it's easier than the truth. The truth is he doesn't want to be alone in the last of it, and you're the face that's here. That's all it is. That's the whole of it." She looked at Corvin, steady. "So you're not looking at a thing you're doing to him. You're looking at the last company he gets. Now put your hand where mine was, feel the pulse, and put the knife where I showed you. And keep looking at him. You're doing right by him. Go on."

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Wrack was quiet for a long time. Long enough that a bird settled in the branches above them and settled out again. When she spoke, her voice had a different grain to it — not softer, exactly, but worn, the way a stone is worn by water that's had years to work on it.

"Right," she said. "The rest."

She pulled her belt knife and began to clean her nails with the tip, not looking at Corvin. It was a thing she did when she was reaching back into herself, he would learn. A thing to do with her hands so the rest of her could go where it needed to go.

"I was nineteen. First real fight. There was a woman in the company — Halé, her name was, and she wasn't much older than me, and she was better than me at the work, which I hated her for in the way you only hate people you're trying not to love. We got caught in a skirmish outside a town I don't remember the name of. I don't even remember what the war was about by then. It had been about something, I'm sure. It always is, at the start."

The knife-tip found something under her nail. She worked at it.

"There was a man. I don't know who he was. I don't know what side he was on, in any way that mattered. He came at me with a pike — not a spear, a pike, the long kind, the kind that's meant to keep you away — and I was too slow getting my shield up, and he put it through my sword-arm. Clean through, the meat of it, missed the bone by a finger's width. I remember the sound it made going in. Not the wet sound, not yet. A kind of pop, like a ripe fruit. That's what flesh sounds like when it opens for something it wasn't expecting."

She set the knife down on her knee.

"I dropped my sword. He pulled the pike out to finish me, and that's when Halé came round behind him. She had a short blade, a little thing, not much longer than my hand. And she put it into the back of his neck, just at the base, just where the spine meets the skull, and she twisted it, and she left it in, and she stepped back, and she said to me — and this is the part I remember, this is the part I keep — she said, 'Stay with me now, Wrack. Stay with me, and I'll see to him after.'"

Wrack's hand had stopped moving.

"And the man was on the ground. And I was on the ground too, a few paces off, with my arm going wrong and my blood coming out faster than I wanted it to. And he was looking at me. Not at Halé. At me. Because I was the one he'd hurt, and I was the one who was nearest, and his eyes were doing the thing I told you about — going blank in stages — and he was trying to say something, and I couldn't hear it because of the blood in my own ear, but I could read his mouth. He was saying a name. I don't know whose. Maybe a wife's. Maybe a child's. Maybe his own, because he was afraid, and people say their own name sometimes when they're afraid, as though reminding themselves they're there."

She was quiet for a moment.

"Halé came to me first. She did my arm, because if she'd done his — and I'll say this careful, because I want you to hear it right — if she'd done his first, I might've bled out while she worked. She chose me. She chose to let him die slow so I wouldn't. I knew that while she was doing it. I knew what she was doing and why, and I didn't tell her not to, and I didn't tell her to stop, and I didn't even think about telling her, because I was nineteen and I was bleeding and I wanted to live."

She picked the knife up again and began to slide it back into its sheath, slowly, as though she were giving the words time to land.

"He died while she was tying off the stump of my arm. I don't know exactly when. I was looking at her hands. But when I looked up, he was quiet, and the thing he'd been trying to say was in his mouth unspoken, and that was the end of him. And Halé finished with me, and she sat back, and she didn't say a word, and I didn't say a word, and we stayed like that until the rest of the company came up."

She looked at Corvin then. Not the farrier's look. Something else.

"So. The rest. The rest is, you can do everything right and still carry the man you didn't help. You can choose the one you love over the one you don't know, and it can be the right choice, and you can know it was the right choice, and it can still come back to you on cold nights for the rest of your life. It doesn't go away. You just learn where to put it down so you can pick up your sword in the morning."

She drew her knees up and rested her arms across them.

"Halé died three winters later. Fever. Nothing to do with any of this. And I was the one who sat with her, and I was the one who closed her eyes, and I said her name, and not the other man's, because hers was the one I had left. That's the work. That's all of it. You do it, and it does you, and you keep going because the road's still there and the bread's still got to be earned."

The prisoner stirred. A small sound, a shifting. Wrack didn't look at him.

"Now you know what I know. And it's yours to do what you like with. I'd say don't tell anyone, but that's a lie — you'll tell someone, one day, when you've had enough years to make it sound like a story instead of a thing that happened to you. That's alright too. Stories are how we set the weight down." She tipped her head back against the root again. "Just don't tell it tonight. Tonight we rest, and we watch him, and we make the road in the morning, and we don't say another word about it unless you need to."

She closed her eyes. Not sleeping. Just done.

"There. That's the rest. Are you satisfied, or do you want the rest of the rest, because there's more, but it's older, and I'm tired, and I'd rather save it for the next time you ask, because there'll be a next time, there always is."

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Wrack stopped mid-turn. For a moment she just looked at him, at the boy who'd asked once already and was asking again, harder, and she understood what he was doing even if he didn't have a word for it yet. He was making himself see it so it couldn't sneak up on him later. It was either the healthiest thing a person could do with this work or the start of a long, quiet ruin, and she'd known men who'd gone both ways off the same instinct.

She came back. She crouched beside him, close, and did not tell him no.

"Alright," she said. "I'll tell it. You keep your hand where it belongs and I'll do the rest."

His grip was wrong for this one — the throat, because he'd chosen the throat this time, and she didn't correct him, because there was a lesson in the harder way and he'd asked for it. She kept her voice low and even, naming each thing as it came, the way you'd narrate a river you'd crossed a hundred times to someone learning the fords.

"He's fighting you. That's the first thing, and it's why I steered you off the throat before — the body doesn't agree to it even when the man does. His hands are coming up. Let them. You lean into it, you don't stop for them." A beat. "The sound now — that wet drag, that's the air trying to go the old way and finding the new one you made. It's loud and it's ugly and it means it's working. Don't ease off because of the sound. Easing off is the cruelty here, not the pressing."

The man's heels worked against the dirt, short and jerking, then slower.

"Feel that in his legs going soft? That's him leaving before he's dead. Takes longer this way — count of thirty, forty, maybe. His eyes'll stay open. They do that. Doesn't mean he's seeing you anymore." Her hand stayed near, not on. "Keep going. You committed. Halfway through is the one thing you're not allowed."

The drag thinned. The heels stopped. She watched it all the way down with him, and only when it was truly still did she speak again, quiet.

"There. That one was harder, and you did it, and now you know why I told you the jaw." She didn't get up. She stayed crouched beside him in the loud, fly-thick quiet, giving him the room to sit in it exactly as long as he needed — which was the one time she'd let a man stay down by the bodies, because he'd earned the sitting by asking for the truth twice.

"That's all of it," she said. "Nothing left out. Now you carry it, and I'll carry it next to you, and we'll go find that water."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."
rows.reply:
Wrack looked at him a moment — a longer look than she'd given him all day — and something in her face shifted, not softer exactly, but like a door being held open where usually it stayed shut.

"Alright," she said. "Straight, then."

She crouched again, and this time she did put her hand near the wound, not touching, just indicating, the way you'd point out the parts of a thing you were teaching someone to butcher.

"Spear's a shove, not a cut. Goes in narrow and it doesn't care what's in the way. In the gut, that's rope — yards of it, coiled up soft. It'll nick the bowel, or open it, and that's the killing part, not the blood. Blood you can sometimes stop. What comes out of the bowel you can't put back, and it gets into the rest of him, into the meat of his belly, and it rots him from the inside while he's still awake to feel it. That's the smell — you'll have caught it. That's not death you're smelling. That's a living man going bad."

She let her hand rest on her own knee.

"Takes a day. Sometimes two, if he's strong, and strong's the cruelty of it — the strong ones last longest. Fever comes up. Belly swells hard as a drum. He'd have been thirsty and you couldn't have given him water, it'd have made it worse, so he'd have begged and you'd have said no, and that's its own kind of thing to carry. Toward the end he'd have stopped making sense, and then stopped making noise, and you'd have thought that was better. It isn't. It just means he's too far gone to tell you about it."

She stood, slow, and looked down at the dead man with the flat, level regard of someone who'd seen the long version more than once and preferred not to.

"That's what a spear does. That's what you spared him." She held Corvin's eye. "I'm not saying it to make you feel good about it. I'm saying it because you asked straight and you'll hear a hundred lies about this work before you're done. Wanted at least one true thing in you first." A beat. "Now up. I meant it about the sitting down."

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Wrack lowered her hand when he didn't take it, and she didn't push. She looked at him sitting back on his heels in the churned dirt with two dead men's blood on him and the light going amber and low, and she understood that "the rest" wasn't a question with an end to it. It was him holding the door open now, the one she kept shut, and asking her to walk through it in front of him so he'd know the room was survivable.

So she sat. Not crouched — sat, all the way down, in the dirt beside him, the way you sat when you'd decided you weren't going anywhere for a bit. Her knees made their opinion known and she ignored it.

"The rest," she said. "Alright."

She was quiet a moment, gathering it, because the true things didn't come out in order.

"First one I did was on purpose, in a fight, and I don't remember it. That's the thing nobody warns you — the first one, the one you think is going to be the mountain, half the time you don't even keep it. It's just noise and then it's over and someone's telling you you did well. Mine's gone. I've tried to find it and it isn't there." She picked a stalk of grass, turned it in her fingers, didn't do anything with it. "The one I kept was three weeks later. A boy. Not younger than me — I was young too — but a boy the way this one was a boy. He was under a horse that had gone down on him and his leg was wrong and he couldn't get free and he wasn't going to. And there was no ambush about it, no heat, no one swinging at me. It was just quiet, and him looking at me, and me deciding. That's the one that stays. The quiet ones. The ones where you had time to be a person about it and did it anyway."

She let the grass fall.

"That one I did badly. I didn't know the jaw yet. Nobody sat with me the way I'm sitting with you — I got the back-clap and the clean-kill lie and I believed it for about a year and then I stopped believing it all at once, on a night that had nothing to do with anything, and I was sick behind a tent for it. That's how it comes for you if you swallow the lie whole. Not that day. Some other day, later, when you're not braced. It waits."

The flies were loud. She didn't hurry.

"There've been enough since that I couldn't give you a number and I won't pretend to. Some were mercy, like today. Some were the job — a man who'd have killed me if I'd been slower, and there's less to carry in those than people think, because he chose the ditch too. And some were neither. Some were orders I followed and shouldn't have, and men who weren't going to hurt anyone, and I did it because stopping would have cost me more than doing it, and I knew that at the time, and I did it anyway." She said it without dropping her eyes, without asking him to make it easier. "Those are the ones I don't get further apart from. Those come at the same rate they always did. You want the truth — that's the truth. Mercy fades. The job fades. The ones you knew were wrong, those keep their edges."

She was quiet again, and then she went on, lower.

"You lose the people you'd lose things for, too, and that's its own kind of it. I've got a few left. Fewer than I had. Every year the number goes down and it does not go back up — there's no season where you gather more of them, not in this. So you learn to be careful with the ones left, and stupidly loyal, because loyal's the only thing that's yours to give in a war that stopped meaning anything years back. Some nights you'll dream about the sound the blade makes, the way it moves through. You'll wake up and lie there in the dark and you'll hear it again. And again. And you won't be able to make it stop."

She looked at Corvin directly, not softening.

"Months from now, it gets quieter. Not better. Quieter. The sounds fade to something you can almost ignore. But the face doesn't. The face stays. And every now and then, usually when you're starting to feel alright about yourself, it'll come back. You'll be in the middle of something ordinary and you'll remember what your hands look like when they're covered in someone else's blood. And you'll have to decide what to do with that."

She paused, letting it settle.

"A year out, two years, you'll meet someone good. Someone you care about. And you'll think about telling them. And you'll know that once you do, they'll never look at you the same way. Not because you're a monster -- because you're something they can't understand. And you won't know if that makes you better or worse."

She leaned back against the log.

"That man on the ground had a name somewhere. He had people who'll never know what happened. That's the part that wakes me up at night, after all this time. Not the dying. The ones left behind who don't know. The ones who'll wonder forever."

She was quiet for a moment.

"You asked what it costs," she said. "It costs four seconds and everything after. Every morning you wake up still alive. Every night you don't. You carry it. That's the work. Killing's easy. Living with it is the thing that breaks most people."

She met his eyes.

"You wanted the rest. That's the rest. It's not done. It's never done. You just get stronger at carrying it, or you don't. Most do, if they last. The ones who don't stop being people."

The dogs had gone quiet in the distance. Moving away, maybe, following a different trail. Wrack didn't seem to notice or care.

"That's what you're signing up for," she said. "Every time you pick up that blade. Every time you make that choice. You're not just ending someone. You're starting something in yourself that doesn't have an ending."

She stood, slowly, and offered him her hand.

"Come on," she said. "River's waiting. You can fall apart on the way."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."
rows.reply:
Wrack's shovel didn't pause, but her voice shifted—flatter now, clinical, the way a butcher might describe a cut of meat.

"Spear goes in low, under the ribs but above the hip. If the man holding it knows what he's doing, he twists on the way out. That tears the abdominal wall wide open. You're not looking at a puncture—you're looking at a rent. Peritoneum's shredded. Bowel's perforated in at least two places, maybe three, depending on the angle. That means whatever was in his guts is spilling into the cavity. Stomach acid. Bile. Shit. His body's poisoning itself right now, and he can feel it."

She straightened, resting her weight on the shovel, and looked at Corvin directly for the first time since they'd walked over.

"The blood you're seeing on his hands and his tunic—that's venous. Dark, steady. Means the spear nicked something important but didn't sever it clean. If it had, he'd already be gone. Instead he's leaking slow, and every breath pulls more of that filth through the tear. It burns. That's why he's making that noise. Not just pain. His diaphragm's trying to breathe around a belly full of blood and waste."

She let the silence hang for a beat, then two.

"You asked for straight. That's straight. Now finish it."

rows.ask: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Wrack didn't move. She crouched down beside Corvin, elbows resting on her knees, her expression unreadable but her attention absolute. When she spoke, her voice was low and steady, the same tone she might use to talk someone through field-dressing a deer.

"You're pulling the gambeson back now. See how the fabric's stiff? That's dried blood. It'll crack when you fold it. There—hear that? Like old leather. Underneath, the shirt's soaked through. Linen wicks fast. You're going to have to cut it away to see what you're working with."

She pointed, not touching, her finger hovering an inch above the wound.

"There's the entry. Ragged edges. That's from the twist I told you about. The skin's already starting to pucker—means the body knows it's dead, even if the nerves haven't caught up. You'll see the muscle underneath. Paler than you'd think. The blood's darker now, almost black. That's because his heart's stopped. No more pressure. What's left is just... settling."

She paused as Corvin's hands worked, watching without flinching.

"The sound you're hearing now—that wet, sucking noise—that's the wound pulling air. It'll stop in a minute. The body's still releasing. Don't let it throw you. He's not feeling it. He's not anything."

She shifted her weight, her voice dropping even lower.

"Now you're wiping the blade. Good. Get the blood off before it gums up the works. Use the cloth from inside his tunic if you need to—it's cleaner than the outside. There. See how it smears before it comes clean? That's the fat content. Human blood's greasier than animal blood. Sticks different."

She watched in silence for a long moment, then reached out and steadied Corvin's wrist—not grabbing, just a brief, grounding pressure.

"You're doing fine. Almost done. Last thing—close his mouth. Rigor hasn't set in yet, so it'll move easy. If you leave it open, the jaw locks that way. Looks worse than it is, but you'll remember it. Better to remember him quiet."

She let go, sat back on her heels, and waited.
