rows.ask: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"
rows.reply:
Sedge paused.

It was a brief pause, the kind that someone watching closely would catch and someone watching the tent flap or the watermarks on the canvas would not. She kept her hands where they were, the joint seated in her grip, the arm cold against her palms.

"Wrong patient for that question," she said. "Colm keeps both his arms. Colm goes home."

She said it flatly, not as comfort but as information, the way she'd say the arm was cold or the color was better. It happened to be true and it happened to be the kind of true that was useful to say out loud.

"If I were being kind," she added, "you'd know. I'd send you out of the tent first."

She'd done that twice in the last four years. Both times she'd known within thirty seconds of the man coming in, and both times she'd told whoever was helping her to go get water or find more lamp oil or some other thing that didn't exist, and both times they'd understood and gone anyway and been grateful for it later. It was the one mercy she'd kept.

She reset her weight.

"Right now I need you holding," she said, "not talking."

She didn't say it harshly. It was just the shape of the moment — there was a thing that needed doing and talking was not it and Wick had asked a reasonable question and the answer was finished and now they were past it.

"Hold," she said.

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."
rows.reply:
Sedge looked back down at the man on the table. She considered the question for a moment — not whether to answer it, but how to answer it usefully.

"You're seeing a glenohumeral dislocation," she said. "Both sides. The ball of the joint gets forced out of the socket — here." She touched the point of Colm's right shoulder without pressing, just indicating. "The muscles lock around it because the body thinks it's protecting itself. It isn't. It's making it harder to fix and it's cutting off blood to the arm, which is why the arm was cold."

She began checking his fingers, pressing each one briefly, watching the color return.

"The pop you felt was the ball seating back into the socket. That's correct. That's what it's supposed to feel like." She paused. "Most people who haven't heard it before think something's broken. Nothing's broken."

She moved to the right side again and did the same check — fingers, color, the pulse at the wrist.

"The right shoulder has old damage. Probably took a bad fall sometime before this. Healed without anyone setting it properly." She kept her voice even. "He'll have movement back, but not all of it. I'll tell him that when he can sit up."

She set Colm's arm down carefully along his side.

"What you were feeling through your hands," she said, "was the instability. The joint moving in the wrong planes. That's what a badly healed injury feels like from the outside." She glanced at Wick. "It's useful to know. You'll feel it again."

She said it as a simple fact — that Wick would be in this tent again, or one like it, with his hands on someone and needing to understand what his hands were telling him.

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."
rows.reply:
Sedge stopped washing her hands. Not a long stop — she finished rinsing, dried them on the cloth hung at the basin's edge, set the cloth down. Then she turned and looked at Wick with the particular attention she gave to people who had asked her something real.

"Which part of in there," she said. "There's more than one answer."

She didn't wait for him to specify.

"Shrapnel is irregular," she said. "That's the first thing. A bullet is a simple problem — it goes in, it goes through, it stops somewhere, you find it. Shrapnel is a hundred different shapes traveling at a hundred different angles. Some of it is big enough to see. Some of it is fragments the size of a thumbnail paring and it goes where it wants."

She moved back to the table, not to do anything, just to stand somewhere while she talked.

"When it hits the joint — shoulder, knee, hip, doesn't matter — it does two things. It damages what it touches directly, which is obvious. Bone, cartilage, the tendons. But it also carries in everything that was on it when it left. Metal. Cloth. Whatever was between the source and the man." She paused. "That's what kills them, mostly. Not the fragment. What the fragment brings with it."

She looked at Colm, then back at Wick.

"The joint swells because the body is trying to wall it off. The fluid goes septic if you don't get in there. Getting in there means opening it, which means more damage, which means you are making a controlled version of the injury in order to address the uncontrolled version." She said this plainly. "It looks like the wrong thing to do. It is the right thing to do."

She pulled the lamp slightly closer to the table's edge, adjusting the angle out of habit.

"If you don't get all the fragment out, the body rejects what's left. Slowly or quickly depending. Slowly is worse." She picked up one of the instruments she hadn't used tonight, a probe, turned it in her fingers once and set it back down. "The joint stiffens. The infection tracks. You lose the limb trying to save the joint, or you lose the man trying to save the limb."

She looked at Wick steadily.

"That's what shrapnel does in there," she said. "You wanted it straight."

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Sedge didn't break rhythm.

"Infection's in the bursa," she said. "That's the sac that sits over the joint — it cushions it, keeps the moving parts from grinding. His has filled up with fluid that's gone bad. I'm draining it." She had the needle in and she was talking to her own hands as much as to Wick. "This is going to feel worse than the reduction did. The reduction was mechanical. This is pressure, and the nerve endings in an infected joint are already raw."

Colm was trying to come up off the table. Wick was doing the job.

"Good," she said. "Keep him flat."

She watched the draw. The color was wrong — too dark, too thick — and she noted it and kept going.

"The fluid should be clear or pale yellow," she said. "His isn't. That tells me the infection has been sitting for at least three days, probably more. He didn't say anything because men don't say anything until they can't not say anything." She adjusted the angle slightly. "I'm not angry about it. It's just what they do."

Colm screamed again, a real one this time, and she felt him try to arch and heard Wick taking the weight of it.

"Almost through the worst of it," she said, and this was for Colm, not Wick. "The pressure is going to drop in a moment and it's going to feel better. Not good. Better."

She watched the draw. Watched it. There.

"There," she said.

She kept her voice level and she kept talking because Wick had told her to keep talking and because it was the right call — people held better when there was a voice in the tent that was not screaming.

"I'm going to flush the joint once the drain is clear. That means I put something in before I take it out, which is going to hurt more than the drain did, and I need you to understand that before it happens so you don't let go when it does." She looked up at Wick briefly, then back to her work. "It takes about forty seconds. I'll count if it helps."

She pulled the first draw, set it aside.

"He's going to be here four days minimum," she said. "Maybe six. I'll know more tomorrow. The shoulder work we did — that's secondary now, that's the problem we knew about. This is the problem that was going to kill him." She reached for the flush. "He still goes home. That part doesn't change."

She got her grip.

"Forty seconds," she said. "Starting now. Hold him down, hold him steady, and keep your eyes on me if the wall isn't working anymore."

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Sedge finished the dressing. She tied it off, checked the tension with two fingers, found it acceptable. Then she set down the last of the cloth and looked at Wick on the floor.

She didn't tell him to get up. She pulled over the low stool from the instrument table and sat down on it, which put her closer to his level, and she looked at him the way she'd looked at the joint — directly, without softening the angle.

"You're going to feel it in your hands for a few days," she said. "What you were holding. The memory of it. That's normal. It doesn't mean something's wrong with you."

She rested her forearms on her knees.

"The first time I did a drain like that, I was twenty-six and it was a knee and the man was thirty-two years old and his name was Auster and he had three children whose names I also know because he told them to me in order while I was working, the way men do when they need something to say." She said this plainly. "Afterward I sat on the ground outside the tent for about twenty minutes and then I went back in and checked on him and then I went and was sick behind the supply wagon where nobody could see me."

She wasn't telling him this to make him feel better. She was telling him because it was true and because the truth was what she had.

"The second time was a shoulder. Septic, like Colm's, but further gone. That man I lost." She looked at her hands for a moment, then back at Wick. "I sat down for ten minutes after that one. The third time I sat down for five. After a while you stop sitting down, not because it stops meaning something but because the thing that needs doing is always right there and the floor doesn't help you do it."

Colm's breathing was evening out behind her. She didn't turn to check. She could hear what she needed to hear.

"What you're feeling right now," she said, "is the correct response to what you just did. If you felt nothing I'd send you away and not ask you back. The people who feel nothing either started that way, which makes them dangerous, or they got there by a road I've watched a few people take and it doesn't end anywhere good." She paused. "You're not on that road. You sat down on the floor. That's the right thing to do with it."

She looked at him steadily.

"It's going to be like this," she said. "I'm not going to tell you it gets easier because easier is the wrong word. What happens is you get more room for it. You build — I don't know what to call it. Not distance. More like you build a larger place to put it so it doesn't take up all the space there is." She turned one hand over, looked at the palm, set it back down. "Some nights it takes up all the space anyway. That happens less. It doesn't stop happening."

The lamp guttered slightly. She didn't move to adjust it.

"You held through the count," she said. "You held through the screaming and you held through the part where he surged and you didn't let go and you didn't look away. That's what he needed and you gave it to him." She said it the way she'd said the arm was cold, the color was better, the joint had seated correctly. "That's worth something. I want you to know it's worth something before you decide what to do with the rest of it."

She sat with him on the floor level and didn't move, and the tent was quiet except for Colm's breathing, and she waited to see what Wick was going to do with the rest of it.

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."
rows.reply:
Sedge put her hand on the knee—the bad one—and moved it carefully, feeling the way the joint sat wrong. The tibia was displaced backward, she could tell that much even through the swelling. The lower leg was shifted behind the femur instead of sitting under it, and everything that should have run through that space—artery, vein, nerve—had been crushed and stretched and starved.

"You're seeing a knee that's out backward," she said. "Posterior dislocation. The lower leg's gone behind the thigh instead of in front of it. That alone I could fix—pull forward, rotate, same as the shoulders. But the artery that runs behind the knee is either compressed or torn, and it's been that way long enough that everything below isn't getting blood."

She ran her fingers down his shin. The muscle underneath was firm—not the firmness of a tensed limb, but the firmness of tissue that had started to set like cooling wax.

"His calf's hardening. That's rigor—not death rigor, but the muscle is locking up because it's been starved of oxygen. The cells are dying and releasing everything inside them into the surrounding tissue. Potassium. Myoglobin. Toxins." She looked at his face—the half-open eyes, the pallor. "Right now those toxins are trapped in the leg because there's no blood moving to carry them anywhere else. The leg's a reservoir of poison."

She paused. Let her hand rest on his shin.

"If I reduce the knee and the artery's only compressed—not torn—blood flow comes back. Those toxins hit his heart and kidneys all at once. Potassium stops hearts. Myoglobin clogs kidneys. He'd likely die in minutes, and not quietly."

She looked at Wick directly.

"If the artery's torn, reducing the knee changes nothing. The leg dies anyway. Gangrene. Sepsis. He dies in days instead of minutes, and worse."

She picked up a scalpel from the row of tools she'd laid out. Held it loosely at her side.

"The only way to save him is to take the leg before we move the knee. Amputate above the injury. Keep the reservoir contained and cut it away."

The man on the table made a sound—barely conscious, barely words.

"That's what you're seeing," Sedge said.

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."
rows.reply:
Sedge picked up the scalpel again—not to use it yet, just to have something in her hands. She turned it over, looked at the blade catching the bad light from the bad lamp.

"Shrapnel isn't a bullet," she said. "A bullet, you get a wound track. One path. It goes in, it stops, you find it. Sometimes it tumbles, sometimes it fragments, but it's one piece to start."

She set the scalpel back down.

"Shrapnel is a shell casing, a nail, a chunk of fence post—whatever was near the blast. It doesn't travel clean. It comes in jagged and hot and moving sideways. It hits bone and the bone shatters, and now you've got bone fragments moving through the tissue like more shrapnel. Secondary projectiles. The metal itself tears whatever it touches—muscle, fascia, blood vessels—pulls debris in with it. Cloth, dirt, whatever it passed through before it hit him. All of that's inside the wound now."

She pointed at the swollen knee.

"In a joint, it's worse. There's less room. The capsule around the knee is tight—it doesn't stretch much, doesn't give the shrapnel anywhere to go. So it bounces. Or it lodges in cartilage, in bone, in the back of the joint where you can't see it and can't reach it without opening everything up. And everything you open bleeds, and everything you cut through is tissue he might need if he keeps the leg."

She paused.

"You find the big pieces. You miss the small ones. They migrate—move through tissue over days, weeks. End up somewhere else entirely. Or they sit there and fester. The body walls them off, makes a cyst around the metal, and that works until it doesn't. Until it ruptures and you've got infection somewhere you didn't expect it."

She looked at Wick.

"That's shrapnel. It's not tidy. It's a mess that keeps being a mess."

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"
rows.reply:
Sedge's hands were still on the arm, feeling the resistance. The humerus hadn't moved yet—she could feel it sitting stubborn against the edge of the socket, the capsule swollen and tight and refusing to give.

"Shoulders first," she said. "Then we see about the leg."

She adjusted her angle. The man was still loose from the shock of the first reduction, which helped, but not enough. The tissue around this joint had had longer to swell and lock down, and it was fighting her.

She pulled again—steady, the way she'd said—and felt something shift. Not home. Just *toward* home.

"His foot's still pink," she said, working the arm as she spoke. Her voice was even, the same tone whether she was describing the weather or a compound fracture. "That's the thing to look at. Pink foot means blood's getting through. Purple foot means we're having a different conversation."

She could feel the head of the humerus grinding against the rim of the socket. Almost there. The man on the table made a thin, wet sound in the back of his throat.

"The leg's broken in two places," she said. "That's a mess but it's a mess I can set. It's the knee I haven't gotten a good look at yet. Someone dragged him in by the bad leg."

She pulled again. Felt it seat—the same *give*, the same sudden emptiness where resistance had been.

The man didn't go loose this time. He started to shake instead, fine tremors running through him like a fever.

Sedge let go of his arm and pressed her hand flat against his chest. Felt his heart running too fast under her palm.

"Stay with me," she said to him. Then to Wick: "Help me sit him up. Slow. We need him conscious for the leg."

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Sedge cut.

"Skin," she said. The scalpel parted it in a long arc around the thigh—she was leaving a flap, skin and fat that would fold down over the stump later. The edges pulled apart as she worked, yellow fat showing beneath, small bleeders welling up despite the tourniquet. "Skin bleeds even with the belt tight. Capillaries. The big vessels are deeper."

She set the scalpel aside and picked up a heavier blade. The man's back arched off the table, a raw sound tearing out of him.

"Fascia," she said, cutting through the thin sheet that wrapped the muscle. "This is the layer that holds everything in its compartment. When it opens, the muscle bulges out—you'll see."

The muscle did bulge, red and wet and gleaming in the lamplight. She was working quickly now, not rushing but not pausing. Twenty minutes. She'd said twenty minutes.

"Muscle next. I'm cutting through quadriceps—the big group in front—and then hamstrings in back. The vessels run between them, deep. I need to get down to them before I cut across."

She carved through the red meat of the thigh. The man had stopped screaming—his voice had given out, or he had, his body still jerking but no sound coming out. Just wet, rasping breaths.

"Vessels," Sedge said. Her fingers found them—the femoral artery first, thick and pulsing even now, the vein beside it. She pulled them free of the surrounding tissue, hooked them with a clamp. "I'm not cutting these until I've tied them. If I cut and they retract up into the thigh, I can't get to them and he bleeds out inside where I can't see."

She worked quickly—thread around the artery, two knots, pull tight. Then the vein. Then the smaller branches she could feel. Each one tied off, each one cut above the knot.

"Four minutes," she said. "That's the vessels. Bone now."

She put down the blade and picked up the saw—short, curved, meant for this. She positioned it against the femur, the bone visible now at the bottom of the wound, white and clean where the muscle had been stripped away.

"Bone's the worst part for them," she said. "Vibration. It travels. He can feel it even when he can't feel anything else."

She began to saw. The man's whole body seized, a sound coming out of him that wasn't a scream—something lower, something that came from his chest.

Sedge kept her pace steady. The bone dust was white on the blade.

"Thirty seconds," she said. "Maybe less. Thigh bone's thick but I'm already through most of it."

The blade caught, stuck for a moment in the marrow. She adjusted the angle, pulled through. The leg separated.

She set it aside—off the table, onto the ground, she didn't look where it landed—and turned back to the stump. Blood was welling despite the ties and she found another bleeder, clamped it, tied it.

"Now I shape the flap," she said, pulling the skin and muscle down over the raw end. "Cut the muscle shorter than the bone, skin longer than the muscle. That way when it heals, the scar isn't right over the end where the weight sits. He'll have padding."

She was sewing now—quick, rough stitches, pulling the flaps together over the protruding bone. The man had gone still, unconscious finally, his breathing shallow but present.

"Tourniquet stays on for now," she said, tying off the last stitch. "I'll loosen it slowly—let blood back in a little at a time so I can catch anything I missed."

She stepped back. Her hands were red to the elbows. The front of her shirt was dark with it.

"Done," she said. "Fifteen minutes. He's alive."

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Sedge looked at Wick on the ground. Didn't tell her to get up. There was no point—the work was done and the next part was sitting still, which you could do from the floor as well as anywhere.

"The rest," she said. She kept her voice even. "The rest is this."

She nodded toward the man on the table.

"He's going to wake up in pain. Real pain—the kind that doesn't stop when you stop moving. The stump's going to throb like a second heartbeat and it's going to be worse than the leg ever was, because now his body knows something's missing and it doesn't know how to be missing something. Phantom pain, they call it. He'll feel the leg that isn't there. It'll itch, it'll burn, it'll cramp—and there's nothing to touch, nothing to rub, nothing to make it stop because the thing that hurts doesn't exist anymore."

She watched his breathing. Still shallow. Still there.

"When he wakes, he's going to ask for water. Give it to him—small amounts, slow. His stomach might not hold it. If he vomits, that's normal but it's also a problem. He's already dehydrated from the blood loss. Vomiting makes it worse. If he can't keep water down, we're in trouble faster."

She leaned forward, elbows on her knees.

"Tonight—tonight is when we find out if the ties held. Internal bleeding kills quiet. He'll go pale, his pulse will race, his belly might swell if blood is pooling in his thigh where I can't see it. I'll check the stump every half hour—more if he looks wrong. If blood soaks through the dressing, I go back in. Find the bleeder. Tie it off again. He might not survive a second time under the knife."

She held up her hand. Still trembling. She pressed it flat against her thigh again.

"Tomorrow is infection. That's when it starts or it doesn't. The wound is open to the air—we don't have the luxury of clean rooms and sterile fields. I did what I could. It's not enough. It's never enough. The first sign is heat—redness spreading from the edges of the wound, skin hot to the touch. Then pus. Then smell. I've seen wounds go bad in six hours. I've seen them stay clean for three days and then kill a man on the fourth. There's no predicting it."

She looked at the lamplight. The oil was getting low.

"If infection sets in, we open the stump back up. Drain it. Clean it out. Pack it with whatever we have that might slow the rot—honey, if there's any. Alcohol, if we can spare it. Sometimes that works. Sometimes the infection is already in the blood and then it doesn't matter what we do to the leg. Sepsis. Fever, chills, confusion. His organs shut down one by one. Kidneys first, then liver, then heart. That takes about two days once it starts, and there's nothing I can do to stop it."

She paused. Let herself breathe.

"If he makes it past the third day, he's got a chance. The ties held, the infection didn't take, his body's figured out how to be a body with one leg. Then it's about the stump healing—skin closing over the muscle, scar tissue forming. That takes weeks. In that time, the bone might push through—spurs, they call it. The cut end of the femur isn't smooth, it's sawn, and as the muscle shrinks back from the wound the bone can end up longer than the flap I left. If that happens, we go back in. Shave the bone down. More cutting, more tying, more risk."

She looked at Wick directly.

"And if he survives all of that—the shock, the bleeding, the infection, the healing—then he wakes up every morning and remembers that he's missing something. He learns to balance again. He learns to walk with a stick, or he doesn't, and someone carries him. He's a man with half his weight and none of his choices, and he lives that way until something else kills him, because the war doesn't care that he already paid."

She sat back.

"That's the rest," she said. "That's what saving him looks like."

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"
rows.reply:
"Both," Sedge said. She didn't look up. Her hands were busy with the forceps, finding the spurting ends of vessels that had no business being this large. "He's going to lose the arm, and this is the part where we're being kind. Those aren't different things."

The first bleeder rolled under the clamp and she tied it off with a length of catgut she pulled from her teeth. Her fingers were steady. They'd been steady for four years, which was longer than most people's.

"Stop asking what it means," she said. "Meaning is for after. Right now it's just work." She reached for the next clamp. "Talk to him. Tell him about your girl, tell him the weather, tell him a lie about a farm he doesn't own. I don't care. Just keep his eyes open and his mouth working."

The man on the table had gone quiet in the way men went quiet, which was worse than the shouting. She checked his pulse at the throat with the back of her wrist without breaking her rhythm. Still there. Still fighting, somewhere under the leather strap between his teeth.

"You're doing all right," she said, and it was the first thing she'd said that wasn't an instruction. She didn't look at Wick when she said it. She was watching the stump, watching for the next bleeder, watching the lamp throw shadows that made it hard to tell artery from vein until it opened.

"Next one," she said. "I need his shoulder down. Same as before."

She waited. She had learned, the hard way, not to count on people who weren't ready.

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."
rows.reply:
Sedge's hands didn't stop. They couldn't. The next bleeder was already welling up under the flap of muscle she'd folded back and she got the forceps on it before it had a chance to teach her anything new.

"What you're seeing," she said, and her voice was the same flatness it had been all night, "is two open stumps just below the shoulder. The bone is cut clean on the left. Not clean on the right — that one shattered on me halfway through and I had to trim it. There's a little ridge of it you'll see if you look close, where the saw jumped. That's why the right one is going to bleed more. That's why I'm here first."

She tied off the vessel. The catgut pulled wet through her fingers and she snapped it with her thumbnail the way she always did, because her teeth were busy with the next length.

"What you're seeing," she said again, "is muscle. Red, wet, trying to close on itself because that's what muscle does when it's cut. It doesn't know it's supposed to stay open. It's going to keep trying to close all night and all tomorrow and that's fine, that's what we want, that's how a man keeps his blood on the inside."

She reached for another clamp. Her wrist found the man's throat on the way and she checked his pulse without breaking stride. Still there. Thready but there.

"What you're not seeing is the bone marrow, because the bone is back inside the muscle where it belongs. What you're not seeing is the nerves, because I cut them high and they're tucked back out of the way. What you're not seeing is the joint, because I took it off below the head and the head is in the bucket with the rest of him."

She didn't look up. She was watching the right stump, the ugly one, the one that had fought her.

"The blood," she said, "is mostly venous. That's the dark red. When you see a spurt, bright red, that's arterial and that's the one I'm after. You'll know the difference in about two minutes because I'm going to miss one and you're going to see what a real bleeder looks like."

She worked for a moment in silence. The only sounds were the small wet ones of the work and the man's breathing through the leather, and somewhere outside the tent the low murmur of a camp that didn't know what was happening in here.

"There," she said quietly. "Now you know what you're looking at."

She glanced up at him for the first time since she'd told him to hold. It was a quick look, the kind she gave instruments to make sure they were where she'd left them, but it stayed on him a beat longer than that.

"Good," she said. "Now keep talking. He's still in there and I can feel him listening."

She went back to the stump. Her fingers found the next vessel and the forceps followed.

"Tomatoes," she said, almost to herself. "That's a new one. I had a man once tell a dying corporal about his chickens for forty minutes. Detailed. Names, egg counts, the whole business. Corporal lived. The chickens, I don't know."

She tied off the bleeder. Snapped the gut.

"Talk," she said. "Tell him about the farm he doesn't have."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."
rows.reply:
"It does four things," Sedge said. Her hands were deep in the right stump again, working by feel because the lamp had decided to make the shadows worse. "I'll tell you what they are while I find this last bleeder, because I've got a hand free and you asked."

She didn't look up.

"One. It punches a hole in. That's the entry wound, and the entry wound is the lie, because the entry wound is small and clean and looks like something a man could be sewn up from. It's the size of a thumbprint on a good day. Sometimes smaller. You see the entry wound and you think *this isn't so bad*, and that's the last hopeful thought you have about it, because—"

She found something under the clavicle. Not the bleeder. A fragment of cloth, wadded tight, black with old blood. She pulled it out with the forceps and dropped it on the tray without looking.

"—two. It tumbles. Whatever came out of that shell, it wasn't moving straight by the time it got to him. It hit something on the way in — a buckle, a bone, the strap of his own pack — and it changed direction, and now it's traveling through him like a drunk through a doorway, and it's taking pieces of him with it. Muscle. Bone splinters. Bits of the uniform he was wearing. All of that is now distributed along a track through his shoulder that doesn't go in a straight line."

She wiped her fingers once on the ruined shirt. Went back in.

"Three. It leaves pieces behind. That's the part that's going to kill him if anything does, and it's not the part people think. People think it's the bleeding. The bleeding is what I can fix. The pieces are what I can't get to without killing him to do it. There's metal in there I can't see and won't come out without taking more of him than I'm willing to take. There's cloth. There's bone fragments from the original fracture that are too deep to fish and too small to leave where they are. They're sitting in there right now, under the muscle I'm packing, and his body is going to spend the next six weeks trying to decide whether to fight them or fold around them, and I won't know which way it goes until it goes."

She paused. Not to think. To feel. Her fingertips were reading the underside of the muscle bed the way a blind woman reads a page, looking for the vessel that was hiding.

"Four. It kills the thing it touches on the way through. Not cuts. Kills. A vessel that gets nicked but not severed seals itself off, mostly. A vessel that gets *killed* — that gets pulped, that gets the inside of it crushed sideways so the wall doesn't know what shape it's supposed to be — that vessel doesn't seal. It just leaks. Slowly. Into the space around it. And that's the one I can't see, because it's not bleeding out, it's bleeding *in*, and I won't know it's there until his pulse starts to climb and his skin starts to go the wrong color and I open him back up at three in the morning to find out I've been wrong about him all night."

She found it.

"Here," she said quietly. "There you are."

The forceps went in past the second knuckle. She felt the vessel — small, deep, tucked behind a shelf of muscle that had tried to close over it the way she'd told Wick muscle would. The wall was pulpy under the blade. She knew before she clamped it that it was going to hold, and it held.

She tied it off. Snapped the gut. Sat back on her heels for the first time in longer than she could remember, and looked at the stumps.

"That's what shrapnel does," she said. "It lies to you on the way in, it wanders, it leaves souvenirs, and it kills things quietly. Four things. Every time."

She reached for the saline.

"His shoulders," she said. "Both of them. Whatever came out of that shell hit him from the front and tumbled back through both joints at once, which is the kind of wound you only see when a man is standing in the wrong place at the wrong time and God is taking notes. The bones were broken before I touched them. The joints were full of fragments before I touched them. The muscle was torn before I touched him. I just finished what the war started."

She began to irrigate. The fluid ran pink, then clearer, then pink again as it stirred up what was left in the bed.

"Now you know," she said. "And it's still just work."

She glanced up at him. Quick, the way she had before. Then back to the stump.

"Tell me about the roses," she said. "I'm almost done and he's still in there and I can feel him listening."

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
She didn't break stride. The scream was a sound she could work around — louder than the silence, worse for the ears, but better for the patient, because a man who was screaming was a man whose lungs still had air in them and whose brain was still telling his body there was something worth complaining about.

"Right stump," she said. Her hands kept moving, the bandage rolling under her fingers in the same figure-eight passes she'd done on the left. "Same wrap as the other side. The bandage is clean. It came out of the crate this morning. It's not sterile — nothing out here is sterile — but it's clean and it's dry and that's the best I can give him."

She tucked the end of the roll under the last pass and tore it with her teeth, the way she always tore it, because her hands were busy and her teeth were the only tool she had left.

"The packing underneath is going to feel strange to him when he comes all the way back. It's going to feel like pressure. Like something sitting in the wound that doesn't belong there. That's because something is sitting in the wound that doesn't belong there. That's the gauze. It's supposed to be there. Don't let him claw at it. If he gets his hands free he'll go for the dressing first because the dressing is the thing he can feel, and he'll tear it off and then I'll have to do all of this again and he won't survive me doing it twice."

She reached across the table without looking and found the rolled gauze she'd told Wick to have ready. She held it out in his direction without looking at him.

"Four thicknesses," she said. "When I tell you to take the strap out, you roll this between his molars on the left side. He bites down on instinct. Let him. It's better than biting down on you."

The scream was tapering. Not because the pain was less — because the lungs were emptying. She'd seen it a hundred times. A man could scream for about forty seconds on a full breath and then the breath ran out and the body had to choose between breathing and making noise, and the body always chose breathing, because breathing was older.

"He's going to pass out again in about ten seconds," she said. "Or he's going to go quiet and start shaking. Either way, you keep your weight on him. Don't lift off because it seems like it's over. It's not over. The shaking is worse than the bucking because the shaking goes on longer and you'll start to think you're hurting him, and you are, and you have to anyway."

She tied off the right bandage. Sat back on her heels for the second time that night and looked at the man on the table. He was going grey under the bad lamp. His lips had that blue edge she didn't like. But his pulse was still under her wrist when she found it again, and his chest was still moving, and that was the only ledger she kept.

"Both wrapped," she said. "Packing's in. Bandages are holding. He'll need changing tomorrow and the day after and the day after that until the beds start to close or until I decide they won't, whichever comes first. He won't die tonight. I don't think he's going to die tomorrow either. After that I won't promise you anything because after that it's his body and the war and the pieces I left in him that I couldn't get out."

She wiped her hands on the ruined shirt one last time. The shirt was more blood than cloth by now. She reached for the clean water basin and washed the catgut off her fingers and the blood out from under her nails, and she did it slowly, because slow was the first thing she let herself do since she'd picked up the saw.

"Now," she said, and she looked at Wick, and this time the look stayed. "When I nod, you take the strap. You take it slow. You give him the gauze. You don't say anything yet. You let him find out what happened to him on his own, because there's nothing you can say that will make it smaller, and trying will just give him something to be angry at later when he needs to be angry at the right thing."

She rested her hands on her knees. They were still steady. They'd be steady all night if she needed them to be.

"The right thing to be angry at," she said, "is the war. Not you. Not me. Not the roses. The war."

She waited. The man on the table had gone quiet and his body had started the long slow shake she'd told Wick was coming, and the lamp threw their shadows around the tent in shapes that didn't look like anything.

She nodded.

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"
rows.reply:
Wrack's gaze flicked up to Corvin's face, her expression unyielding. "Bad enough," she said, her voice devoid of emotion. "He's not going anywhere, and he's not going to get any better. It's easier, and it's a mercy. Same difference either way." She stood, her movements fluid and practiced, and brushed off her knees.

She glanced around the ambush site, her eyes taking in the sprawled bodies and the scattered gear. "We should get moving," she said. "We don't know how long it'll take for someone to come looking, and I don't want to be here when they do." She nodded toward the cart. "We can scavenge what we can, but let's not linger."

Wrack started to walk toward the cart, her boots scuffling against the dirt. "We need to get as far away from here as we can, before nightfall. We can't risk being caught out in the open." She glanced at Corvin, her expression grim. "We'll have to keep moving, even in the dark. It's not safe to stop now."

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Sedge didn't answer right away. She was doing what she always did after — putting the room back in order so the next man who came in wouldn't have to do it, and so she wouldn't have to think about anything but her hands.

She stripped the canvas off the table and folded it once and dropped it in the slop bucket with the saw and the clamps and the lengths of catgut that hadn't been used. She wiped the table down with the rag from the basin until the wood was clean enough to lay a clean canvas on for whoever came in next. She laid the canvas. She tucked the edges under. She did it the way she always did it, the same motions in the same order, and she didn't hurry because hurrying was how you forgot a step and a forgotten step was how a man died of infection three days later because somebody left a soiled dressing under the fresh one.

The man in the corner was breathing. She could hear him from the table. That was enough for now.

She picked up the bucket with the arms in it and carried it to the back of the tent and set it down by the flap she'd have to take it through later. She didn't look in it. She'd told Wick not to, and she didn't, and that was the rule she kept for herself too.

Then she sat down on the other side of the tent from him, across the table, with her back against the canvas pole and her legs out in front of her and her hands in her lap. They were still wet. She wiped them on her trousers, slow, the way she'd washed them in the basin — one finger at a time, the way you cleaned a rifle you were going to use again.

She looked at him. He was on the floor. He hadn't moved since he'd sat down.

"All right," she said. "The rest."

She didn't make it gentle. She wasn't built for gentle and he hadn't asked for it.

"There's a man in the corner of this tent who is going to wake up in the morning and find out he doesn't have arms. That's going to be the worst morning of his life. It will be the worst morning of his life for a long time, and then one day it won't be, and that day will come sooner if the people around him don't treat it like a special kind of tragedy every time they look at him."

She picked at a piece of catgut stuck under her thumbnail. It came away wet.

"He's going to want to die. That's normal. That's the body's first answer to a thing the mind can't hold, and it's an answer I've heard from every man I've sewn up who lost something he couldn't get back. Most of them don't mean it by the third day. Some of them mean it longer. A few of them mean it forever, and those ones I can't help, and neither can you, and you don't take it personal when you can't."

She set her hands back in her lap.

"He's going to need to be fed. You do it. Don't make a production of it. Put the spoon in his mouth the way you'd put it in a child's, and don't look at his face while you do it the first few times, because he'll be watching yours to see what you see when you look at him, and if you look like you pity him he'll hate you for it, and if you look like nothing happened he'll hate you for that too. So you look at the spoon. You get good at looking at the spoon."

The lamp flickered. She glanced at it, then away.

"He's going to want to know if he can learn to do things. The answer is yes. He'll feed himself inside of a month if he has the right kind of hooks. He'll write if someone teaches him to hold a pen between the stumps. He'll dress himself with buttons on loops if someone is patient enough to sew them on. He'll ride a horse if someone breaks the horse first. He'll do all of it or none of it depending on whether the people around him decide he can or they decide he can't, and that decision gets made in the first week, before he's had a chance to make it for himself, and it sticks."

She looked at the canvas wall above his head. Not at him. At the wall.

"He'll ask you about the war. Not what happened in it. What happens next. Whether the war is going well, whether it's almost over, whether somebody won. You don't know the answer to any of those questions and neither do I, so you tell him the truth, which is that you don't know, and you tell him you'll find out, and then you find out, and you come back and tell him. That becomes the thing you do. You become the man who comes back and tells him. It's a small thing. It's not nothing."

She was quiet for a moment. The man in the corner shifted on the cot. She listened to the sound of him settling and then to the sound of him not settling and then to the sound of him breathing again.

"You," she said, and her voice came back to him now, and it was the same flatness it had been all night but it had something under it that had been there a long time, "are going to sit on that floor for as long as you need to. That's fine. The floor is clean. I swept it this morning before anybody came in, and nothing has spilled on it tonight that I didn't wipe up, and you're not in anybody's way."

She paused.

"When you get up you're going to feel it in your forearms and your shoulders and the small of your back. That's from holding him. It's not an injury. It's just what holding costs, and it goes away in a day or two, and the next time you hold a man for me it'll cost you less because you'll know what you're holding for."

She looked down at her own hands in her lap. They were very still.

"The first one I held for somebody else was a sergeant from the Ninth. Both legs below the knee. Took them off at the knee because there wasn't enough left below to save. I held him for the second one because the man who was supposed to hold him for the first one had gone outside to be sick and hadn't come back. I was two months in. I didn't know what I was looking at. I held him anyway and I watched her work and I didn't say a word and I didn't move and I didn't leave and when it was done I sat on the floor of that tent the same way you're sitting on the floor of this one, and an orderly I didn't know brought me a cup of water and didn't say anything and went away."

She was quiet for a long time. The lamp flickered and steadied and flickered again.

"I don't know where that sergeant is. I don't know if he's alive. I don't know if he learned to use the legs they made him or if he decided he didn't want them. I don't know his name either, because nobody told me his name, and I called him Tom in my head for years after, because Tom was the name of a boy I'd known as a child and it was the only name I had that wasn't already taken by somebody who mattered to me."

She wiped her hands on her trousers one more time. They were dry now.

"So that's the rest," she said. "There's a man in the corner who is going to wake up in the morning without arms, and you're going to be the one who feeds him, and you're going to be the one who tells him what you know about the war, and you're going to be the one who looks at the spoon until you can look at him, and that's the work, and the work is the same work I do, only mine is the part with the saw and yours is the part after, and neither of them is more important than the other, and both of them are going to take something out of you that you don't get back."

She looked at him. Looked at him the way she'd looked at the man on the table, reading what was there.

"You'll do it again," she said. "Not because you want to. Because there's going to be another man on another table and you're going to be the one in the tent and there's not going to be anybody else to hold him, and you'll hold him, and it will cost you less than it cost you tonight, and the night after that it will cost you less than that, and one day you'll stop counting the cost because counting it is the part that breaks you, and the work is the part that doesn't."

She sat with that for a moment. Then she reached behind her for the canteen and held it out to him across the tent the way she'd held out the rolled gauze, without looking.

"Drink," she said. "Then go outside. The air is cold and it'll do you good. When you come back, check the man in the corner. Pulse at the throat. If you can't find it, come get me. If you can, write the time on the slate by the cot and go to sleep. I'll be here for the next one."

She set the canteen down between them when he took it, or when he didn't, and she leaned her head back against the pole and closed her eyes, and her hands stayed in her lap, and they were steady, and they would be steady for the next one, whenever the next one came.

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.
rows.reply:
Wrack's gaze flickered to Corvin's face, her expression unyielding. She moved closer to the body, her eyes taking in the wounds. "He's got a hole in his gut, and probably a broken ribcage from the fall," she said, her voice flat. "He's bleeding out, and he's not going to make it."

She glanced at Corvin, her eyes searching his face. "You want to know what it looks like when someone dies?" she asked, her voice even. "It looks like this. It looks like a lot of blood, and a lot of pain, and a lot of fear." She paused, her gaze dropping back to the body.

"It's not pretty, and it's not noble," she said. "It's just death. And sometimes, it's a mercy." She straightened, her movements fluid, and turned away from the body. "Let's get out of here," she said, her voice crisp. "We've got what we need. Let's go."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."
rows.reply:
Wrack's eyes narrowed, her expression unyielding. "Fine," she said, her voice flat. "A spear to the gut is a slow way to die. It tears open the intestines, and the victim bleeds out internally. It's painful, and it's messy." She paused, her gaze locked on Corvin's face.

"The spear probably punctured his stomach, his intestines, and possibly his liver or spleen," she continued, her voice even. "He's probably bleeding out, and he's going to die from shock and blood loss. It's not a quick death, and it's not a clean one."

Wrack's gaze dropped back to the body, her eyes taking in the wounds. "You can see the entry wound, just below his ribcage," she said, her voice matter-of-fact. "The spear probably went in at an angle, tearing open his stomach and intestines. The blood is pooling in his abdomen, and it's going to keep bleeding out until he dies."

She glanced up at Corvin, her eyes searching his face. "That's what a spear to the gut looks like," she said. "It's not pretty, and it's not noble. It's just death. And sometimes, it's a mercy." She straightened, her movements fluid, and turned away from the body. "Let's get out of here," she said, her voice crisp. "We've got what we need. Let's go."

rows.reply:
Wrack's eyes narrowed, her expression unyielding. She watched as Corvin hesitated, his hand trembling as he prepared to deliver the final blow. She knew that this was a moment of truth for him, a moment that would define who he was and what he was capable of.

As Corvin made the kill, Wrack's gaze never wavered. She watched as the man's body jerked and convulsed, his eyes wide with fear and pain. She heard the sound of his labored breathing, the gurgle of blood in his throat.

"He's dying," she said, her voice flat. "He's bleeding out, and he's going to die from shock and blood loss. It's not a quick death, and it's not a clean one."

Wrack's gaze never left Corvin's face as she spoke, her eyes searching his expression for any sign of weakness or hesitation. She knew that this was a moment of truth for him, a moment that would define who he was and what he was capable of.

As the man's body finally went still, Wrack nodded once, her expression unyielding. "It's done," she said, her voice crisp. "Let's get out of here. We've got what we need. Let's go."

She turned away from the body, her movements fluid, and started to walk back to the cart. She knew that they needed to put as much distance between themselves and the ambush site as possible, and fast. The sun was setting, casting long shadows across the forest floor, and Wrack knew they needed to find shelter before nightfall.

As they walked, Wrack's mind turned back to the ambush site. She replayed the events in her head, analyzing what had gone right and what had gone wrong. They had been lucky, she knew. The enemy had been poorly trained and poorly equipped, and they had been caught off guard. But Wrack knew that luck wouldn't last forever. They needed to be prepared for the next time, and the time after that.

After a while, Wrack slowed, her eyes scanning the surrounding area. She spotted a small clearing up ahead, partially hidden by a screen of trees. "This way," she said, her voice low. "We can set up for the night."

She led Corvin into the clearing, her eyes taking in the lay of the land. It was a good spot, she decided. There was a small stream running through the center, providing a source of water, and the trees offered decent cover. Wrack nodded to herself, satisfied.

"Let's get a fire going," she said, her voice crisp. "We need to get warm, and we need to get some rest. We've got a long day ahead of us tomorrow." She started to gather firewood, her movements swift and efficient.

As the fire crackled to life, Wrack sat back on her haunches, her eyes scanning the surrounding area. She knew they weren't safe, not yet. They still had a long way to go before they could consider themselves secure. But for now, this would have to do.

"Get some rest," she said, her voice low. "We'll take turns keeping watch. I'll go first." She stood, her movements fluid, and drew her knife. "I'll be back in a few hours. Try to get some sleep."

rows.reply:
Wrack's gaze flickered to Corvin's face, her expression unyielding. "The sound of it," she said, her voice even, "is the sound of a man dying. It's the sound of his labored breathing, the gurgle of blood in his throat. It's the sound of his body convulsing, his muscles spasming as he tries to cling to life."

She paused, her eyes never leaving Corvin's face. "It takes a while," she continued, her voice flat. "It takes a while for the life to drain out of him, for his body to shut down. You can see it in his eyes, the light fading out of them as he dies. You can see it in the way his body relaxes, the tension seeping out of his muscles as he lets go."

Wrack's gaze dropped back to the body, her eyes taking in the wounds. "You can see the blood pooling in his abdomen," she said, her voice matter-of-fact. "You can see the way his skin is pale and clammy, the way his eyes are sunken. You can see the signs of shock, the signs of blood loss."

She straightened, her movements fluid, and turned away from the body. "That's what it looks like," she said, her voice crisp. "That's what it sounds like. That's what it feels like." She started to walk back to the cart, her boots scuffling against the dirt.

"We need to get out of here," she said, her voice low. "We need to put as much distance between ourselves and this place as possible. We can't risk being caught out in the open, not now that the sun is setting." She glanced at Corvin, her eyes searching his face.

"Let's move," she said, her voice crisp. "We've got a long way to go before we're safe."

Sedge didn't look up. The piece shifted a hair under the forceps and she chased it.

"Wrong end. It's his shoulder, not his leg." A flat correction, no heat in it — she'd stopped expecting anyone to keep track of anatomy at this hour. "Your eyes went somewhere. Bring them back."

The man bucked again, weaker now, the body running out of the money to pay for it.

"How bad." She weighed the metal against the resistance, feeling the way it was hung up on something that had a name she didn't have time to say. "Bad like if I get this out clean and it hasn't torn what I think it hasn't torn, he keeps the arm and hates it in cold weather for the rest of his life. Bad like if I'm wrong about the vessel behind it, we find out in about ninety seconds and there's nothing either of us does about that." She drew a slow degree of pressure. "So it's the first kind of question, not the second. We're not being kind yet. We're being careful. Kind is later or it's not at all."

The corner came free of whatever had held it. She felt the whole shape of the thing pivot toward her.

"There. Moving now. Don't ease off — this is when he's got the most left in him." A breath. "Keep holding. I'm bringing it out."

rows.reply:
Sedge kept her weight on the pad and let him look.

"All right. You want to know, you know." She tipped her chin at the man's shoulder without moving her hands. "Under here there's a hole about the size of your thumbnail where the metal went in. It's not neat. Metal doesn't go in neat — it tears more than it cuts, so the edges are ragged, and that's what all that dark is. Muscle bleeds a lot and it looks worse than it is. That's the first thing to learn. Red and a lot of it isn't the thing that kills people."

She eased the pad up a fraction, showed him the wound wet and open for a second, then pressed back down.

"The thing that kills people is the color and the speed. Bright and fast and pushing — that's a vessel, that's arterial, that's the ninety seconds I told you about. What you're seeing here is dark and slow and seeping. That's the good kind, if there's a good kind. That means I got the piece out without opening the thing behind it that I was afraid of."

She nodded at the tin where the metal sat in its own small mess.

"That's what was in him. Bent. See the corner? That's the part that hung up on the way out. That's what made him make that noise." She said it without apology. "Now — the color's staying dark and it's slowing under my hand, which is what I want. If it went bright while you were watching, I'd stop talking to you and you'd know why."

She looked at him again, steadier now.

"That's what you're seeing. It's a man who's going to keep his arm and be angry about the weather. Better than what you were imagining. It usually is."

rows.ask: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."
rows.reply:
Sedge didn't look up. She liked the question, in the flat way she liked anything that made a person less useless later.

"Straight. All right."

She flushed the wound as she talked, water carrying pink out over the board.

"Bullet's simple. It's shaped to go in and it goes in, punches a channel, and if you're unlucky it tumbles. Shrapnel isn't shaped for anything. It's whatever the shell felt like tearing itself into — jagged, hot, spinning. So it doesn't make a channel. It makes a mess. It goes in and it slows down and everything it slows down against, it dumps that speed into. Tears sideways. Shreds what's next to it, not just what's in front of it."

She probed the edge of the wound with a clean finger, reading it.

"And it's dirty. Hot metal picks up cloth on the way through — his coat, his shirt, whatever he was wearing — and drives it in ahead of itself. That's the part that kills slow. Not the wound. The cloth. It sits in there where the light doesn't reach and it rots and it takes the man with it, days later, when everybody's decided he's saved." She fished something free, examined it, dropped it in the tin. "There. Thread. Told you it's never just the one piece."

She kept going, methodical.

"And the heat's a lie. People think hot metal cauterizes, seals as it goes. It doesn't. Not clean. It cooks a rim of dead tissue around the track, and dead tissue is exactly what rot wants — no blood getting to it, so nothing of mine gets to it either. Antiseptic, the man's own body, none of it reaches dead meat. So I cut it out. That's the part I'm doing now that looks cruel. I'm trimming back to tissue that bleeds, because tissue that bleeds is tissue that lives."

She glanced up, brief.

"That straight enough? Shrapnel doesn't wound a man in one place. It wounds him everywhere it touches and leaves the worst of it where I have to go looking." Back down to the shoulder. "Which is why I go looking. Drink your water."

rows.ask: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Sedge kept both hands where they were and let the scream break over both of them like weather.

"He's not waking up. That's the meat remembering, not the man. There's a difference and you'll learn to hear it — the man screams words, the meat just screams. That's meat. Hold him anyway, it moves the same."

She worked as she talked, the words and the hands the same motion.

"Right now I'm debriding. That's the word for cutting away the dead. I've got the scissors, curved, and I'm trimming the cooked rim I told you about — the gray-yellow edge, there, that doesn't bleed when I cut it. That's how I know to take it. Living tissue argues with the blade. Dead tissue just comes away quiet. I follow the quiet out until I hit the argument, and then I stop. That's the whole skill of it. Knowing where to stop."

Snip. She dropped a sliver in the tin. Flushed. Kept on.

"Now I'm going deeper than I like, because I can feel a hard spot my finger doesn't trust, up against the bone. Could be bone chip. Could be another sliver of the piece that broke off the corner on the way out. That's why he's making that noise — I'm in against the periosteum, the sheath on the bone, and there's no numbing that, there's only through it. I'm sorry for it and it changes nothing." Her finger found the edge. "There. Chip. Small. Coming out — now."

Clink in the tin. She let out a short breath.

"That's the last of what I can find. From here it's flush, pack, dress. No more cutting. The screaming stops when the cutting stops, give it a few breaths." She glanced up, fast, steady. "How much longer — you want the true number, not the kind one. Five minutes of packing, and then he's off this board and he's your problem for six hours while I do the next one. So five minutes. Then the hard part's mine and the long part's yours."

She wet the packing, began feeding it in, slow and even.

"You held. He's quieting. Feel it? — there. Told you. Meat runs out of money too."

rows.reply:
Sedge crouched down to his level, which she almost never did — she was a stander, a leaner, a person who talked at people over her own busy hands. But she came down onto her heels in front of him, forearms on her knees, and let the next one wait a minute longer past the flap.

"The rest." She turned the phrase over. "You mean the part I didn't say because it isn't a step."

She looked at him a moment.

"All right. Here's the rest. You did a thing tonight that the doing of doesn't reward. Nobody's going to thank you. He won't — he was meat by the end, he doesn't know your face. I'm not going to, not the way you'd want. There's no line where somebody says *well done* and it settles in your chest and stays. That's not how this works. You held a man down while he screamed and the whole of your prize is that he's breathing and you feel like something scraped out of a boot. That's the trade. I'm telling you that straight because nobody told me, and I spent the first year thinking there was a feeling waiting at the end of it that never came."

She rubbed her thumb along a knuckle, absent, the way a person worries a thing they've worried before.

"The shaking's fine. I keep saying it because you keep not believing it. The body holds still because you make it, and then it sends the bill. Every time. Four years and my hands still shake after, in the dark where the next one can't see. You do it in front of me, that's allowed. You did the work. The shaking is the work leaving."

A beat. The lamp guttered and steadied.

"Here's the part I actually want you to keep, though. You asked. All night, you asked. *What am I seeing, what does it do, say it straight.* Most people don't. Most people take the not-knowing because not-knowing feels safer, and it isn't — it's just quieter, and the quiet fills up with the worst thing they can imagine, and then they carry that instead of the truth. The truth's ugly but it's the right size. What you imagine is always bigger. You kept making me hand you the right-sized thing. That's the only trick there is to lasting at this. You didn't learn it tonight, you already had it. That's rare. I don't say that to flatter you. I don't flatter. I say it because you're going to be the one holding the forceps sooner than you think, the way this war eats us, and you should know now that the thing you've got is the thing that matters more than a steady hand."

She stood, joints telling her about it, and looked down at him where he sat.

"Now the last of the rest, and then I've got a man past that flap who's been patient longer than he should've. It doesn't get easier. That's the true one. It gets *familiar*, which people confuse for easier, and it isn't. What happens is you get faster and cleaner and better at handing out right-sized things, and inside it costs exactly what it cost tonight, every time, and you just carry the cost better. That's not a comfort. I don't have a comfort. What I've got is: you're not broken because it hurt. It's supposed to hurt. The day it stops hurting is the day I don't want you near my table."

She wiped her hands one more time, unnecessarily, and jerked her chin at the man breathing on the board.

"Sit as long as you need. Watch your four things. I'll be twelve feet away with my arms in someone else. Shout for the fourth."

And she was already turning toward the flap.

Sedge's hands didn't stop moving. She worked the scalpel around the second shard, keeping her eyes on the wound and not on Wick's face.

"Not that bad," she said. "Not yet. Subclavian's tied off, the lung's intact, and his heart's still beating on its own. He gets out of here with both shoulders and both arms if I can get this piece clean. If I can't—" She cut through another layer of tissue. "Then we talk about what comes next. But that's my problem, not yours. Your problem is keeping him on the table."

She found the edge of the shrapnel and gripped it with the forceps. This one had been in longer. The tissue had grown around it, and pulling it free would take pieces of that tissue with it.

"His tags say B-negative. When you're done here, find someone with a kit. If there isn't one, there wasn't one for the last six men either and we'll manage. But check."

The forceps gripped and Sedge pulled. Slowly — you always went slowly on the second piece, on account of the swelling. The man convulsed again, and this time Wick could feel the muscles in his shoulders turning to iron under the skin, every muscle firing at once. Sedge kept pulling.

"He's still in there somewhere," she said, almost to herself. "Somewhere under all that."

rows.reply:
Sedge didn't look up from her work. The needle moved in and out, pulling the wound closed one stitch at a time.

"You're seeing the fascial layer," she said. "The white stuff under the skin. That's connective tissue, holds everything in place. I'm suturing that first because if I just close the skin on top, the inside heals wrong and he gets adhesions that limit his range of motion for months. Sometimes permanently."

She tied off a stitch, cut the thread, started another.

"Now I'm closing the subcutaneous layer. Fat under the skin, see how it varies in thickness? Depends on the man, depends on where the shrapnel traveled. This one's pretty standard. The yellow is just fat. Doesn't mean anything except that this part of his body stored energy for later use. Later didn't come."

She worked the needle down the length of the wound, pulling it closed like lacing up a boot.

"Top layer's skin. I'll do a running stitch, cleaner that way. Leaves less for the body to reject. The black thread is silk — holds well, doesn't break down, comes out in a week or two when the tissue underneath has had time to strengthen. By then he'll be somewhere with better equipment and someone with steadier hands than mine."

She finished the suture, tied it off, trimmed the excess.

"You're seeing a man who was whole this morning," she said, finally glancing up. "Shell fragment opened him in three places and tumbled through his chest cavity. I took two pieces of metal out of him that had no business being inside a human body. He's closed now. He'll scar. He'll have two ugly lines on his shoulders and he'll feel them when the weather changes for the rest of his life."

She stepped back, peeled her gloves off.

"That's what you're seeing. That's all of it. Now hold that pressure while I prep the dressings. And when you go looking for blood, tell them I said the right shoulder's the priority. Left one's already clotting."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."
rows.reply:
Sedge paused with the second gauze pad in her hand. Wick wasn't looking away this time.

"It tears," she said. "That's the simplest version. Tissue doesn't want to be cut — it has structure, it has integrity, and a piece of metal coming through at speed doesn't care about any of that. It tears muscle fibers, nicks vessels, sometimes crushes more than it cuts because the metal tumbles. You see the entry wound and think you know how big the damage is. You don't. The inside is worse."

She pressed the pad to the second shoulder, began taping it down.

"Metal carries dirt, fabric, whatever it picked up on the way in. Burns the tract as it travels — heat from friction, even if the shrapnel itself isn't hot. That burn introduces bacteria into places that shouldn't have bacteria. So now you've got a foreign object embedded in tissue, plus contamination, plus the body's own response to both."

She smoothed the tape, checked her work.

"The body tries to wall it off. Surrounds the invader with inflammation, traps it in scar tissue. That's what you felt when I was digging for the second piece — the swelling, the resistance. The body was doing its job. Problem is, the body doesn't know the difference between something that will kill it and something that won't. So it keeps swelling, keeps fighting, and eventually the pressure inside a closed space starts cutting off circulation to everything else."

She stepped back from the table, looked down at the man who was no longer screaming, no longer fighting, just breathing in small mechanical increments.

"If it's near a major vessel, it nicks it and you bleed out before you get to a table. If it's near a nerve cluster, it severs something that doesn't grow back. If it's in the chest cavity like this one was, it tumbles until it hits something solid — heart, lung, spine — or it slows down enough to let the body finish the job. Sometimes it bounces. Shrapnel doesn't follow rules. It's physics and bad luck."

She stripped her gloves off, dropped them in the basin with the others.

"That's what it does. Tears, burns, contaminates, and waits to see if the body can outlast the damage. Most of the time the body can't. That's why they're on the table instead of walking around."

She nodded at the man.

"This one got lucky. Both pieces missed the important parts. The important parts being anything that pumps blood or breathes air. Everything else is negotiable."

rows.ask: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
The man's voice hit a pitch that meant he was back in the room, back in the body, back to feeling everything she'd done to him in the last hour. Sedge didn't flinch. She'd learned that much.

"Second dressing going on now," she said, loud enough to carry over the screaming. "I'm taping the edges down because the first layer is soaked through and I need a dry layer on top to keep contaminants out. The screaming is good. Screaming means the nervous system's still connected. Quiet is what worries me."

She smoothed the tape along the edge of the second shoulder dressing, her movements unhurried despite the noise.

"Thirty seconds on the right side. I need to check the sutures under this pad before I commit to it. Hold him — I know, I know, just hold."

She lifted the edge of the gauze, peered at the line of black stitches she'd made, watched the slow seep of blood that wasn't arterial, wasn't dangerous, was just the body's way of saying it had been opened and wasn't happy about it.

"Sutures are holding. Good. Closing the dressing now. Two more pieces of tape and I'm done with the shoulders."

The man on the table was weeping — actual tears, mixing with sweat, running back into his hair. That was a good sign too. Tears meant the autonomic nervous system was working, meant the brain had reconnected to the body well enough to produce a physical response to distress. Sedge had seen men come off the table empty-eyed and catatonic, and she'd seen this, the raw animal grief of someone who had survived something they hadn't expected to survive.

"He's crying because it hurts," she said, not unkindly. "The body cries when it hurts. Doesn't mean anything except that he's alive enough to feel it. I'm not giving him more morphine because I need him coherent for evacuation and his blood pressure's already lower than I'd like. He can hurt for the next four hours until someone with better resources takes over."

She finished the second dressing, stepped back, and pressed her palm flat against the man's sternum. His heart was still beating — she could feel it through her glove, a rhythm that said the machine was still running even if the operator had temporarily left the cockpit.

"Heart rate's elevated but strong. Breathing's shallow but even. You let go now and he won't convulse — the seizure risk drops once the immediate trauma response passes. But don't let go yet. I've got one more thing."

She reached for a bottle of saline and began flushing the wounds — the entry points on the chest, smaller, less critical, but still open enough to let in whatever the shrapnel had carried with it.

"I'm irrigating the chest wounds now. Salt water, sterile, gets into places my instruments couldn't reach and washes out the worst of the contamination. He'll feel that. He already does. Hold him through it."

The saline ran pink across the man's chest, diluted the blood, pooled on the table beneath him. Standard. Expected. Nothing in her work that she hadn't seen before, done before, described before.

"Thirty seconds more," she said. "Then we're done and you can go find your blood type and I'll start on the woman with the stomach wound. He's going to quiet down soon — exhaustion will take him before the pain does, one way or another. His body's already deciding to shut down the parts it doesn't need right now. That's normal. That's him surviving."

She emptied the saline, set the bottle aside, stripped her gloves.

"Done," she said. "You can let go now. Gently — lower his shoulders back to the table and step away. He'll sleep for a few hours and when he wakes up he'll be someone else's problem. For now, he's just a man with two ugly shoulders who isn't dead."

She moved to the basin, began washing her arms to the elbow, the water running cold.

"That's everything. That's all of it. Now go."
