rows.ask: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"
rows.reply:
"He’s not going to die of a pair of bad shoulders, Wick, and he’s keeping his legs," Sedge said, her voice flat and even as she reached for the boy’s right wrist. "But if we leave this one out, he won't be able to feed himself with his right hand, let alone hold a pike. He'll be a cripple by winter, and the army doesn't feed cripples."

She didn't look up to see if her words registered. She was already examining the right shoulder. It didn't look like the left one; instead of a bulging lump in the front, the front of the shoulder was hollowed out, flat as a board, while the back of the joint was swollen and deformed. 

"A posterior dislocation is stubborn," she explained, her fingers digging into the boy's cool, sweaty flesh to find the landmarks. "The head of the arm bone is hooked right behind the rear rim of the socket. If I just pull straight back, I’ll chip the bone or tear the rotator cuff to ribbons. We have to unlock it first."

She took the boy's right wrist in both of her hands, bending his elbow to a right angle. 

"I need you to shift," she ordered Wick. "Get around to his left side, reach across his chest, and get your palms behind his right shoulder blade. The scapula. When I start to pull down toward his hips, you are going to push that shoulder blade forward, toward me. We have to lever the ball out from behind the socket before it can slip back in."

She waited a beat for Wick to move, her boots digging into the dirt floor of the tent for traction. The boy on the table groaned, a low, bubbling sound in the back of his throat as consciousness flickered back toward the surface.

"Do it now, before he wakes up enough to fight us again," Sedge said. "Once you're in place, don't just lean. Push like you're trying to shove his shoulder blade right through his chest."

rows.ask: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."
rows.reply:
Sedge shook out the long strip of coarse linen, her fingers moving with the steady, unthinking rhythm of a woman who had tied the same knot ten thousand times. She looked from the bandage to the boy's bare, bruised torso, then up at Wick.

"You're seeing a pair of pockets that have been stretched out until they're loose as old sacks," Sedge said, her voice flat and instructional. She pointed a blunt, dirt-rimmed finger at the boy’s right shoulder. Already, the skin there was beginning to puff up, turning a dull, angry plum color under the greasy lantern light. 

"The ball at the top of the arm bone belongs in a shallow little cup on the side of his shoulder blade. It’s not a deep socket like the hip. It’s barely a saucer. The only thing keeping the arm attached to the trunk is a sleeve of tough, fibrous tissue—the capsule—and a few bands of muscle. When we pulled those bones back into place, we didn't heal them. We just put them back in the starting line."

She reached down, taking the boy's limp right wrist and laying his forearm flat across his stomach. 

"Right now, that fibrous sleeve is stretched thin and torn in places. It's wet paper. If he rolls over, or if his arm dangles off the edge of this table, the weight of the limb alone will pull the ball right back out of the saucer. There's nothing to stop it."

She stepped closer, holding one end of the linen band. 

"So we bind him. In an hour, his body is going to realize what's happened. It's going to flood both joints with fluid. They'll swell up until they're hard as rocks, hot to the touch, and he won't be able to move them an inch without screaming. That swelling is his body's way of casting the joint. It's ugly, it's painful, but it's the only thing that will hold the bones steady long enough for the tissue to start scarring over."

She looked up, her gray eyes fixing Wick over the boy's chest. 

"Get your hands under his left hip and his left shoulder blade. We need to tilt him toward you—just an inch or two off the wood—so I can slide the bandage under his back. Don't let his right arm drop when you do it. Keep it pinned to his ribs."

rows.reply:
Sedge didn't stop laying out instruments. Her hands kept moving — forceps, sutures, gauze, the same arrangement she used every time, muscle memory that didn't require her attention.

"The rest of what," she said. Not a question. She knew what he meant.

"Everything. What happens when we leave. What happens if he doesn't make it. What happens to us."

Sedge set down the forceps. Turned. Looked at Wick on the floor of the tent, back against the canvas, legs stretched out in front of him like a child who'd worn himself out playing.

"You want the rest of it," she said. "Alright."

She pulled a stool over and sat, not across from him but adjacent, close enough that she didn't have to raise her voice. The lamp threw her shadow across the table where the man lay breathing his shallow mechanical breath.

"When we leave, he'll wake up in pain and confusion and probably ask where he is. The answer changes depending on who answers — a field hospital, a aid station, a place where people go to not die. He'll get water if he can keep it down, broth if someone's made any, and a cot that will feel like concrete after what his body's been through. Someone will check his dressings in an hour. Someone else will check them in two. He won't remember our faces. He won't remember yours. That's normal. That's how it's supposed to work."

She interlaced her fingers, rested her hands on her knees.

"If he doesn't make it — if the subclavian clot breaks loose, or the infection takes hold, or his blood pressure drops and doesn't come back — someone will note the time. They'll write his name on a tag and tie it to his wrist. The tag goes with him to wherever they take the bodies. That's not morbid. That's administrative. Someone has to account for everyone, and the tags make sure no one gets lost."

She watched Wick's face in the lamplight. He wasn't crying. He was just sitting, breathing, being present in the way someone is present when they've used up everything they had and there's nothing left to spend.

"What happens to us is we move to the next one. The woman with the stomach wound is awake and asking questions she doesn't need answers to. I need to get her stable before she tears something open by worrying. The arm case is wrapped wrong and if I don't fix it in the next three hours he'll lose the hand. The fever case — could be nothing, could be the start of something that moves through the camp like fire through dry grass."

She leaned forward, elbows on her knees.

"That's what happens to us. We don't sleep enough and we eat when there's time and we stop thinking about the ones who came before because there's no room in your head for ghosts and live patients at the same time. You pick the live patients. Every time. You pick them until there aren't any left to pick."

She stood, walked back to the instrument table, resumed her work.

"You did something tonight you probably didn't think you could do. You held a man together while I cut him open and you didn't look away and you didn't let go. That's not nothing. That's not small. But it doesn't change anything except that this one man will wake up with two ugly shoulders instead of bleeding out on a table. The war keeps going. The bodies keep coming. We keep cleaning up the mess until we can't anymore."

She picked up the scalpel, tested its edge against her thumbnail, set it down.

"That's the rest of it, Wick. There's no meaning in it. There's no lesson. There's just the next thing that needs doing and us doing it. You can sit on that floor for five more minutes or you can get up and find me B-negative blood and help me keep three more people alive tonight. Either way, tomorrow comes and we start over."

She turned back to the table, began arranging the second set of instruments. The woman with the stomach wound had gone quiet — either sleeping or getting worse, and she wouldn't know which until she checked.

"The floor's cold," she said. "And I'm going to need you standing up when I start on the next one. Up to you how long you take to get there."

The lamp flickered. The man on the table breathed. Somewhere outside, someone was calling for a medic, voice thin and distant, one more voice in a war that had run out of voices to answer it.

She didn't flinch as the acid bit into her raw skin. She simply rubbed her hands together, the sharp smell of the vinegar briefly cutting through the heavy, greasy stench of sweat, wet wool, and old blood that filled the tent.

"You want it straight," she said, her voice flat as a plank. "Fine."

She wiped her hands on the least-stained corner of her apron, her movements methodical. 

"A sword or a pike is clean. It cuts. It divides the meat, and if you're lucky, it goes between the ribs and misses the vitals. Shrapnel isn't clean. It’s lazy, and it’s hot."

She reached down to pick up a pair of iron forceps from her tray, squinting at them in the bad light before wiping them down with a vinegar-soaked rag. 

"It’s jagged iron, usually torn off a shell casing that’s been sitting in a damp wagon for six months. When the powder goes off, those pieces don't fly straight. They spin. They tumble through the air. By the time a chunk hits a man, it isn't a blade; it’s a hammer with teeth."

She looked up at Wick, her gray eyes dead and level. 

"It doesn't slide in. It punches. It takes a patch of his dirty wool coat, his greasy shirt, the lice in his seams, and whatever mud he was lying in, and it rams the whole mess six inches deep into his thigh or his belly. If the iron doesn't kill him, the wool will. In three days, the fibers rot inside the muscle, and the leg turns green."

She set the forceps down with a dull clink. 

"And inside the meat, it doesn't stop. If it hits a bone, it doesn't chip it. The force is too high. It shatters the shaft into fifty white splinters. The bone itself becomes secondary shrapnel. The jagged little needles get driven outward by the impact, shredding the nerves and the deep arteries from the inside out. You can pull the iron out, but you’ll spend an hour fishing for the pieces of the man's own femur with your fingers, and you'll miss three of them. Then those three rot, too."

She stepped toward the tent flap, lifting the heavy, wet canvas with one shoulder to look out into the grey, drizzling dark where the next stretchers were waiting. 

"The heat of the iron cauterizes the vessels as it tears through them," she added, her voice dropping a fraction. "Which means they don't bleed out on the field. They live long enough to get to this table, with a cup of dead, black meat cooked inside their shoulder or their hip. And then I have to cut the dead meat out until I find red, healthy blood, or the gangrene takes the rest of them."

She let the canvas drop, turning back to Wick. 

"That's what it does. Now go get the bucket. The next one has a hole in his ribs the size of my fist, and I need to be able to see my own fingers inside him."

"Here’s the rest. If he survives the night without his lung filling with blood and drowning him from the inside, his body will start to heat. By tomorrow noon, he’ll have a fever that will make his skin feel like a hot brick. That’s the inflammation. She rubbed her palms together, the sharp smell of the vinegar rising between them.

If we're unlucky, the discharge will be thin, dark, and smell like a ditch at low tide. That’s the hospital gangrene. It eats the tissue faster than a dog eats grease. It turns the red muscle to grey slime, and then the slime turns black."

She looked at the lantern, her eyes flat and unblinking. 

"If that happens, there is nothing to sew. The skin goes soft. The stitches I just put in his ribs will simply tear through the rotting flesh like thread through wet bread. The wound will open back up, and he’ll lie on that straw in the corner and whistle through his chest again until his heart gives out from the strain."

rows.ask: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"
rows.reply:
Sedge had the forceps in and was already working, her wrist turned at an angle that would have looked wrong to anyone who hadn't watched her do it a hundred times. She didn't answer right away. She got her fingers around the ball first, felt it shift, felt the give of the tissue around it, and only then spoke.

"Neither, if I get it out clean and the bleeding stops when I take my hand off. Both, if I nick the artery going after it." She adjusted her grip. "So somewhere between. Ask me again in ten minutes."

The man tried to sit up. Sedge had said he would. His stomach came off the table in a slow hard arch and Wick's arms took it and held, and Sedge kept her hands exactly where they were, moving only the two fingers that mattered.

"Good. That's good holding. Don't ease."

She got the ball moving. It came up through the track slower than she wanted, catching once on something she couldn't see, and she made a small sound in her throat and worked it sideways until it came free. She dropped it in the tin dish without looking. It rang.

"Out," she said. Then, because the next part mattered more than the first: "Now we find out."

She took her hand away from the thigh. Watched. Counted, silently, the way she counted everything.

Blood welled up but it welled — it didn't jump. She let out a breath through her nose.

"Meat wound," she said. "Just meat. He keeps the leg. Probably keeps the rest of him too, if the fever doesn't get clever." She was already reaching for the needle. "You can breathe now. Don't let go yet, but you can breathe."

rows.ask: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Sedge didn't argue. She'd already turned back to the table before he finished speaking, and her hands were moving before her mouth caught up.

"He's woken because I moved him wrong when I checked the pulse. My fault. Happens." She had the apron back on, tied one-handed at the small of her back while the other hand was already at his thigh, palm flat, feeling. "Bandage is spotted, not through. Good. Stitches held. That's what the screaming's about — he's feeling the stitches pull because he's tensing the leg. Not a new wound. Just the old one talking."

She reached for the small brown bottle at the end of the row, uncorked it with her teeth, and tipped a careful measure into a tin cup with water already in it.

"Laudanum. Not enough to kill him, not enough to take the pain fully, enough to take the edge off and put him under again in about four minutes. Any more and his breathing slows past where I want it, and I've watched enough men stop breathing from too much of this to be careful with the pour." She set the bottle back. Corked it. "I'm going to get it into him now. You keep his shoulders. His head'll thrash. Turn it to the side if he vomits — he might, on this — and don't let him choke on it. That's the only new thing I'm asking of you."

She got her hand under his jaw, thumb at one hinge and fingers at the other, and pressed inward. His mouth opened. She poured. Not fast. Steady, the way you'd water something you wanted to keep alive.

"Swallow, damn you. There. There he goes."

Most of it went down. Some came back at the corner of his mouth and she wiped it with the back of her wrist and kept her hand at his jaw a moment longer to make sure he wouldn't spit the rest.

"Four minutes. Maybe three. Keep holding. He'll fight harder before he goes softer — that's the drug meeting the pain in the middle, they wrestle for a bit before one wins." She was already checking the bandage again, lifting only the top edge, peering underneath with the lamp tilted close. "Stitches are clean. Nothing weeping that shouldn't. He's just angry with what's already been done, not with anything new."

The man arched. Wick's arms took it. Sedge braced her hip against the table without thinking.

"What I'm doing now — nothing, is what I'm doing. That's the truth of it. Watching. Waiting for the drug. The worst part of this work isn't the cutting, it's the standing still while a man screams and knowing the right answer is to do nothing to him for four minutes. Everything in you says fix it. But there's nothing left to fix in this minute. Just the waiting."

She counted, silently, the way she counted everything.

"Two minutes gone. He's slowing. Hear it? The screams are coming further apart. That's the drug finding him." She adjusted her grip on his jaw, gentler now. "One more minute and he's out. Then I check the bandage properly, re-wrap if it's shifted, and we go back to sitting. That's all. No more knife tonight unless something opens under the wrap, and it won't. I'd feel it already."

She glanced up at Wick, at his white knuckles, at his face.

"You're doing it right. Keep holding. Don't ease till I say."

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."
rows.reply:
Sedge wiped her hands on the apron and then, because that was worse than nothing, on the inside of her sleeve. She didn't move to cover the leg. If he wanted to look, she'd let him look.

"All right." She set her fingertip near the wound, not on it. "This here — the long line, that's my cut. Clean edges. That's what you want. Ragged means you sawed, and sawing tears more than it opens. The stitches are close together because thigh meat pulls when he walks and I don't want it opening on him in a week."

She moved her finger.

"That darker red, deeper in — that's muscle. Healthy muscle looks like that. Wet, dark, like raw beef. If it looked grey or brown you'd be seeing something dead and we'd be having a different conversation." She indicated the paler tissue at the edge. "That yellow's fat. Some men have more, some less. Doesn't bleed much. Cuts like soft cheese."

Her finger moved again, tracking the line of something under the skin he wouldn't have picked out on his own.

"That ridge, there — that's the artery. What I was worried about. You can see how close I was working. Half an inch off and we'd be mopping the floor instead of stitching him." She said it without drama. It was just where the artery was. "The ball was sitting just past it. That's why I went slow."

She straightened, rolled her shoulder once, and reached for the strip of linen she'd laid out at the start.

"The blood on his tunic and on you — most of that's from before I started. Wounds bleed hardest in the first minutes, then they slow. What I opened bled less than what the ball did going in. Looks worse than it is because it's on cloth. Cloth wicks. Makes a spoonful look like a cup."

She began to wrap the thigh, firm, not tight.

"That's what you're seeing. Man with a hole in his leg, closed up, going to hurt like the devil for a month and then he'll walk. Nothing mysterious about any of it, once you've had your hands in a few."

She tied the bandage off and finally, briefly, allowed herself to lean her weight on the edge of the table.

"You asked the right question, by the way. Most don't. Most would rather imagine, and then they see it worse in their heads for years."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."
rows.reply:
Sedge stopped with her hand still on the apron nail. She turned, considered him for a moment — not weighing whether to tell him but whether he'd asked because he wanted to know or because he wanted to prove something. She decided it didn't matter. Either way the answer was the same.

"All right." She sat down on the stool herself, since she was going to be talking, and rolled her sleeves back down over the red at her wrists.

"A ball like the one I just took out — round, lead, slow — that's the kindest of them. It punches a hole roughly its own size, drags cloth and skin in with it, stops when it runs out of push. Meat closes up behind it more or less. That's what he had. That's why he keeps the leg."

She wiped her palm absently on her knee.

"Shrapnel's different. Shrapnel isn't shaped. It's whatever the shell was made of, torn into pieces, and every piece has edges. Some spin. Some tumble. They don't punch, they tear. A piece the size of your thumbnail goes in and it doesn't make a hole, it makes a cavity — pushes the meat aside going in and the meat doesn't spring back, it stays open, full of blood and cloth and whatever was on the ground when he fell. Grass. Dirt. Bits of the other man next to him, sometimes. All of it in there."

She kept her voice level. She was describing a road.

"And it doesn't stop where you'd think. Metal that shape hits bone and it skips. Goes sideways. I've pulled a piece out of a man's back that went in at his hip. I've pulled a piece out of a lung that went in through the arm. You can't track them by the entry. You have to feel for them, and half the time you don't find them at all, and they sit in there and fester until either the body walls them off or it doesn't."

She paused. Looked at the man on the table.

"The tearing's the worst of it, though. A ball crushes tissue. Shrapnel shreds it. Muscle doesn't knit back from shredded the way it knits back from a clean cut. What you get is a mess of scar and dead meat, and dead meat rots whether it's still attached to a living man or not. That's when I take the leg. Not because of the wound. Because of what the wound turned into three days later."

She rubbed her thumb across the pad of her forefinger, feeling for something that wasn't there.

"And it's hot. People forget that. The metal comes off the shell hot enough to cook what it touches on the way through. So you get a wound that's torn and dirty and burned, all at once. Body doesn't know which one to fight first. Usually loses."

She looked up at him.

"That straight enough?"

rows.ask: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Sedge looked at him where he'd gone down. She didn't tell him to get up. She didn't offer a hand. She'd learned early that when a man put himself on the floor after his first bad one, the floor was where he needed to be, and pulling him up before he was ready just meant he'd go down again later somewhere worse.

She moved the stool closer to him instead. Sat on it. Rested her forearms on her knees and let her hands hang between them, palms up, because they'd started to ache and open was better than closed.

"The rest." She said it slowly, like she was deciding where to start. "All right."

She looked at the lamp for a moment. Then at him.

"The rest is that you'll do this again tomorrow. Not maybe. Will. There's a push coming from the south road and I've been told to expect twenty by nightfall and it'll be forty. That's how the arithmetic runs here. Whatever they tell you, double it. Whatever you plan for, plan for twice. You'll hold another man down before this time tomorrow, and probably three more before the day after, and the one after that you'll stop counting because counting stops helping."

She rubbed at the base of her thumb with the opposite hand, working something loose in the joint.

"The rest is that the first one is the one you feel. The second one you feel less. By the tenth you're doing it the way you tie your boots, and that frightens people when it happens to them, but it shouldn't. It's the body being sensible. You can't hold twenty men down in a week and feel each one the way you felt this one. You'd stop being useful. The body knows. It turns the feeling down like a lamp wick. Doesn't turn it off — turns it down. You'll still feel them. Just quieter. And the quiet isn't the same as not caring, though it'll look like it from the outside and sometimes from the inside too."

She glanced toward the man on the table. His chest rose and fell.

"The rest is that some of them die on you. Not most. But some. And not always the ones you'd expect — the bad ones you save and the small ones you lose, and there's no lesson in it and no pattern, and if you go looking for one you'll find one that isn't there and it'll ruin you. I've watched it ruin better than me. Man who worked this tent before I did — he kept a list. Names, wounds, what he tried, what worked, what didn't. Thought he could learn his way out of losing them. Shot himself in the spring of the second year with the list in his pocket. So no lists. You do the work, and the ones who live live and the ones who don't don't, and you don't carry the ones who don't past the moment you set them down. You can't. There isn't room."

Her voice hadn't changed. She was telling him where the road was muddy.

"The rest is that you'll want to drink. I told you already. I'll tell you again because saying it once doesn't take. You'll want to drink because after a day like today your hands will still be moving when you try to sleep, and drink is the fastest thing that stops the moving. It also stops other things. Stops you being any use in the morning. Stops your judgment before it stops your hands, which is the worst order for it to stop in. I've seen medics kill men because they were drunk when the wound came in and they cut where they shouldn't have. So. Tea. Bad tea, all night if you need it. Not drink."

She paused. Looked at him properly.

"The rest is that you'll go strange. Not mad. Strange. You'll stop being able to talk to people who haven't done this. Your family, if you have one. Friends from before. They'll ask how you are and you'll open your mouth and nothing will come out that fits in the room you're in. That's normal. That's every one of us. You'll find that the only people you can talk to are the people who were in the tent with you, and even then not about the tent. About other things. The weather. Card games. You'll sit next to a man who watched you hold someone's shoulders down and you won't mention it, either of you, and that not-mentioning will be the closest thing to friendship you've got for a long time. Take it. Don't ask it to be more than that. It's enough."

She was quiet a moment.

"The rest is that you'll get better at it. That's the part nobody warns you about, because it sounds like praise and it isn't. You'll get faster. You'll get calmer. You'll cut on two without being told. You'll pour laudanum without measuring because your hand knows the weight. And one day you'll do something that would have made you sick in the first month and you won't notice you did it until hours later, and when you notice you'll feel — not sick. Something worse than sick. You'll feel like you've lost track of who you were before, and you'll try to find him, and he won't be there, and that's the day you'll want to drink most of all and you still can't."

She let out a breath.

"The rest is that some of them thank you. Not many. Most don't remember you well enough to. But some do, later, when they've healed and they come looking. And you'll think you want that, when it hasn't happened yet — you'll think a thank-you would balance some of it out. It doesn't. It puts a face on the ones who lived and the ones who didn't stay faceless, and that's a bad trade. I don't take visitors any more, if I can help it. That's not shame. That's arithmetic. The math doesn't work in favour of remembering."

She looked at her hands. Turned one over. Looked at the back of it.

"The rest is that this is work. That's the last of it and the most of it. It's not a calling and it's not a punishment and it's not making you into anything you weren't already. It's work. Somebody has to do it. Today that's us. Tomorrow probably still us. If you can hold that in your head — that it's work, the way ditch-digging is work, the way baking bread is work, and that the work matters and that's all — you'll last. If you make it more than that, if you make it holy or make it damning, you won't."

She stopped. The lamp guttered again and she reached over without looking and adjusted the wick.

"That's the rest. Or most of it. There's more but you don't need more tonight. You need water and you need to wash and you need four hours on your back before the next one comes in."

She stood up. Her knee cracked again.

"Get up when you can. No hurry. I'll take this watch. Man on the table isn't going anywhere and neither am I."

She went to the basin herself and began to wash her own hands, slow, methodical, under the nails first.

rows.ask: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"
rows.reply:
Sedge glanced up at Wick, just for a second, before returning her attention to the arm. "It's a shoulder, not a leg. He'll keep the arm if I do this right." She repositioned her hands, one on the man's wrist, the other braced against his chest. "But if the joint stays out much longer, the nerves and blood vessels get compressed. Tissue starts dying. Then it's not a shoulder anymore—it's a problem that spreads."

She began to pull, slow and steady, rotating the arm just slightly. The man's screaming had worn down to a ragged, animal keening.

"This is the part where we're being kind," she said. "But it won't feel like it to him. Ready?"

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."
rows.reply:
Sedge didn't look up from the needle, already making the first small, precise stitch through the edges of the wound. The man's breathing was ragged but steadier now, the tension draining out of him in waves.

"You're seeing a clean incision, about two inches long, just below the acromion process—that's the bony point at the top of the shoulder." She pulled the thread through, tied it off with a quick, practiced motion. "The bleeding's already slowing. That's good. Means I didn't hit anything major."

She gestured with the needle, not quite pointing. "The swelling you see there, that puffiness around the joint—that's from the dislocation. Fluid buildup, torn ligaments. It'll look worse before it looks better, but the joint's back in the socket now. That's what matters."

Another stitch. Another knot. The man had stopped keening and was just breathing now, shallow and wet.

"When you see a shoulder that's been out this long, you look for a few things. The deltoid muscle goes flat—see how his isn't rounded like it should be? That's because the head of the humerus isn't where it belongs. Or wasn't. And the arm sits wrong. Too long, turned out at a bad angle." She tied off the last stitch and reached for a bandage. "None of that now. It's back where it goes. He'll be in a sling for weeks, but he'll use it again."

She pressed the bandage into place, then finally looked up at Wick. "Second shoulder's been out since yesterday. There's more swelling. I'll have to cut deeper to release the pressure, and the reduction's going to be harder. He's tired. You're tired. But it has to be done."

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Sedge's hands didn't falter, even as the screaming started up again—weaker now, more breath than sound, but still awful. The man had come back around just as she'd begun cleaning the second wound, and she didn't waste time on comfort.

"He's awake," she said, flat and clinical. "That's the adrenaline. Body's still convinced it's dying. It's not wrong to be worried, but it's wrong about the timing."

She reached for a clean cloth—cleaner, anyway—and pressed it against the incision. "I'm packing the wound now. Not deep, just enough to keep it open. If I close it all the way, fluid builds up underneath. That's how you get an abscess. So I leave a drain, let it weep for a day or two. Looks ugly. Smells worse. But it works."

The man thrashed weakly, and she waited a beat for Wick to steady him before continuing.

"Now I'm checking the joint. Feeling for the head of the humerus in the socket." Her fingers pressed into the swollen flesh, and the man keened. "It's in. I can feel it seated. That's the good news. Bad news is the ligaments are shredded. Anterior capsule, probably the labrum too. That's the cartilage rim that keeps the joint stable. Without it, this shoulder's going to want to pop out again. Every time it does, it gets easier. More damage. Eventually it won't stay in at all."

She withdrew her fingers, wiped them on her apron, and reached for a roll of bandages.

"I'm going to immobilize it now. Sling first, then a swathe to bind it to his chest. He'll hate it. He'll want to move it, test it, prove to himself it still works. Don't let him. The muscles need time to stop spasming, and the ligaments need time to scar down. That's weeks. Months, maybe. He won't listen. They never do."

She began wrapping, her movements quick and practiced, the bandage pulling tight around the man's chest and arm.

"How much longer? I'm almost done. Two minutes, maybe three. Then we move him off this table and onto a cot. Then we watch him. Fever, check every hour. If the wounds start smelling sweet or the skin turns red and streaks, you come get me. That's infection spreading. If his fingers go cold or blue, you come get me faster. That's the artery shutting down."

She tied off the bandage and stepped back, finally still. The man's screaming had subsided into ragged, hitching breaths. His eyes were open but glassy, staring at the canvas ceiling without focus.

"There. Done. Both shoulders reduced, both incisions closed, both arms immobilized. He's stable for now. That's all I can give you. The rest is up to him."

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"
rows.reply:
Sedge gave the crooked shoulder one flat look.

“Arm,” she said. “If he loses a leg from this, I’ll be impressed.”

She shifted her grip on the wrapped wrist.

“Bad like if this stays out, he may keep the arm and lose the use of it. Bad like if there’s a break hiding under the swelling and I drag it wrong, I can make him worse. Bad like kindness is not the word for any of this.”

Her jaw set. She leaned back, putting her weight into a straight line through his arm, slow and even. No flourish. No anger. Just force applied where force had to go.

“This is repair,” she said. “Ugly repair. If I thought the kind thing was a knife, I’d say knife.”

The man’s body went rigid under the pull. His breath broke into a ragged, animal sound. Sedge kept her eyes on the shoulder, on the skin, on the way the joint resisted.

“There’s the spasm,” she said. “Shoulder’s trying to guard itself after already losing the war. Stupid thing, but bodies are mostly stupid things with opinions.”

She eased the arm a fraction outward, then held traction steady. The muscles jumped under the skin. The shoulder did not go.

“No,” she muttered. “Not that way.”

She changed the angle by inches, lowered the elbow, then drew again, patient and hard. Sweat had started down the side of her face. She ignored it.

“If it was mercy work, he’d be quiet by now,” she said. “This is the part where he gets a chance to hate us later with both hands.”

The joint shifted under her fingers, not the neat little clunk the left had given, but a thick, reluctant slide. Sedge stopped moving at once and felt with her thumb over the head of the bone.

“There,” she said. “Halfway. Don’t let him twist.”

She rotated the arm slowly inward. For one breath nothing happened.

Then the shoulder went home with a deep, ugly thunk.

Sedge froze with both hands still on the arm, listening through her fingers more than her ears. No grinding followed. No sudden slackness. The limb lay wrong from pain but not from dislocation.

“In,” she said.

She lowered the arm across the man’s chest as if setting down a loaded weapon. Then she found his pulse at the wrist.

“Still there.”

She pinched the fingers, one after another, harder than pity would have allowed. The hand twitched weakly.

“Still feels.”

Only then did she exhale.

“Bad,” she said, “but not kind yet.”

rows.ask: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Sedge looked at Wick, sitting on the packed dirt floor of the tent with their back against a supply crate, hands still trembling in their lap. She didn't tell them to get up. She didn't tell them it was fine. Instead, she pulled a wooden stool over and sat down across from them, elbows on her knees, close enough that she didn't have to raise her voice over the distant rumble of artillery.

"You want the rest," she said. "Alright."

She gestured toward the man on the table, now unconscious and swathed in bandages, his breathing finally even.

"He's going to wake up in a few hours. He's going to be confused and scared and in more pain than he's ever felt in his life. He's going to ask what happened, and he's not going to remember most of it. That's a mercy. The body does that—blacks out the worst parts. The mind, too, if you're lucky."

She wiped a smear of blood off the back of her hand, absently, like brushing away a fly.

"You're going to tell him his shoulders were dislocated. You're going to tell him we put them back. You're not going to tell him he screamed for forty minutes straight. You're not going to tell him he pissed himself on the table. He'll figure that out on his own. Let him keep whatever dignity he's got left."

She leaned back slightly, her spine cracking in the silence.

"Then the real work starts. He's going to be useless for weeks. Can't feed himself, can't dress himself, can't wipe his own ass. Someone's going to have to do all of that. If he's lucky, he's got friends in his unit who'll step up. If he's not, he's going to sit in his own filth until the infection takes him or the depression does. I've seen men survive surgery just fine and then stop eating. Stop drinking. Just... stop. Because they can't see a future where they're whole again."

She let that sit for a moment, watching Wick's face.

"He's going to hate the slings. He's going to try to take them off. He's going to swear he feels fine and he just wants to stretch, just for a minute, just to prove to himself he's not broken. You're going to have to stop him. Every time. He'll get angry. He'll call you names. He'll say you're keeping him crippled on purpose. You're going to have to let that roll off you, because he's not angry at you. He's angry at his own body for betraying him, and you're just the one standing there."

She paused, tilting her head slightly.

"And then there's the infection watch. I wasn't exaggerating about that. Fever, chills, red streaks, sweet smell—any of that, and we're cutting him open again to drain the pus. That's worse than what you just saw. The smell alone will make you gag. And if the infection hits his bloodstream, there's nothing I can do. We don't have the antibiotics for sepsis. We never do. So we'll watch him die slow, over days, while he burns up from the inside. That's the worst-case scenario. It happens more often than I'd like."

She stood up, walked over to a battered footlocker, and pulled out a canteen. She took a long drink, then offered it to Wick.

"You asked about us. About walking away." She sat back down, closer this time. "You don't walk away. You can't. Because if you walk away, he dies. Maybe not tonight, maybe not tomorrow, but eventually. Someone has to change the bandages. Someone has to check the incisions. Someone has to hold the cup to his lips so he can drink. That someone is you. That someone is me. That's the job."

She rubbed the back of her neck, a rare gesture of fatigue breaking through her usual composure.

"But here's the part nobody tells you. The part you don't figure out until you've been doing this too long." She met Wick's eyes, her gaze steady and unblinking. "You're going to carry this. Not just tonight. Not just this man. All of it. Every scream, every wound, every time you held someone down while I cut into them. It's going to sit in your chest like a rock. You're going to see his face when you close your eyes. You're going to hear the sound that joint made when it popped back in. You're going to wake up in a cold sweat six months from now because you dreamed about the smell of blood and iodine."

She leaned forward, elbows on her knees again.

"And you're going to have to find a way to live with it. Some people drink. Some people pray. Some people get hard and mean and stop feeling anything at all. I don't recommend that last one. It works, but it costs you everything else. You stop feeling the bad, sure. But you also stop feeling the good. And there is good. There are the ones who make it. The ones who walk out of this tent on their own two feet. The ones who write you letters afterward, years later, saying they're alive because of you. You have to hold onto that. You have to let it be enough."

She stood up, her joints popping, and looked down at Wick on the floor.

"That's the rest. That's all of it. It's ugly and it's heavy and it doesn't get lighter. You just get stronger. Or you don't, and you break. Either way, the war keeps going. So you decide now. You decide if you can carry this. Because if you can't, there's no shame in it. Walk away tonight. Go back to whatever you were doing before they pulled you into this tent. I won't judge you. Nobody will. But if you stay—" She gestured at the man on the table, at the blood on the floor, at the instruments laid out on the tray. "—if you stay, you're in it. All the way. No halfway. No quitting when it gets hard. Because it's always hard. That's the only thing about this job that's guaranteed."

She held out her hand, not to pull Wick up, but offering them the choice.

"So. What's it going to be?"

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."
rows.reply:
Sedge wiped her thumb clean on the edge of her apron and looked at the man as if he were a map with bad weather drawn all over it.

“You’re seeing a body after too much force went through too few joints,” she said. “Both shoulders were pulled out. They’re back in now. That does not mean fixed. It means the bones are where they’re meant to be, and everything soft around them is angry.”

She pointed with two fingers, not touching yet.

“Here. Right shoulder first. Swollen high. That bulge is bruising and torn muscle complaining. Joint capsule stretched, maybe torn. Tendons strained. Could be a chip of bone in there, but I didn’t feel grinding when it went back, so either there isn’t one or it has the manners to stay quiet.”

Her hand moved to the man’s arm.

“The arm lying across his chest is on purpose. If it hangs, the weight pulls on the shoulder. If it drifts outward, it can slide loose again. Sling keeps the elbow close and the joint lazy. Lazy is what we want.”

She touched the fingers of his right hand and pressed a nail until it paled, then let go. Color crept back.

“That is blood returning. Slow, but returning. If it stayed white or went blue, we’d worry the swelling was choking the vessels. If the hand went cold, same. If I couldn’t find the pulse here”—she tapped the wrist—“we’d stop talking and start cutting bandage, loosening anything tight, and praying to whatever useless thing was nearest.”

She pinched the pad of one finger. The hand gave its weak twitch.

“That twitch means the nerves are still carrying messages. Badly, maybe. Insulted, certainly. But carrying. If he wakes and says his hands burn, tingle, or feel full of needles, I’ll listen. If he says he feels nothing, I’ll listen harder.”

Sedge shifted to the left shoulder.

“This one went home cleaner. Less swelling. Still ugly. Do not trust the prettier wound. Pretty wounds kill from manners. But between the two, I hate the right more.”

She looked over the man’s face next.

“Pale skin. Sweat. Lips dry. That’s shock and pain. He’s not bleeding out in a grand way, but bodies don’t need a fountain to panic. Pain can make the pulse run thin. Fear too. Cold makes it worse. That’s why the blanket matters.”

She lifted the edge of it, checked that it covered his legs properly, then let it fall.

“You’re also seeing exhaustion. He shouted until he had nothing useful left to shout with. That does not mean he is safe. Quiet men die all the time. Loud men too, but quiet ones are sneakier.”

Her gaze moved down over the abrasions, the torn skin at collarbone and upper arms, the grime pressed into the scrapes.

“These cuts are small, which is not the same as clean. Mud in a wound is an invitation. Fever, rot, swelling, pus. I washed what I could. I’ll wash again when he has enough sense to curse me for it. If red lines start running away from the cuts, if the skin goes hot and tight, if he shakes with chills under blankets, that is infection coming in with its boots on.”

She set the dirty rag aside and took a cleaner one.

“You’re seeing a man who survived the first trouble. That’s all. First trouble was the shoulders being out and the pain trying to drive him stupid. Next trouble is swelling. After that, fever. After that, whether the nerves forgive him.”

Sedge paused, then added, bluntly, “And whether he obeys.”

She looked back at the slings.

“If he tries to push himself up, he can throw one out again. If he rolls wrong, same. If some officer decides he can carry a pack in three days because both arms are still attached, I will break that officer’s nose with professional regret.”

She checked the pulse once more, counting silently for a few beats.

“Fast. Not worse.”

Then she leaned closer to the man’s mouth and listened to the breath.

“Breathing’s rough but not wet. That matters. If his ribs were smashed bad enough to fill his lungs, we’d hear it. If he starts coughing pink froth, that is a different nightmare. He is not doing that.”

She straightened.

“So. What you’re seeing is not a miracle and not a corpse. It is a repair held together with cloth, swelling, stubborn blood, and our attention. He keeps both arms tonight if we keep him warm, keep him still, give him water like he’s an infant and not a soldier, and watch his hands like they owe us money.”

Sedge’s eyes went back to the man’s face, where pain still moved under the skin even in near-unconsciousness.

“He will hurt when he wakes,” she said. “A lot. That will not mean we failed. It will mean his body noticed it is still alive.”

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."
rows.reply:
Sedge’s eyes moved from the man’s shoulders to the torn places in his skin, then back again.

“Shrapnel is not a knife,” she said. “A knife is polite by comparison. It goes in one line, if the hand holding it has any manners. Shrapnel is metal with no education.”

She picked up a small blackened fragment from a tray nearby, one she had dug out of someone else earlier and not yet thrown away. It was jagged, no bigger than a thumbnail.

“It enters spinning, hot sometimes, filthy always. It does not cut so much as tear and shove. Skin opens. Muscle splits. Fat bruises. Blood vessels get nicked, ripped, or pinched shut by swelling. Nerves get stretched, crushed, or sliced. Bone, if it meets bone, may chip, crack, or explode around it.”

She turned the fragment once between finger and thumb.

“And it drags the world in after it. Cloth. Mud. leather. splinters. Bits of whatever poor bastard stood near the blast. That is the part fools forget. They see a small hole and think small wound. Inside, it can be a dirty tunnel full of dead meat.”

Sedge set the shard down with a dull click.

“If it goes shallow, I wash it, cut away what won’t live, pull out what I can see and reach, and leave a drain if it needs leaking. If it goes deep, the trouble starts. Digging blind can do more harm than leaving it. Metal sitting quiet in muscle may stay there for years. Metal sitting beside a vessel, a joint, the gut, the lung, or the spine is a loaded pistol.”

She nodded toward the man on the table.

“In a shoulder, shrapnel can chew the joint surface, nick the vessels under the collarbone, bruise the nerve bundle that feeds the whole arm. A piece no wider than a fingernail can make a hand useless if it finds the right nerve. Not dramatic. Just permanent.”

Her mouth tightened.

“Blast does its own work too. Even if the metal misses, the force can dislocate joints, tear ligaments, burst eardrums, bruise lungs. Men come in proud because they are not leaking much, then cough pink foam an hour later because the inside of the chest took the blow instead.”

She wiped her fingers on a rag.

“So straight: shrapnel makes holes that lie. The outside may look like a puncture. Inside may be torn muscle, clotted blood, dirt, dead tissue, and metal waiting to shift. Infection loves it. Fever loves it. Rot loves it. I do not.”

Sedge looked back at the patient’s hands, checking color by habit.

“If the fragment is easy, I take it. If taking it means I cut through something he needs more than he needs my pride, I leave it and watch him like a debt collector. Pain, heat, swelling, stink, pus, red streaks, numbness, weakness, fever. Those tell me whether the body is winning or the dirt is.”

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Sedge’s head snapped to the shoulders first, not the mouth.

“Good,” she said, though there was nothing kind in it. “He has air. Now I find out whether he has ruined anything.”

She put one hand flat above the man’s breastbone, not pressing hard, only feeling the lift and fall under the screaming. Her other hand went to the right wrist.

“First thing: I am not cleaning while he thrashes. I am checking whether the screaming means pain, panic, or a joint out again.”

Her fingers found the pulse.

“Fast. Faster than I like. Still regular enough. That says pain and fear more than bleeding out. If it went thready and weak, if his skin went colder, if his eyes rolled and stayed rolled, we would be having a different conversation.”

She leaned over the man’s face.

“Shoulders are back in,” she told him, hard and plain. “Do not move them. You are in the aid tent. You are not under fire. You are not dying this minute. Waste the noise if you must, but keep the arms still.”

The man screamed again, hoarse now, torn at the edges. His heels scraped against the table.

Sedge did not flinch.

“Now the hands.”

She pressed the nail of his right thumb until it blanched, then let go. The color returned slowly.

“Right hand has blood. Slow, but there. I am checking because swelling after a dislocation can choke the vessels. If that happens, the hand goes pale, blue, cold, or stupid. This one is still answering.”

She pinched the pad of his forefinger. The hand jerked.

“He feels that. Nerves still carrying. That is not comfort. That is information.”

She crossed to the left without haste, because haste made hands clumsy. Same nail press. Same pinch. Same watch.

“Left is better. Warmer. Color comes back faster. He will not thank us for that tonight. He may thank us later if he has manners and memory.”

The man tried to twist his head away. Sedge caught his jaw, turned his face just enough to look at his pupils, then let go.

“He is awake enough to suffer. Not awake enough to reason with. That is common. Pain drags the mind up before sense gets its boots on.”

She took the slings between finger and thumb and checked the knots.

“Now I am making sure the bindings did not shift. The right arm stays across the chest. Elbow tucked. Wrist supported. If the elbow drops, the shoulder takes the pull. If the arm swings outward, it can come out again. It has already had one foolish adventure tonight.”

She slid two fingers beneath the cloth at his neck, then beneath the sling near the wrist.

“Not too tight. I can fit fingers under. Skin not pinched. No blue hand. That means I leave it alone. Pain alone does not earn him loose bandages.”

She looked at the raw scrapes across his upper arm and collarbone, then reached for the boiled water again.

“Now I keep cleaning. This will hurt. I am not doing it because I enjoy noise. I take no pleasure in this. I am doing it because dirt left in skin becomes fever, and fever kills men who were proud of surviving the first thing.”

She poured water over the rag, wrung it once, and pressed it to the torn skin.

The man’s scream broke into a choked curse.

“Yes,” Sedge said. “That is the part where water finds open flesh. It feels worse than it is. The wound is shallow. The filth is not.”

She wiped in short strokes away from the wound, not back into it.

“I am dragging mud out, not rubbing it deeper. Brown is dirt. Red is blood. Grey threads are cloth. Anything that does not belong has to leave if I can persuade it.”

She changed the rag when it smeared more than it cleaned.

“Dirty rag goes down. Cleaner rag comes up. If I use the same filthy cloth because I am tired, I might as well spit in the wound and call it medicine.”

She bent closer to a scrape near the collarbone, separating the edges with two fingers.

“This one is ragged. Not deep. No pocket I can see. No metal. No tendon showing. It will sting like sin and look dramatic, but it is not the worst thing on him.”

She rinsed again.

“How much longer? For the cleaning, a few minutes if he holds still enough. Longer if he fights. After that I dress the cuts. Then water if he can swallow. Then watching. The watching lasts all night.”

Another hoarse shout tore out of the man as she worked grit from a crease in the skin.

“There,” she said. “That was a pebble. Small bastard. Small bastards cause large infections.”

She held the speck up briefly between the rag and her thumb, then dropped it into the waste bowl.

“I am not sewing these shut. Hear that clearly. Closing dirty scrapes makes a pretty trap. I would rather have an ugly wound that drains than a neat one rotting underneath.”

She took a clean pad and laid it over the worst of the abrasions.

“Now dressing. Pad over the open skin. Not tight. Its job is to drink blood and keep the tent out of him. It is not a tourniquet. If I bind it hard, swelling has nowhere to go and the hand pays for my tidiness.”

She wrapped the bandage around the upper arm carefully, avoiding the shoulder joint and sling support.

“One turn. Flat. No wrinkles if I can help it. Wrinkles become sores. Sores become another job. Two turns. Enough to hold. Not enough to strangle.”

She tucked the end, then pressed his fingers again.

“Still pink. Still warm enough. Dressing did not steal the hand.”

The man panted now between cries, each breath ragged but moving.

“Breathing is rough from pain. I am listening for wet. Wet means blood or fluid where air should be. I do not hear wet. That is one less knife at our backs.”

She moved to the next scrape, cleaned it the same way, speaking without pause because the words had a purpose.

“This one near the left shoulder is dirt and skin torn by friction. Ground wound. It looks broad because the surface peeled. Surface wounds hurt like liars. Lots of nerves in skin. It does not mean deep damage by itself.”

She washed. Changed cloth. Washed again.

“If he faints, I keep him on the table, check breathing, check pulse, check hands. If he vomits, his head turns, not his shoulders. If his arms pull against the slings, they get held still until sense returns.”

She laid another pad.

“Almost done with the cuts. Not done with him.”

The man made a broken pleading sound. Sedge’s face did not change.

“I know,” she said to him. “Knowing still does not change the job.”

She tied the last dressing and checked both wrists again, right then left.

“Pulse at the right. Pulse at the left. Fingers answer. Color returns. Shoulders still seated by shape and by the way the arms lie. If one had come out again, the shoulder would look wrong, the arm would sit wrong, and his pain would have a new edge to it. I do not see that.”

She reached for the cup and poured a finger’s breadth of water.

“Now I see if he can swallow. Not much. A mouthful. If he gulps, he vomits. If he vomits flat on his back with both shoulders bound, he can choke like a fool after surviving like a stubborn man.”

She leaned close enough for the man to hear through his own noise.

“Water,” she said. “Small. Swallow or don’t. But don’t fight the cup.”

She wet his lips first, then gave him only a little. Most stayed in his mouth. Some went down. He coughed once but did not choke.

“Enough. That tells me he can manage a swallow, poorly. We do not reward poorly with more.”

She set the cup away from reach.

“Now pain.”

Sedge looked toward the small stoppered bottle on the crate and did not touch it at once.

“I have something that can dull the edge. Not erase it. Erasing it would mean more risk to his breathing and more foolishness when he wakes muddled. I will give enough to keep him from tearing against the slings if he stays awake and fighting. I will not drown him in mercy because the sound offends us.”

She watched the man for several breaths. His screaming had fallen into harsh, exhausted sobs, his body still tense but no longer surging as hard against restraint.

“Not yet,” she said. “He is coming down. If he climbs again, I dose him.”

She pulled the blanket higher over his legs and tucked it around his sides without disturbing the shoulders.

“Warmth now. Shock hates warmth because warmth helps blood behave. Cold makes clotting worse and turns frightened bodies stupid.”

She placed the man’s hands where they could be seen easily.

“Hands stay visible. Do not bury them under the blanket. They are the warning flags. Color, warmth, movement, feeling. Every quarter hour. More often if he changes.”

Sedge straightened, then looked over the whole of him again: face, breath, shoulders, slings, dressings, hands.

“So the count is this,” she said. “Shoulders are in. Cuts are cleaned and dressed. No sign right now of shrapnel hiding where I can find it. No sign right now of a dead hand. No wet breathing. He is in shock from pain and injury, but not falling off the edge in this breath.”

She picked up the dirty rags and dropped them into the waste pail.

“How much longer until he is safe? Wrong question. He is safer than he was. He is not safe. The next hour matters. The hour after that matters. Morning will tell us what swelling intends. Fever will tell us later whether the dirt left any friends behind.”

The man gave another weak cry, smaller now, almost swallowed by exhaustion.

Sedge looked down at him.

“That sound means he is still alive enough to hate this,” she said. “I don’t require him to be grateful. I require him to stay still.”

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Sedge did not look offended. Offense took spare blood, and nobody in the tent had any to lend it.

“It isn’t over,” she said.

She took the charcoal back long enough to mark the first strokes herself, one on the right sling, one on the left. Hard black lines on dirty cloth. Then she set it down where it could be found in bad light by a worse hand.

“This is the part that feels over because the loud work stopped. That feeling kills people.”

She crouched beside the table again, knees cracking under her. She ignored that too.

“Here is the rest.”

Sedge took the man’s right wrist between two fingers.

“Right pulse present. Fast. Thin. Not vanishing.” She moved to the left. “Left pulse present. Better. That means both arms are still getting blood. If one of these goes missing, the hand is being starved or the pressure has changed. That is not wait-and-see. That is get-me-now.”

She pressed his right thumbnail until it went pale, then released it and watched.

“Color back. Slow.” She did the same to the left. “Left faster. Write that if it changes. Not because ink saves him. Because tired minds lie. Marks don’t, unless fools make them.”

The man’s breath hitched. His face tightened, but he did not rise into another scream. Sedge watched him through the whole breath, waiting to see whether pain became motion.

It did not.

“Pain will come in waves,” she said. “First wave was the shoulders. Second was cleaning. Third will be when the swelling remembers its purpose. That may be soon. It may be in an hour. It may be when he drifts toward sleep and his body decides to report every insult at once.”

She adjusted the padding beneath the right wrist by less than an inch.

“This wrist was drooping. Droop pulls the forearm. Forearm pulls the shoulder. Shoulder complains. Complaint becomes spasm. Spasm can drag the joint wrong again if the world feels especially spiteful.”

She checked the sling knot behind his neck, then slid two fingers under it.

“Still room. Knot padded. If the cloth saws his neck raw, that becomes another wound. Another wound becomes another door. Infection likes doors.”

The lamp made a small wet pop. Sedge looked up at it.

“Lamp’s low but living. Same as him.”

She rose, crossed two steps to the crate, and sorted the supplies into a stricter order: clean cloths to the left, dirty bowl to the right, water behind the cup, charcoal in front, bottle away from careless reach. Each movement had the clipped economy of long habit.

“If he wakes with sense, he gets told the same thing every time. Shoulders back in. Arms stay still. Hands get checked. Water comes slow. If he argues, he is awake enough to be useful and stupid enough to be dangerous.”

She glanced down at the man.

“He may not remember any of this. That does not make it gentler. Pain without memory still takes its payment.”

Sedge picked up the stoppered bottle and held it to the light. The liquid inside moved dark and thick.

“This is for pain. It is not mercy in a bottle. It is a tool with teeth. Too little and it does nothing. Too much and he breathes shallow, vomits, or sleeps so hard he forgets to protect his own airway. In a proper hospital, with proper lamps and proper help, I might be kinder with it. This is not that.”

She set the bottle down again without opening it.

“He is not fighting the slings now. So I leave him with his pain. I don’t like it. I don’t enjoy it. But pain tells him not to move. Pain tells me when something changes. Silence purchased too cheaply can cost an arm.”

The man swallowed, dry and rough. His lips moved without shaping words.

Sedge leaned closer, not tenderly, just near enough to see his mouth and hear his breath.

“Not yet,” she told him. “Mouthful later. You kept the last one down badly. Badly is not an invitation.”

She wet a clean rag, squeezed it until it would not drip, and touched it to his lips. Not enough to drink. Enough to ease the cracking.

“There. That is wet, not water. Learn the difference.”

She straightened again.

“Next thing: shock. He is still in it. Pale face. Sweat. Fast pulse. Hands not cold yet, which I’ll take. Shock is the body pulling blood toward the middle and making poor decisions about the edges. We keep him warm, flat, and still. We do not lift him to prove anything. We do not sit him up to drink. We do not let him walk because he says he can.”

She pulled the blanket higher over his thighs and tucked it under the table edge so it would stay without covering his hands.

“If he shivers, more blanket. If he sweats through everything but his hands stay warm and his mind stays present, we watch. If he goes cold and clammy and his pulse gets weaker, that is the slope. You fetch me before he reaches the bottom.”

She put her hand lightly above his abdomen, then over the lower ribs, feeling the rise of breath through cloth and dirt.

“Belly soft enough. Ribs moving. No wet cough. No bubbling. No pink froth. That is what we have now. It can change. Blast injuries are liars. A man can look like he only had the sense knocked out of him, then drown from inside his chest while someone congratulates him.”

She bent her head and listened near his mouth again.

“Air in. Air out. Rough, not wet.”

Then she touched the bruising at his right shoulder, around it rather than on it.

“Swelling will grow here. It will make the shoulder look worse before it looks better. Bruising will spread down the arm and chest. Black, yellow, green, ugly as old meat. That alone does not mean rot. Heat, stink, red lines, pus, fever, worsening pulse, dead hand — those mean trouble.”

She moved to the left.

“Left will swell too. Less, I hope. Hope is not a plan. Same checks.”

The man groaned once, low in his throat.

Sedge watched his arms. They stayed where she had put them.

“Good,” she said, and the word meant only that one thing had not failed.

She took a clean cloth and wiped sweat from his temple.

“That is not comfort,” she said. “Sweat runs into eyes. Men wake blind with sweat and think the world has ended. Then they thrash. I am preventing work.”

She dropped the cloth aside and picked up the charcoal again. On a scrap of torn packaging, she wrote in blocky marks, speaking each word as she made it.

“Both shoulders reduced. Right worse. Pulses present. Movement to pain both hands. Color returns. Cuts washed. No obvious retained metal. Watch for swelling, numbness, cold hand, fever, wet breathing, vomiting.”

She pinned the scrap under the cup so it would not blow away in the tent’s damp breath.

“That is for whoever tries to relieve you and claims they were told everything. They were not. The note will shame them a little. Shame is useful if applied early.”

Sedge finally let herself sit on the edge of an overturned crate. She did not slump. She sat like a tool set down but not put away.

“The next hour goes like this,” she said. “At the first mark, hands. Right then left. Look, touch, press nail, pinch. Pulse if you can find it. Then breathing. Then face. Then bandages. Then water only if he is awake enough to ask and swallow. Then nothing. Nothing is part of it. People hate that. They start fussing. Fussing kills.”

She pointed toward the dressings.

“Do not peel those up. Blood on the outside does not mean you need to see the inside. If the pad blooms red and keeps blooming, add another over it. If blood pulses or soaks fast, call me. If it just stains and stops, mark it and leave it. Wounds prefer being left alone by amateurs and inspected by people with a reason.”

Her eyes moved to the slings.

“Do not improve my knots. Every man who has ever ruined a dressing was improving it. If a finger swells around cloth, loosen the cloth near the finger. Not the sling. If the neck knot bites, pad it. Not undo it. If he says the sling hurts, believe him and still leave it on.”

The man’s eyelids fluttered. Sedge leaned forward.

“You are in the aid tent,” she said to him, each word blunt and separate. “Both shoulders are back in. Do not move your arms. Breathe. Be angry later.”

His eyes did not focus. His mouth opened, closed, and the sound that came out was more breath than speech.

Sedge waited. When he did not surge, she sat back.

“He heard something. Maybe none of it. Still worth saying. Minds under pain catch scraps. Give them useful scraps.”

She rubbed at the heel of one hand, where traction had reddened the skin.

“Tomorrow, if he earns tomorrow properly, he wakes mean. That will be better than noble. Noble men pretend. Mean men tell you where it hurts. I’ll check the shoulders again. If the right feels loose, if the joint shifts under my hand, if he cannot lift later when he should, then something tore badly. Ligament. tendon. nerve. Maybe the rim of the socket. Some of that heals ugly. Some never does.”

She looked at the right hand.

“If the nerve bundle took insult, he may have weakness. Maybe numb over the outside of the shoulder. Maybe fingers that burn. Maybe a hand that does not grip right. Sometimes nerves sulk for days and come back. Sometimes they don’t. I will not promise him a clean arm because I put the bone back where it belonged.”

A pause. The tent canvas snapped softly in the wind.

“If infection comes, it will likely come later. Heat first. More pain after pain should be settling. Skin tight and shiny. Pus. Stink. Fever. Chills. Confusion. Red streaks running from the wounds. Then I open what needs opening, drain what needs draining, cut away what is dead, and try to keep the living parts from joining it.”

Her voice did not change on dead.

“If the joint itself gets infected, that is worse. Deep pain. Fever. Shoulder refusing any touch. Then we are in a bad room with no door. A rotten joint can ruin the whole arm. It can kill him if the blood takes the filth everywhere. That is why I washed shallow scrapes like they had insulted my family.”

She reached over and checked the right fingers again though the quarter hour had not passed.

“Still warm.”

Then the left.

“Still better.”

She let the hands rest where they could be seen.

“There is also the ordinary stupidity to guard against. He may roll in sleep. He may wake thinking he is somewhere else. He may try to scratch, piss, pray, fight, or stand. He may decide shame matters more than instruction and try to prove he is not badly hurt. Shame has killed more soldiers than enemy steel. At least steel is honest about entering the body.”

She shifted the cup farther from the table edge.

“If he needs to piss, he does it lying down, with help, and hates every breath of it. Better humiliation than shoulders out again. If he needs to vomit, head turns. If he tries to turn his whole body with the arms bound, stop him at the hip and chest. If he chokes, clear the mouth with cloth around your fingers and keep the arms still. If he bites, let him bite cloth, not you. Human mouths are filthy.”

The man’s breathing roughened for a moment. Sedge stood immediately, watched, counted, then waited until it evened.

“No wet,” she said. “Just pain catching.”

She remained standing.

“That is the rest people don’t want. It is not one brave act. It is hours of boring vigilance over a man who may be ungrateful, insensible, or foul-mouthed. It is pinching fingers while he curses you. It is denying water. It is keeping him warm while he sweats. It is calling for help early and feeling foolish rather than calling late and being correct beside a corpse.”

She took the charcoal and added another tiny note beneath the first.

“No draught given yet.”

“There,” she said. “So no one doses him twice because they like quiet.”

Her expression hardened at that thought.

“If someone comes in and tells you to give him more for mercy, ask whether they plan to breathe for him. If they do not, they can keep their mercy in their own mouth.”

The man’s eyes opened again, wider this time, wild and unfixed. His chest rose sharply.

Sedge was beside him before the breath finished.

“Stay down,” she told him. “Shoulders are in. Arms still. You are hurt, not dying. Do not spend my work.”

His jaw trembled. His hands flexed weakly inside the limits of the slings.

Sedge watched the fingers.

“Movement both sides,” she said. “Good.”

He made a raw sound.

“I know,” she said. “It hurts because the body is not dead. That is the bargain. Poor bargain, but the only one on the table.”

She did not touch his shoulders. She put one hand flat on the center of his chest until his breathing followed the pressure down by degrees.

“Breathe under my hand. In. Out. Smaller. You tear nothing by breathing. You tear plenty by fighting.”

When his eyes drifted again and the panic loosened, Sedge withdrew her hand.

“That will happen again,” she said. “Maybe ten times. Maybe more. Each time is the same. Orient him. Keep him still. Check the hands after. Panic can do injury if it gets arms involved.”

She looked toward the dark tent flap.

“And if the camp gets shelled, you put your body over his middle and keep his arms from being thrown. If fire comes through the canvas, then we move him because burning outranks shoulders. Otherwise he stays. Triage is just cruelty with arithmetic, and fire changes the sum.”

She took a breath, then another. Her face had gone grey with fatigue, but her hands stayed steady.

“The second hour is the same as the first unless it is worse. If it is better, do not trust it too much. If he sleeps, check him anyway. Sleep is not permission to stop. If he snores wet, wake me. If he cannot be roused, wake me. If his lips turn blue, wake me. If one pupil goes wide and stupid while the other behaves, wake me. I do not expect a head injury from what I saw, but expectation is not evidence.”

She touched the bruised cheekbone with the back of her fingers.

“He took some knock. Not the worst. Still, if he vomits without reason, grows confused after being clear, complains of a splitting head, or will not wake, that joins the list.”

The list had become long enough to stand in the tent like another person.

Sedge seemed to see it too and snorted once without humor.

“Yes,” she said. “It is a lot. Keeping people alive is mostly noticing all the ways they are trying not to be.”

She picked up the waterskin, weighed it, then set it down.

“Water in another few minutes if he rouses. Not before. If his tongue swells dry and he cannot drink, wet rag. If he keeps two mouthfuls down over time, good. If he vomits once, we slow. If he vomits twice, no more by mouth until I say. Vomit steals more water than it gives.”

She checked the first mark on the sling and glanced toward whatever sense of time she kept in her bones.

“Not quarter yet. Feels longer. It always does.”

The man lay shivering now, small tremors running through him.

Sedge laid another blanket over his legs and belly, carefully leaving the hands out.

“Shivering. Warm him. Do not cover the hands. Warning flags stay visible. If he complains his hands are cold while they feel warm, nerve insult. Note it. If they are cold to touch, worse. Fetch me.”

She pressed her knuckles into the small of her own back until something clicked.

“By morning, if he has no fever, hands still working, shoulders still shaped right, and breath dry, I will call him stubborn and continue. Then he gets binding for travel if travel cannot be avoided. He does not march. He does not carry. He does not get thrown in a wagon without padding. Every jolt will try to undo us.”

Her mouth twisted.

“Someone will say there are worse wounded. They will be right. That will not make his shoulders stronger.”

She went back to the crate and opened the bottle at last, only to smell it, judge it, and stopper it again.

“Still no draught. He is not quiet because he is well. He is quiet because he is spent. There is a difference. If he starts straining again, I use it. If he sleeps with decent breath, I don’t.”

The first true quarter hour arrived by Sedge’s reckoning. She took the charcoal and pointed.

“Now. First check after the first mark.”

She did it aloud.

“Right hand: visible. Pink enough. Not blue. Warm.” She pressed the nail. “Color returns slow but returns.” She pinched. The fingers twitched. “Moves to pain. Pulse present.”

She marked a second small line beside the R.

“Left hand: visible. Pink. Warmer. Nail returns faster. Moves to pain. Pulse present.”

She marked the L.

“That is how boring it should sound. If the words change, the night changes.”

She set the charcoal down again.

“There. That is the rest for now. The rest after that is doing it again. And again. And again. Until dawn or trouble.” 

Sedge looked at the man’s face, then at his hands, and her voice went a shade lower, though no softer.

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."
rows.reply:
Sedge didn't pause in her work, but something in her expression shifted—a flicker of acknowledgment, maybe even respect. Most people didn't want it straight.

"Shrapnel doesn't just cut," she said, pressing the scalpel deeper, finding the fascia. The man's screaming had gone hoarse, breaking apart into something that barely sounded human. "A bullet makes a hole. Clean entry, maybe messy exit, but it's a line. Shrapnel tears. It's irregular—jagged edges, sharp corners. When it goes in, it doesn't just push tissue aside. It rips it. Muscles, tendons, blood vessels. It chews through whatever's in its path."

She found the tight membrane and sliced. A rush of dark fluid welled up, and she wiped it away without flinching. The pressure release was visible—the swelling began to ease almost immediately.

"And it doesn't stop at the entry wound. Shrapnel fragments. A single piece can break apart inside the body. So you're not looking for one path of damage—you're looking for ten, fifteen, twenty little pieces that scattered in different directions." She set the scalpel down and reached for a pair of forceps, probing gently. "Sometimes it hits bone and the bone itself becomes shrapnel. Splinters of femur, rib, scapula—they become secondary projectiles. They do their own damage."

She found what she was looking for—a small, dark fragment she'd spotted earlier in the swelling—and pulled it out. It clinked against the metal tray. "There. That's been in there since yesterday, causing trouble. Not big enough to kill him, but big enough to keep the inflammation going."

She set the forceps aside and moved her hands into position for the reduction, one on his wrist, one braced against his chest.

"That's what shrapnel does," she said. "It turns a single injury into a dozen injuries. It hides. It makes you dig. And half the time, even when you think you've got it all, there's something left behind that'll fester and kill them slow instead of fast." She met Wick's eyes. "This one's not shrapnel, though. This is just a shoulder that's been out too long. The worst of it is already done."

She began to pull, harder than before. The man's body bucked. "Hold."
