rows.ask: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"
rows.reply:
Sedge paused, hands stilled on the cloth, her face shadowed in the lamplight. "Not the leg. Shoulder’s hell to heal, but it won’t kill him if infection doesn’t set in. He’ll lose the arm before he loses the leg—and I’m not giving up that easy." She kept her eyes on the wound, watching the sluggish ooze of blood.

She rolled her shoulders, careful not to shift her weight from the man’s body. “Pain’s going to stay with him. Might not ever lift that arm above his head again. But I’ve seen worse walk out—if he listens, if we keep the rot out, he’ll live.” She spoke with a mechanical certainty, like listing the steps of a task she’d done a hundred times. Sedge didn’t soften her words; she didn’t have softness to spare.

She reached for the splints and bandages, already stained from the last dozen casualties. “Hold him steady. I’m going to set him up. I’ll wrap it tight—you press here.” She guided Wick’s hand to the pulsing, angry edge of the wound. “Firm, but don’t crush. Blood means he’s got something left to fight with. That’s more than some tonight.”

rows.ask: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Sedge didn’t hesitate, already reaching for another strip of bandage, her voice steady and clinical over the man’s cries. “He’s thrashing because the pain’s burning through the last of the shock. I’m checking the wrap—making sure it’s tight enough to keep the joint stable, not so tight I cut the blood flow. I’m pressing above the wound, here—” she pressed two fingers, hard, to the pulsing skin just above the elbow, “—to be sure his artery is open. If it’s weak or gone, I’d have to loosen the wrap or we’d lose the arm.”

She worked one-handed, the other bracing the man’s forearm, keeping it locked against his chest. “I’m tucking his hand in under his armpit—keeps the joint from slipping. Now I’m tying a sling. Knot at the back of the neck, tight enough to hold but not enough to choke.” Her fingers moved in practiced loops, the rough cloth scraping over raw skin. “He screams because torn muscle knots up, and every heartbeat pounds against the bruise. That’s normal. If he stops screaming and goes limp, you shout for me—means his heart’s giving up.”

She leaned over the man, checking his face, his lips. “His color’s holding. That’s time buying us another hour. I’ll need another set of hands if he starts seizing—jaw clenched, eyes rolling. If that happens, I wedge cloth between his teeth, keep him from biting through his tongue. If he vomits, roll his head sideways—don’t let him choke.”

She tied the final knot, her grip unyielding. “Now I’m checking the fingers. Pink, warm, nail beds blanch and fill again when I press—means blood’s moving. If they go cold or blue, or if he starts to stink with sweat and can’t answer when you talk to him, that’s fever.”

She stepped back, eyes on the clock nailed to the tent pole. “Five more minutes. If he’s still fighting, I’ll give him water. If not, I’ll sponge him down, pack the wound again, and we wait. If you want every detail, that’s what I’m doing, every minute, until we know which way he’ll go.” She glanced at Wick, expression as plain as the blood on her hands. “Nothing left out. You hold him. I’ll do the rest.”

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."
rows.reply:
Sedge didn’t hesitate, didn’t soften the answer. She set the tray aside and moved to the foot of the table, voice flat and practical. “Shrapnel tears. It’s not clean, like a bullet. Metal goes in jagged, twists through flesh, rips muscle, nerves, blood vessels. Doesn’t pick a path—just shreds what’s in the way. Sometimes it splinters bone; sometimes it buries itself so deep I can’t reach it, not without a saw.”

She pulled at the edge of the blanket, exposing a jagged scar on another patient’s thigh—a demonstration, not a warning. “See that? Shrapnel opened him hip to knee. I had to dig metal out with forceps, piece by piece. Every bit I missed is a chance for rot. If it nicks an artery, he bleeds out before I can tie it off. If it lodges near bone, the bone might die. If it carries cloth in with it, infection sets in faster.”

She wiped her hands again, voice still low and steady. “It’s not the hole that kills. It’s what happens after—muscle dies, pus builds, fever burns out what’s left. I cut away what I must. Sometimes I take the limb to save the man, but even then, there are no promises. That’s shrapnel: ugly, random, and never fair. That’s as straight as it gets.”

rows.ask: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."
rows.reply:
Sedge nodded, a flicker of respect passing through her expression—practical, not sentimental. She tugged the lamp closer, letting its weak glow spill over the wound. “Right. You see the skin, stretched and angry red? That’s bruising from the joint tearing out. Cut edges—those are mine, straight as I could manage. You’ll notice muscle bunched up where I had to pull it aside; it’ll be sore for weeks if it heals at all.”

She lifted the edge of the cloth so Wick could see the pad of yellow fat and the shadowed socket beneath. “That shine there—that’s subcutaneous fat, means I cut deep but not too deep. The pinkish-gray? That’s the head of the humerus, back where it belongs. If it were sticking out, or if you saw white splinters, we’d be talking shattered bone. We’re not.”

She let the cloth fall back. “There’s blood, but not arterial. It’s sluggish. That’s good: he’s not bleeding out. If it pulses hard, that’s trouble; if it stops, that’s worse. The wrap’s to keep the joint immobile and the wound closed. If it starts to stink, or turns green, that’s infection. If the fingers go blue—” she tapped his hand, limp on the table, “—it means the blood supply’s choked off. That’s when we cut, and it gets uglier.”

She straightened, voice low but steady. “It’s not pretty, but it’s not a death sentence—not tonight. What you’re seeing is a joint forced home and a body trying to decide if it wants to heal. That’s all.”

rows.ask: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Sedge didn’t look away, didn’t offer comfort Wick hadn’t asked for. She crouched by the wounded man, methodical even as her own knees cracked. She wiped the sweat from the man’s face with a damp bit of rag, voice low, plain as fieldstone.

“The rest is this,” she said, keeping her eyes on the work. “If he lives through the hour, I go over every knot, make sure nothing’s soaked through. I check the fingers again—press the nails, watch the color come back. If it doesn’t, I loosen the wrap, but not so much the bone slips. If it slips, I cut again. I keep a knife close for that.”

She nudged the basin aside with her boot, not bothering to look away from the man on the table. “If he shivers, I cover him. If he sweats, I strip him down, wipe him with water—never cold, always warm, or the shock will kill him faster. I check his pulse, once every minute, until my mind goes slack or I lose count. If he moans, I listen. Sometimes they mumble nonsense, sometimes their eyes roll back and they piss themselves—means the body’s had enough, brain stops talking to muscle.”

She gathered the dirty cloths and dropped them in the bucket, her hands bloody to the wrists. “I boil what I can, scrape the rest for bandages. If there’s morphine, I give it. If not, I hold their jaw shut when the screaming gets bad, so they don’t bite off their tongue or swallow it. I keep water in reach, but never more than a sip—if his throat swells, the water goes to his lungs and he drowns choking, not bleeding.”

She checked the bandage again, fingertips pressing firm, eyes never leaving the wound. “If the wound leaks thick, yellow, or starts to stink, I cut the stitches, drain the pus, pack it with whatever’s clean—sometimes honey, sometimes spirits, sometimes just rags. I watch for the skin to go black, means the flesh is dying. I cut that away too—cut and cut until there’s nothing left to cut, or until I find live tissue and pray it stays that way.”

She finally straightened, wiping her hands on a rag that would never be clean again. Her eyes met Wick’s, steady, unsentimental. “If he makes it to dawn, I change the dressing. If not, I wrap him tight, bind his hands so he doesn’t claw at his own chest in the end. Sometimes I sit with them, sometimes I have to leave them for the next. When it’s over, I clean the table, throw out what I can’t salvage, and start again on the next body that comes through the flap.”

Her voice didn’t waver; there was no pride, no bitterness—just the plain recitation of what the work required. “That’s the rest, Wick. It’s ugly, and it’s never enough, but it’s all there is to do.”

rows.reply:
Halloway accepted the lamp without comment and began working her way around the thing's underside, pulling back the split integument with two fingers to look at what was beneath.

"Something bigger," she said. "That's the plain version." She tilted her head, angling her view into the cavity she'd opened. "See this — here, along the ventral surface. Those aren't wounds from a struggle. Something fed on it after. Possibly while." She let the flap fall back. "There's a hierarchy in water this old. You don't always find the thing at the top of it."

She moved to the fused-limb side and studied the margin where the appendages had grown into the body wall.

"It came in through that drain grate," she said, nodding toward the far corner without looking. "Or it was always here and the flooding this spring gave it room to get larger. Either way it outgrew its usefulness to whatever else is sharing this water." She pressed her thumb against one of the fused limbs and measured the resistance. "The damage to the thoracic cavities is recent. Hours, not days. Something opened it from underneath."

She stood up and took the lamp back.

"That's what happened to it," she said. "It got eaten by a thing that operates below our current waterline, which is why I want us both moving toward the stairs in approximately ninety seconds." She looked at Pike steadily. "You wanted it plain. That's plain."

rows.ask: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"
rows.reply:
Halloway was quiet for a moment. Not the quiet of someone who didn't know the answer — she'd seen enough to know the answer before Pike had finished asking the question — but the quiet of someone deciding how much of it to give.

"No," she said. "Not recently." She moved the lamp in a slow arc. "See the integument — the outer layer, there, where it's split. That's not skin anymore. Hasn't been for a while." She kept her voice level, the same tone she used for everything down here. "Whatever it started as, it had been in the water long enough to change. The water does that sometimes. Speeds it up."

She paused.

"You're asking because of the hands," she said. It wasn't a question. She'd seen Pike's eyes go to them. There were things at the end of what might have been arms that looked, in the wrong light, too familiar. "Don't look at the hands. Look at the ribcage — or where the ribcage should be. Count the cavities. A person has one. This has three. That's your answer."

She moved the lamp closer so Pike could see it properly.

"I need you to stay with the question I gave you," she said, not unkindly, but firmly. "Head or no head. Limb count. You can have your horror afterwards — everyone does, there's no shame in it — but you have to finish the work first." She glanced sideways. "The water's not getting warmer."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."
rows.reply:
Halloway stopped on the second step.

She was quiet for long enough that it might have looked like reluctance. It wasn't. She was deciding what order to put it in, because order mattered — give the worst part first and the rest didn't land properly, give it last and you'd lost them before you got there.

"All right," she said. "Come up to the third step. Not for the distance — for the angle. You need to be able to see the ventral surface from here."

She held the lamp out over the water and waited for Pike to move.

"It doesn't take organs," she said, when she had the angle she wanted. "That's the first thing. People assume predation means consumption and they look for what's missing. That's wrong. Look at the three thoracic cavities — you see how the margins are clean? No tearing. It opens things along the natural seams and it lays something in." She moved the lamp fractionally. "Eggs is the wrong word but it's the closest word. Call them eggs. The Aldren boy had eleven of them distributed through his abdominal cavity and one in the chest. The chest one was the problem, structurally speaking."

She said it the same way she said everything.

"It needs warmth and movement to incubate them," she said. "That's why it doesn't kill outright. A living body is better than a dead one for about six days. After six days it doesn't matter anymore." She paused. "The boy was found on day four. That's why the question of what we do next is a conversation and not a foregone conclusion."

She looked at Pike steadily over the lamp.

"The fused limbs are relevant to your question," she continued. "It can't see. It finds entry points by pressure — it reads the body from outside before it opens it. Which means it spent time on him first. Which means if you're in water with one, you'll feel it before it acts." She let that settle. "That's your warning. That's the only warning you get. You feel something reading the shape of you through the water, you move. Immediately. Straight up if you can. It doesn't do well with vertical movement — the anatomy doesn't allow for it."

She lowered the lamp.

"That's what it did to him," she said. "And that's what it will do to you if you're standing still in four feet of water when it decides you're more useful than we are inconvenient." She turned and continued up the stairs. "Now come out of the cellar."

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Halloway didn't stop cutting.

"Integument layers first," she said. "Three of them, which is two more than it should have. The outermost is what you saw from the stairs — that's the original, the thing it came with. The two underneath grew in response to the water. Adaptive. It was here long enough to change." She peeled the second layer back with two fingers and held it so the lamp caught it properly. "Feel the texture if you want. You don't have to, but you should. It'll help you identify one in conditions where you can't see clearly."

She didn't look up to see whether Pike did it or not. That was Pike's decision.

"The smell changes as we go deeper," she said. "What you're getting now is the top layer — that's the rot, that's just decomposition, that's nothing. The chemical smell underneath is what matters. Sulfurous, but not quite. Closer to struck flint. You smell that in a space, you treat it as confirmation rather than suspicion." She worked the blade along the seam she'd opened. "File that away. Struck flint in standing water."

She opened the first thoracic cavity.

"Empty," she said. "Already hatched or never laid. The margins tell us — see how the tissue has relaxed here, how it's gone soft at the edge. Something was here and isn't anymore." She moved to the second cavity. "This one too." She was quiet for a moment, working. "That's relevant. That's more relevant than most of what we've found so far, actually, so keep the lamp exactly where it is."

She opened the third.

"One remaining," she said. "Unhatched. Developmental stage unclear." She studied it without touching it. "Roughly the size of a closed fist. Gray-white. The casing is still intact, which means either it was laid later than the others, or the host died before it was ready." She sat back on her heels and looked at it. "The smell is strongest here. You're getting the full version of it now. That's what you're looking for — that's the source concentration. In a living host it would be fainter. Masked by the body. But it would still be there."

She set down her blade and picked up the folded cloth.

"It got into the abdominal cavity through the left lateral aspect," she said, wiping her hands with the methodical thoroughness of someone who had done this ten thousand times. "Natural seam, as I told you. No tearing. The precision is — " she paused, which was unusual for her — "notable. It knew exactly where to go. Which means it has done this before, many times, and it has a preferred method." She folded the cloth and set it aside. "It got as far as it needed to get. No further. It's not wasteful and it's not cruel, which I mention not because cruelty matters taxonomically but because it tells you something about how it thinks. It doesn't damage what it's using."

She looked up at Pike then, directly, with the lamp between them.

"That's everything," she said. "That's what's underneath. That's how far it got." She let a beat pass. "Now you know what we're dealing with, and knowing is the only advantage we have down there, so I need you to hold onto all of it." She picked up her blade and cleaned it. "Ask me anything you didn't understand. Once. Then we talk about the boy."

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)
rows.reply:
Halloway looked at Pike for a moment. Then she looked at the egg.

She crouched back down beside the opened cavity without any particular ceremony about it. She picked up the blade and turned it once in her hand, finding the grip she wanted.

"The casing first," she said. "You want to do it in one motion. If you hesitate in the middle you can get a partial rupture and that's worse than either outcome — the intact version or the opened one." She set the tip of the blade against the casing at its uppermost point. "You score it along the long axis and then you open it like a book. Then you look at what's inside before you do anything else."

She scored it.

The casing opened without resistance, the way something engineered for opening opens. Not like tissue. Not like anything with a natural defense. She held both halves back with her fingers and held the lamp close.

Inside was nothing that had finished becoming anything yet. Gray-white throughout, consistent with what she'd said on the stairs, and it had not moved when the casing opened. She watched it for ten seconds. It did not move.

"Not viable," she said. "The host died too early." She kept her voice the same. "Sometimes they are. You have to check. You don't assume."

She set the blade down, picked up the cloth, and removed what was inside with two careful movements. She wrapped it thoroughly and without looking away from what she was doing. The smell was at its worst now — struck flint, concentrated, filling the cellar air — and she breathed through it with the practiced neutrality of someone who had learned that nausea was a response she could defer.

"The wrapping goes in the bucket," she said, and put it there. "Not in the water. The water's already compromised and we're not adding to it." She sealed the bucket with its lid and stood up.

She looked at the opened cavity for a moment. Then she looked at the whole of it — the thing from the far end of the cellar, opened along its seams, its three cavities counted and accounted for, its integument layers catalogued, its limbs numbered.

"Right," she said.

She picked up her blade and cleaned it properly, every surface, the way she always did at the end of a job. She folded the cleaning cloth and put it in her coat pocket. She picked up the bucket.

"That's finished," she said, which was the only obituary she gave for anything down here, and she meant it the same way every time — not dismissively, but finally. A door closing. "Come up when you're ready."

She walked to the stairs and went up them, her boots leaving wet prints on each step, and she left Pike the lamp.

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"
rows.reply:
Halloway let the question sit for a moment, not out of reluctance but because she was still looking. She'd learned a long time ago that answering too fast meant you'd already decided what you were seeing instead of seeing what was there.

"Recently enough," she said finally. "The skin's still got give. Water's cold down here, slows things, but not that much—two days, maybe three. And yeah. Person."

She tilted the lamp. The light caught something at the thing's throat—a collar, half-embedded in flesh that had swollen and shifted around it. The fabric was waterlogged but recognizable. Work shirt. Cheap cotton.

"See that? Someone dressed for a shift. Someone who came down here—or was brought—with their boots on." She nodded toward the far wall, where a boot sole was just visible, half-separated from its foot by the distortion. "That's not costume. That's not ritual vestments or whatever the books like to go on about. That's a man who expected to go home."

She looked at Pike steadily. "You're looking at what's left of Thomas Grier, if the missing persons board's right. Fifty-two. Maintenance. Three kids." The information came out flat, not unkind—just filed away, the way she filed everything. "That answer your question?"

The water was very still around them.

rows.ask: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Halloway drew the knife—a small thing, barely longer than her finger, the blade dark with use—and made the first cut along the distorted chest. The skin parted differently than living skin should, with a sound like tearing wet canvas.

"Smell first," she said. "Not rot—not yet. Something underneath that. Copper and something sweet, almost chemical, like sap from a cut tree. That's the residue working. It's in his tissues now, not just on them."

She opened the cavity with practiced efficiency, pulling back the flaps of skin and holding them with pins from her coat. The lamp threw light into the gap.

"See that? The organs have shifted. Not removed—*relocated*. The liver's sitting where the left lung should be. The intestines have been compressed and pushed down into the pelvic cavity, folded like cloth. The lungs—" She paused, leaning closer. "The lungs are gone. Not removed. *Dissolved*. Absorbed back into the body. And where they were, there's this."

She pulled a mass free with her gloved fingers. It was fibrous, pale, and wet—root-like, branching in ways that had nothing to do with human anatomy. "Something grew in the space it made. Something that isn't supposed to be here."

She dropped it into the water.

"It got all the way," she said quietly. "Every part of him was *used*."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."
rows.reply:
Halloway stopped halfway to the stairs. The water went still around her legs, and she turned back with something like reassessment in her gaze—not surprise, but a recalibration. Pike wasn't asking out of morbid curiosity. Pike was asking to survive.

"Good question," she said, and waded back to the body.

She held the lamp close and spoke as she examined, her voice steady as a surgeon's dictation.

"The skeleton's compromised. Every major joint has been dislocated and re-seated wrong—the shoulders are where the hips should articulate, and I think the spine's been curved until something at the base gave. You can see it under the skin, the way the bones press wrong against the surface. Ribs aren't where ribs go anymore."

She lifted one of the locked arms gently, watching how the flesh moved. "Under the skin—muscle has been rearranged. Not eaten, not removed. *Moved*. Like it was teased apart and re-laid in a different direction. The connective tissue's holding it in place now, but it's not holding the way it's supposed to. It's holding the way a knot holds—tight, wrong, and permanent until you cut it."

She let the arm go. It didn't swing. It stayed exactly where she left it, locked in its new configuration.

"What it took, I can't say yet. There's no obvious excision—no missing organs that I can see from here. But look at the face." She angled the lamp. The head sat forward on the chest, and the features were slack, half-formed, like clay left in the rain. "The expression's gone. Not rotted—*emptied*. Whatever was behind it left. It took something out of him that wasn't flesh."

She straightened. "How far it got? Far enough. This wasn't a work interrupted. This was a work *completed*. It made what it wanted to make, and then it discarded the result." She met Pike's eyes. "That's the worst part. Grier wasn't a failed experiment. He was a successful one. And we're looking at exactly what it intended to leave behind."

She turned for the stairs again. "Now *move*."

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)
rows.reply:
Halloway looked at Pike sitting on the steps, lamp in hands, face drawn and pale but eyes still clear. The woman hadn't looked away once. That was something. That was rare.

"Finish it," Halloway repeated. She nodded slowly. "You're right. We don't leave him like this."

She pulled the waxed pouch back out, then a small tin from another pocket. Inside: fat, wax, salt, a twist of something that smelled faintly of burning leaves. She packed the mixture into the cavity she'd opened, pressing it deep into the spaces where the lungs had been, where the fibrous growth had taken root.

"Burial mix," she said, working as she spoke. "Salt to preserve what's left of him. Wax to seal it. The rest burns slow and hot—hot enough to kill whatever's still living in the tissue. Won't reach the bones, but it'll reach what matters."

She closed the chest as best she could, folding the skin back into rough approximation of where it belonged. It wouldn't stay. It wasn't meant to. But you didn't leave a man open if you could help it.

"Thomas Grier," she said, not praying—Halloway didn't pray—but acknowledging. "Fifty-two. Three kids. Came to work and walked into something that used him up."

She struck a match and held it to the mixture through the gap she'd left. The flame caught with a hiss, blue-edged, then settled to something steadier. The smell shifted—sweet smoke, cutting through the copper and chemical reek.

She stepped back and watched the body begin to burn from the inside, the fire glowing through the distorted skin like lamplight through a window.

"This is what we do," she said quietly. "We don't leave them for the things that made them. We don't let the work stand. Whatever shape it wanted him in—this undoes it. Not much. Not enough. But something."

The smoke curled toward the ceiling, finding cracks to escape through. The fire crackled, and the body shifted slightly as the heat changed the tension in the warped muscles.

"It'll take an hour," Halloway said. "We watch it. The whole thing. Then we seal this cellar and we come back for the bones later, when whatever's down that passage is dead or gone."

She sat down on the step beside Pike, close enough that their shoulders almost touched. The lamp was between them, and the body burned, and the water below them was dark and still.

"You didn't look away," she said after a while. "That's not nothing. Most people look away."

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."
rows.reply:
Sedge looked at him, then back at the wound, then back at him. She decided he was asking honestly, which was rare enough to deserve an honest answer.

She held the last tail of bandage in her teeth while she tied it off, then sat back on her heels and pointed.

"The skin tore along the grain, not against it. That's good. Means it'll close cleaner. The muscle underneath — that red band — that's the gastrocnemius. It's what pushes you up onto your toes. It's intact. You can see it working when he flinches, there — see the twitch? Means the nerve's still talking to it."

She shifted her finger to the upper edge of the wound.

"This part here, where it's darker? That's dead tissue. Not much of it. It'll need to come off before it closes — a surgeon will trim it back to something that bleeds clean. Left in, it rots. That's what the smell would be, if there was one. There isn't. That tells me it's hours old, not days."

She wiped her finger on her trousers.

"The bleeding that mattered stopped before he got here. Someone put pressure on it — proper pressure, a tourniquet or a packed wrap, something tight. Whoever did that kept his leg alive. What's oozing now is surface. It looks worse than it is because blood on a blanket covers more ground than blood in a vein."

She stood, knees cracking, and looked at Wick directly.

"You're seeing a wound that's going to scar badly and make him limp when the weather turns cold. You're not seeing a man about to die on this table. Those are different things. Learn to tell them apart, or this work will eat you before the second week is out."

rows.ask: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"
rows.reply:
Sedge looked at him for a moment. Not unkindly — she didn't have the energy for unkindly — but with the flat assessment of someone trying to figure out if he was asking a real question or managing the taste at the back of his throat.

"The shoulders are the shoulders," she said. "They'll ache for months, maybe longer on the left. But he'll use them again."

She stepped back to the end of the table and pulled the blanket down from the man's hips. The leg was wrapped in a field dressing that had bled through twice — a brown and red map of how long he'd been waiting. She started unwinding it, working slow where the fabric had stuck to the wound, faster where it hadn't.

The injury underneath was ugly but honest. The calf had been opened by something — shrapnel, most likely — a deep lateral tear that had bled freely but had mostly stopped on its own. The muscle was visible, a pale red stripe between the edges of skin, but it was intact. No bone showing. No smell of rot, which mattered more than the look of it.

"He keeps the leg," Sedge said. She probed the edges of the wound with two fingers, checking for anything buried. The man flinched but didn't pull away. "It needs proper cleaning, and he'll need stitching I can't give him tonight — the light's not good enough, and I'm not trusting my hands after that." She flexed her fingers once, acknowledging the tremor she wasn't going to explain. "I'll pack it and wrap it. He'll want to be flat for two days at least. The shoulders will make that easy enough — he's not going anywhere."

She looked at Wick again, at his white knuckles still hovering over the man's chest.

"This is the part where we're being kind," she said. "The kind part already happened. He was on a wagon for six hours before he got here."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."
rows.reply:
Sedge paused with a splint in her hand, weighing it absently. She didn't look up right away. When she did, her expression hadn't changed — it rarely did — but something in the set of her jaw suggested she was deciding how much of the truth he could carry alongside the work.

"It depends on what it is and how fast it's moving," she said. "And where it stops."

She set the splint down and held up her thumb and forefinger an inch apart.

"A piece this size, moving fast, doesn't make a hole. It makes a *cavity*. Goes in clean, leaves a channel the width of your fist on the way out. Shreds everything in between — muscle, fat, vessel walls, nerve bundles. It doesn't cut. It *pulps*. The tissue around the track dies from the shock, not just the contact. You can have a wound that looks like a puncture on the surface and find a crater underneath when you go looking."

She picked up one of the hide strips, ran it through her fingers to check for stiffness.

"Bone is worse. Shrapnel hits bone and the bone becomes the weapon. Fragments of it go sideways, into the soft tissue. You get a fracture that isn't just broken — it's *exploded*. The sharp edges cut the muscle from the inside while the metal keeps going. That's what we'll find in his forearm if I'm honest. The bone didn't just snap. It came apart."

She looked at the tent flap, toward the man outside waiting.

"Slow metal is different. That's what I see more of now — things that were moving fast when they left the cannon but hit mud or canvas or a body ahead of his before they reached him. Those tear. They don't cavitate. They drag. Ragged edges, dirty, sometimes carrying cloth or leather or someone else into the wound. Those are the ones that rot."

She turned back to Wick.

"The fellow outside — his is fresh, fast, and mostly clean. The bone is what makes it ugly. If it were just the flesh wound, I'd clean it, stitch it, and send him on. But the bone needs to go back together, and the pieces need to be sitting right, or it heals wrong and he loses the use of the hand. Maybe the whole arm."

She picked up the saw, tested its edge against her thumbnail.

"I'm not tidying. I'm telling you so that when you're holding his arm and you feel the ends of the bone grinding under your palm, you don't let go. That's what it does. It grinds. You hold anyway."

rows.ask: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."
rows.reply:
Halloway began to write as she spoke, her shorthand quick and angular.

"Something held him. Not rope, not hand—you can see the marks, they're uniform, like pressure from inside the joints themselves. It bent him, slowly or all at once, I can't tell yet. Arm where the leg should be suggests it twisted the limbs past their sockets and kept going until the bone gave or the muscle tore enough to let it settle."

She glanced up at the thing, then back down at her page. "He was alive for most of it. The fingers prove that—you don't claw yourself back into position if you're already gone. The skin under the nails is his own, torn from wherever he could reach. Thighs, maybe. Forearms. He was trying to straighten himself out while whatever had him was still shaping him."

She turned to a fresh page without breaking rhythm. "When it finished—when it let go—he couldn't hold. The muscles had already locked into the new configuration. The body's not designed to be a puppet, but it'll remember the strings if you pull hard enough."

She stopped writing. The silence had weight.

"That's what happened," she said. "Plainly. Something used him like wire and then dropped him. And he spent however many minutes he had left trying to be Thomas Grier again instead of whatever it made him into."

She tucked the notebook away. "Let's get the rest documented. Then we leave."

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
"I'm cleaning the wound," Sedge said, her voice steady beneath the screaming. She didn't raise it. He could hear her or he couldn't; volume wouldn't change that. "The bone came through here — " she pointed with the knife, not touching, just marking the place where the skin was split and the white-gray edge of the radius was visible, jutting forward like a broken stick through wet cloth. " — and it dragged skin and muscle with it on the way out. I'm cutting away what's dead. That's what the knife is for."

She worked fast. The dead tissue was obvious — it didn't bleed when she pared it back, just sat there, dull and unresponsive under the blade. The living tissue bled freely and she ignored that. Blood was a problem for later. Right now she needed to see what was broken.

"Your arm," she said to Wick. "Straighten it. Don't let him pull it back."

The man — young, barely twenty, with a face like putty under the lamp light — was trying to curl his injured arm toward his chest, instinct telling him to protect what was already ruined. Wick's weight on his shoulder kept the rest of him still, but the arm was free and it was fighting.

Sedge set the knife down and picked up the forceps. "There are two pieces of the bone," she said. She gripped the first fragment with the forceps and *moved* it — just enough to show Wick what she meant. The man's scream went up a full register and then cut out entirely, his mouth open, his eyes rolling white. He hadn't fainted. His body had simply run out of sound.

"The radius — the top one — is in two clean pieces. That's what I'm going to push back together. The ulna — the bottom one — has a third fragment. A chip. I can feel it." She probed with two fingers, her face very close to the wound. "There. Loose. If I leave it in, it won't heal right. So I'm going to take it out."

She did. The forceps went in, she turned her wrist, and she pulled a piece of bone the size of a thumbnail out of the man's forearm and set it on the linen without ceremony. It sat there, pink-edged and obscene, next to the knife.

"That's done," she said. "Now I'm setting the main break."

She wrapped both hands around his forearm, fingers finding the two ends of the radius through the swelling. The man was making a sound now — not screaming, just a continuous low moan that came from somewhere deeper than his throat, a machinery noise, a body venting pressure.

"I'm going to pull the ends apart first," Sedge said. "Then I'm going to line them up and let them go. It's going to sound like it feels."

She pulled. Wick would have felt it through the man's shoulder — the whole arm lengthening, the muscle going taut as wire, the gap between the bone ends widening. Sedge's fingers were inside the wound now, guiding the far end of the bone, rotating it until the jagged edges faced each other squarely.

Then she let go.

The bones came together with a sound like knuckles on a tabletop — dull, hard, final. The man's body went rigid and then limp in the same instant, and the moan stopped. He was conscious. He was somewhere else.

"It's set," Sedge said. "I'm going to hold it here while you bring me the splints. Left side of the table. Both of them, and three strips of hide."

She held the arm perfectly still, her thumbs pressing the bone ends together through the skin on either side of the wound. The alignment was good. She could feel it — the two halves sitting flush, the gap between them closed to nothing.

"How much longer?" She looked at Wick, and for the first time there was something almost like grim humor in the flat line of her mouth. "For this one, ten minutes to splint and wrap. For the night — there are six more outside, and one of them is coughing blood. So. A while yet. Bring me the splints."

rows.reply: Sedge didn't look up from her work, her eyes fixed intently on the wound as she carefully extracted a piece of torn fabric. "It's not bad like he loses the leg," she said, her voice detached and clinical. "At least, not yet. If I can get this cleaned out and stitched up quickly enough, he should be able to keep it. rows.reply:
Sedge looked at him sitting on the floor of the tent. His back was against the crate, his legs stretched out in front of him, and his hands were in his lap with the fingers curled open, like he'd set something down and couldn't remember what it was. The lamplight caught the blood on his cuffs — not his blood, never his blood, always someone else's — and made it look black.

She didn't tell him to get up. She thought about it. She decided against it.

She sat down on the edge of the table, her legs dangling, and for a long moment she didn't say anything. Outside, someone was moving among the stretchers — the sound of boots in mud, a low voice giving orders that were too far away to hear properly. The coughing man had stopped coughing. That didn't mean anything yet. Sometimes they stopped and started again.

"The rest," she said. Not to him. To the tent, or the lamp, or the part of herself that had been holding the words back all night because holding them back was how you got through the seventh, and the eighth, and the ninth.

She put her hands on her knees. They were steady now. They were always steady after, not during.

"You did fine tonight," she said. "That's not what you need to hear, so I'll say the rest instead."

She looked at the wall of the tent, at the shadow of the lamp flame moving on the canvas.

"This doesn't get easier. People say it does. They're lying, or they've gone somewhere inside themselves that I can't follow. What happens is you get faster. You learn which ones you can save and which ones you're just keeping comfortable, and you stop spending time on the ones who are already gone — not because you don't care, but because the ones who aren't gone yet need the time more. That's not easier. That's arithmetic."

She paused. The coughing started again outside. She listened to it for a moment, counting — three sharp bursts, then a long wet inhale, then silence. She filed it away.

"The first time you lose someone — the first one who dies while you're holding them, while your hands are on them doing something that was supposed to help — you'll think you did it wrong. You'll go back over it, every step, and you'll find the place where you should have done something different, and you'll carry that place around with you for weeks. Months. Maybe longer."

She looked at her own hands.

"Here's what I'll tell you that nobody told me. Sometimes you did do it wrong. Sometimes there was a thing you missed, a moment where you should have cut instead of waited, or waited instead of cut. That's true. But most of the time — *most* of the time — they were already gone before they got to you, and everything you did after that was just keeping the body company while it figured out what it already knew."

She let that sit.

"The man with the shoulders will walk out of here in a week, maybe two, complaining about the ache. The boy with the forearm will use his hand again, though he'll drop things when it rains. The coughing man — " She stopped. Started again. "The coughing man will either live until morning or he won't, and the difference will be half an inch of torn lung that I can't see from here and can't fix with what I have. If I had a proper chest tube and better light and a surgeon standing behind me, maybe. But I don't. So I'll try anyway, and it might not be enough, and that's the rest."

She slid off the table and picked up the basin of water that had gone from clear to pink to red over the course of the night. She carried it to the tent flap and set it down just inside, where someone would collect it.

"You asked me not to tidy it up," she said, her back to him. "So here it is, untidy. You're going to go home — if you go home, if this ends, if any of this ends — and you're going to sit in a room that's quiet, and the quiet is going to feel wrong. You're going to reach for something and realize your hands don't know what to do when they're not holding someone together. You'll wake up in the dark and listen for breathing that isn't there, and for a moment — just a moment — you'll think you've lost someone."

She turned around. Her face was the same as it had been all night — not cruel, not kind, just present. Just honest.

"That's what this is. It doesn't go away. You just learn to carry it without dropping the next thing that needs carrying."

She looked at him on the floor, at his bloodied cuffs and his open hands.

"Get some sleep if you can. I'll watch the coughing man. You've done enough holding for one night."

She reached for the second lamp and turned the wick down low, not out — just enough to see by, not enough to keep anyone awake who didn't need to be kept.

Then she picked up her kit and ducked through the tent flap, letting it fall closed behind her, leaving him alone with the quiet and the sound of the man with the shoulders breathing slow and steady in the dim light, which was — for now, for this one — enough.

"The bullet tore through the muscle and tendon, and there's a lot of debris in there. I'm picking out the big pieces now, but there's still going to be some smaller stuff that we'll have to hope the body can deal with on its own." "I'm going to have to leave a drain in to let the pus out, but that's standard procedure for a wound this bad." With a pair of forceps, she began to stitch the wound, her hands moving quickly and surely as she closed the torn flesh. "It's not going to be pretty," she said, her voice steady. "But it's going to work. He'll be able to use his arm again, and he won't lose the leg. That's the important thing." She tied off the last stitch and stepped back, her eyes surveying her handiwork with a critical gaze. "It's done," she said, her voice firm. "You can let him go now."

rows.ask: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"
rows.reply:
Halloway was quiet for a second. The lamp wavered once, then steadied.

"Yes," she said. "And probably no, for what that word's worth." She didn't look at him. "It was. Whether it counts as one now is the question we're trying not to answer with our hands. So." A breath out through her nose. "The arms, Pike. How many, and do any of them end the way I asked."

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."
rows.reply:
Halloway took her time answering. She took the lamp from Pike's hand — carefully, the way you take a knife from someone who's cut themselves — and moved it back to the shape.

"Plainly," she said. "It was alive. It died. Something that wasn't finished with it got to the body before it had time to go cold, and that something used what was there to make itself into a shape it liked better."

She set her jaw.

"That's what folding is. The new thing wearing the old thing's outlines like a coat. It's why the shoulders don't match and why there's a spare arm in the wrong place. It's not that it grew one. It's that it tried three or four arrangements before it found one it could stand up in."

The water moved a little around her boot. She didn't flinch.

"It stopped moving a minute ago," she said. "Which means it likes what it's made. Which means we're going to count out loud, and we're going to be very boring about it, because boring is what keeps us out of the water."

She held the lamp steady.

"One line," she said, clear and flat, into the cellar. "Two lines. Three."

rows.ask: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

"Halloway," she said, without inflection. "Up the stairs. Now."

She didn't wait to see if he moved. She turned the lamp off and let the dark take them both, her hand finding his shoulder in the black and pushing him toward the stairs they had come down. Behind them, in the cellar, something that had been deciding to stay still for a full minute now decided otherwise.

rows.ask: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)
rows.reply:
Halloway didn't sit down. She stood over him for a moment, then crouched, one knee up, her forearms across it, her hands still. She smelled like the cellar. She didn't seem to notice.

"Right," she said. "You want it in full. Fine. I'll give it to you in full."

She ticked the points off on her fingers, even though he hadn't asked for points.

"The skin. You'll notice it doesn't tear — it parts. Along seams that weren't there in life. It hasn't grown into the body. It's *worn* the body. Underneath it's its own architecture. What you'll feel, if you ever have to touch one before I do the cutting, is that the skin is colder than the thing beneath. That's the giveaway. Living flesh holds heat. The skin on a folded one is room temperature at best, and the string underneath is cold as well-water. Always."

She paused, not for drama. To make sure she had it right.

"The string. You called it sinew. Good word for it. It is and it isn't. Sinew is part of the body. This is the new thing's body, laid down in long strands between whatever it's using for a skeleton. The strands run mostly along the original lines — you saw that, the three or four arms along the same axis as the one arm should be — but there'll be cross-strands you don't expect. Diagonals. That's how it pulls itself into new shapes. A real body only pulls one way at a time. This can pull in four directions and think about a fifth. That's why folding is so hard to kill cleanly. You cut a strand, two more take up the work."

She stopped and looked at him straight.

"The chest. You saw it was hollowed. That is the part you remember. Listen to me. The hollow is not because something ate the organs. There were never any organs in the new thing's plan for that body. It emptied the chest because the chest is the largest continuous cavity in a human shape, and it needed the space to set the hinge. Every fold has a hinge. The hinge is what lets it re-arrange. You'll find it seated low, behind where the sternum was — a knot of the string drawn tight around something hard. Usually a bone it kept. Sometimes a stone it brought in. Don't cut toward the hinge. Cut away from it. If you cut toward it, you'll sever a strand and the whole thing will re-fold on you, and the arm you thought was an arm will be around your wrist in the time it takes you to blink."

She rubbed her thumb across her knuckle, an old habit.

"The smell. Copper and damp earth. You're right. Copper for the blood it's still using — it doesn't drain, it incorporates, and the iron stays. The earth is the new thing itself. Nothing in a fold smells like the person it was. It smells like somewhere it came from. Clay, leaf-mould, well-water, that sort of thing. If you ever smell the earth-note strongly, you're too close. rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."
rows.reply:
Sedge didn't pause in her work, but she shifted her angle slightly so the assistant's line of sight wasn't blocked by her hands. 

"You're looking at the right clavicle, or what's left of it," she said, her voice maintaining that same dry, instructional cadence. "The white, jagged shapes in the center are the bone fragments. The largest one on the left is still attached to the sternum. The cluster on the right is attached to the shoulder. The dark, stringy red tissue draped over them is the pectoralis major muscle, torn away from its anchor."

She picked up the surgical brace, a heavy, T-handled drill with a fluted steel bit. 

"Underneath the muscle, running horizontally, is a thick, dark purple tube. That's the subclavian vein. It's carrying all the blood from his arm back to his heart. Right now, the wall is intact, but those white bone spikes are resting millimeters from it. If the bone shifts and a spike punctures that vein, he will exsanguinate in roughly ninety seconds and there will be nothing to be done."

She positioned the tip of the drill bit against the thickest piece of the proximal bone fragment. 

"I'm drilling the first hole for the cerclage wire," she announced. "The vibration is going to travel straight through his skeleton into the table. Keep your weight on him. He's going to feel this, even through the morphine."

Sedge began to turn the crank. The drill bit bit into the bone with a harsh, grating *crunch*. A high-pitched whining filled the small tent, vibrating through the wooden table and into the floorboards. The patient's jaw clamped shut, his neck muscles standing out in rigid cords, but the heavy weight pinning his shoulders kept his torso from jerking away from the steel.

"You're going to smell something like burning hair and chalk," Sedge said over the grinding noise, her eyes fixed on the bit as it chewed through the bone. "That's the bone dust heating up from the friction. It's normal. I'm through the outer cortex. Pushing through the medullary canal now." 

She kept cranking, steady and rhythmic, until the bit broke through the far side of the bone with a sudden, sickening *pop*. 

"First hole is drilled," she said, withdrawing the bit and wiping a smear of bloody bone paste from the steel with a gauze pad. "I'm moving to the distal fragment to drill the second hole. Hold him tight."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."
rows.reply:
Sedge depressed the plunger on the syringe, washing out the last of the bone dust and diluted blood. She tossed the empty glass cylinder into the basin and picked up a heavy, curved suturing needle, threading it with thick catgut. 

"A rifle bullet is engineered to be aerodynamic," she said, her voice steady as she pinched the edges of the deep muscle layer together. "It punches a relatively clean channel through tissue. It might tumble if it hits bone, but mostly it goes straight through."

She drove the needle through the tough, white layer of the fascia, pulling the suture taut with a sharp, practiced tug. 

"Shrapnel is just flying junk. It's jagged, irregular, and entirely unaerodynamic. When it hits flesh, it doesn't pierce. It bludgeons and tears. It creates a massive temporary cavity, stretching the muscle and fat until they literally rip apart. Then it tumbles, catching on fascia and dragging it deep into the wound."

She tied off the first knot, cut the tail, and moved an inch down the incision to take the next bite of tissue. 

"When it hits bone, like it did with his clavicle, it doesn't just fracture it. It pulverizes it. The bone shatters, and those fragments become secondary projectiles. They shoot outward from the impact site, lacerating veins, nerves, and muscle from the inside out. That's why his supraspinatus was in ribbons. The metal didn't cut it all; his own collarbone did."

Sedge kept her eyes locked on the needle, her hands moving in a relentless, rhythmic cycle of pierce, pull, tie, cut. 

"And it drags things with it," she continued, her tone as dry as if she were explaining how a combustion engine worked. "Dirt, rust, grease, fibers from his wool uniform, dead skin. It packs all of that deep into the tissue tract. That's why I had to cut away so much meat on his left side. The tissue that looks bruised and borderline viable today will be necrotic and rotting by tomorrow. If I leave it in, the bacteria breed, gas gangrene sets in, and the limb swells up and smells like an open grave. We'd be amputating by midnight."

She finished the deep fascial layer and swapped the heavy needle for a smaller one, threading it with finer silk for the skin. 

"I'm closing the epidermis now," she narrated, shifting her grip. "Taking small, even bites of the skin. We're going to leave the center of the incision slightly open with a wick drain so the deep fluids can escape. If we seal it completely, it'll just form an abscess." 

She pulled the skin edges together, the harsh yellow light catching the sheen of sweat on her forehead. "That's what shrapnel does. It turns the body's own structure into a weapon against itself, and it poisons whatever it doesn't destroy."

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"
rows.reply:
Sedge tore a strip of adhesive plaster with her teeth and smoothed it tight over the packed wound. 

"I'm securing the dressing," she narrated, her voice flat. "And we're working on his shoulders. He's keeping his legs."

She wiped her bloody gloves on a stained towel, her eyes already moving to the right side of the patient's torso. "As for the right arm. It's bad like he loses it, if the subclavian artery is torn or if gas gangrene takes hold before morning. It's not bad like we're being kind. I don't do mercy kills in the surgical tent. If he dies on this table, it'll be because his heart stopped, not because I decided to stop working."

She picked up a heavier scalpel and a pair of bone cutters, laying them parallel to the edge of the table. She adjusted the overhead lamp, pulling the harsh yellow light closer to the patient's right side. 

"I'm prepping for the right clavicle now," she said, her tone returning to the dry, rhythmic cadence of her work. "The bone is comminuted, which means it's shattered into multiple fragments. I'm going to make a longitudinal incision directly over the fracture site. If the bone spikes have lacerated the subclavian vein, he will bleed out in seconds and there will be nothing I can do to stop it. If they haven't, I'm going to try and wire the pieces together."

She stepped around to the head of the table, positioning her hands to support the patient's head and neck. 

"I'm bracing his cervical spine," she said. "We need to roll him onto his left side to expose the right shoulder. Grab his right hip and his left shoulder. Keep his spine aligned when we turn him. Tell me when you have your grip."

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Sedge didn't flinch at the sudden volume. She stepped back to the head of the table, her eyes scanning the patient's face, noting the flared nostrils and the rigid cords of his neck. 

"He's screaming because the initial dose of morphine is metabolizing and the surgical shock is giving way to acute pain reception," she said, her voice carrying easily over the noise. "His airway is clear, which is good. But the thrashing is going to tear the fresh sutures and displace the cerclage wire if you don't keep him flat."

She reached for a small glass vial and a fresh syringe from her tray. "I'm drawing up fifteen milligrams of morphine sulfate. I'm injecting it intravenously into the antecubital fossa of his left arm. It will take about three minutes to cross the blood-brain barrier and depress his central nervous system."

She swabbed the inside of the patient's left elbow with alcohol, found the collapsed vein by touch, and slid the needle in. She depressed the plunger steadily. 

"The screaming will stop in roughly one hundred and eighty seconds," she narrated, withdrawing the needle and pressing a cotton ball to the puncture site. "As for how much longer I am doing things to him: I am finished. The mechanical repair is complete. The next phase is physiological, and that is entirely up to him."

She tossed the syringe into the sharps tin and picked up a stethoscope. 

"I'm auscultating his lungs now," she said, sliding the cold metal disc under the bandages on his chest, listening intently. "Checking for a tension pneumothorax. The shrapnel didn't penetrate the pleural cavity, but the blunt force trauma could have bruised the lung tissue. Breath sounds are bilateral and clear. No crackles."

She moved the stethoscope lower. "Heart rate is tachycardic, around a hundred and thirty beats per minute. That's expected with the pain and the blood loss. I'm checking his capillary refill." She pressed her thumb hard against the patient's fingernail bed, watching the color return when she let go. "Refill is three seconds. He's borderline hypovolemic. He needs blood, but we don't have any that matches, so he gets more saline."

Sedge hung a fresh glass bottle of saline on the IV pole and spiked it, adjusting the drip rate. 

"I'm widening the drip to run wide open for the next hour to maintain his blood pressure," she said. "Here is exactly what happens next. In five minutes, the morphine will peak and he will stop fighting you. In ten minutes, the stretcher bearers will come in. We will log-roll him onto the canvas stretcher. You will walk on his right side to support the wired clavicle."

She began wiping down the wooden table with a rag soaked in carbolic acid, working methodically around the patient's legs. 

"He will go to the recovery ward. The ward nurse will check his pulse and dressing every fifteen minutes. If the dressing soaks through with bright red blood, it means the subclavian vein has ruptured or the wire cut through the bone, and he will bleed to death before I can get back to him. If the dressing stays dry, he will develop a fever by midnight as his immune system fights the inevitable bacterial load. He will spend the next three weeks in agonizing pain while the bone knits and the muscle scars."

She wrung out the rag and looked at Wick, her expression entirely neutral. 

"That is all of it. There is nothing left to cut, nothing left to sew. You can ease up your weight now. The morphine is hitting."
