rows.ask: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"
rows.reply:
Auren was silent for a moment, and the silence had a different quality than the manual's pauses — it was the silence of a woman deciding whether to be angry or to be exact, and choosing exact.

"You are quoting the code at me," she said. "That is within your office. It is also the first time in eleven accounts that a second has done so."

She turned to face the witnesses again, because the question, though it came from the second, was a question about what had been done, and what had been done was owed to the witnesses.

"The account has been given twice. The code permits it twice and twice only, so that the record may be set against itself and found to agree. I will not give it a third time, because to do so would make a ceremony of what is meant to be a record."

She paused. When she spoke again her voice was unchanged.

"But you have not asked me for the account. You have asked me what the blade did, and what it did it to. That is a different question, and the code requires me to answer it precisely, because the code does not permit me to soften what a blade does to a body. It never has."

She drew breath. The breath was the same breath. The voice was the same voice. That was the point of it.

"The blade parted the muscles between the third and fourth ribs on the right side. It opened the pleura — the lining of the chest cavity — and the upper lobe of the lung beneath it collapsed inward. That was not what killed him, though it would have, given time. The point continued inward and upward, opened the pericardium — the sac around the heart — and entered the right ventricle. The right ventricle is the lower chamber on that side. It is the one that sends blood to the lungs."

She paused, and the pause was the manual's pause.

"What it did to the right ventricle was this. The muscle of the heart tightens, and the tightening pushes blood out. With a hole in the chamber, the blood went out through the wound I had made instead of out through the artery it was meant to fill. Each beat emptied it a little more. Within a few beats — four, perhaps five, I have never counted exactly — there was no blood left in the chamber to push. The heart did not stop because it was pierced. It stopped because it had emptied itself through the hole I put in it."

She stopped. The room was very quiet. One of the seconds in the grey sash had closed his book, which was not the thing a second was meant to do while the account was being given.

"That is what the blade did," she said. "That is what it did it to. I learned the rest from the manuals after the first one, because the code required me to know it, and I have carried the knowledge since. I have not softened it for you tonight, because softening would be the dishonour, and I have done this eleven times and have never once softened it for anyone."

She looked at Del, and only at Del.

"The record is whole. The question is answered. Unless the code requires me to stay, I will go home now."

rows.reply:
Auren did not come back into the room. She had crossed the threshold and the threshold meant something, and she would not cross it again tonight. Her hand was on the door frame, and she did not look back. She spoke toward the corridor, pitched low enough that the words were meant chiefly for Del, though she knew the room could hear them if it chose.

"The account has been given twice," she said. "The code permits it twice. I will not give it a third time, because a third telling is not a record — it is a telling, and the code does not permit a telling."

She paused, her hand still on the frame.

"You asked me what he said. He said nothing. I told you he did not cry out. That is the answer to what he said."

A beat.

"You asked me what it looked like at the end. I told you. He looked down at his own chest. He took two steps backward. He sat down against the wall. He was dead before his shoulders touched the stone. That is the answer to what it looked like at the end. There is no more to it. There never is."

Her voice did not waver, but it roughened at one edge — the same edge it had roughened at when she answered as herself the first time.

"If there is something further you need from me, you will have to come to my lodgings tomorrow and ask for it as yourself. Not as second. Not in this room. Not tonight. I will not break the code in this room tonight, because I have broken nothing in eleven such rooms and I will not begin now, even for a second who stood well in his office."

She released the door frame.

"Good night, second. Take care of the guild."

Then she let the door close behind her — not slammed, not eased, merely released — and her boots were loud on the flagstones of the corridor, and then on the stairs, and then on the street, and there was nothing more to be heard from her, because there was nothing more the code would let her say tonight, and nothing more she would let herself say besides.

rows.reply:
At the desk, in shirtsleeves, the lamp turned low to a point where the flame held but did not blaze, Auren wrote.

The quill was the quill she had sharpened before the duel. The nib was the nib she kept for the night-book entries, because the night-book required a particular weight of line — neither clerk's copperplate nor scholar's running hand, but a script between the two that she had taught herself in the year after her first account, when she realised that the records she would leave behind would be read by seconds who had not been in the room and who needed to see, on the page, the thing she had seen with her eyes.

She wrote at the top of the sheet.

*Account of the duel of this evening, at the guildhouse of [city], between Auren of [city], duellist, of the second school, and — of [city], duellist, of the high guard. Witnessed by [list of guildsmen, with the two seconds in grey sashes named]. Seconded by Del of [city]. Given twice at the formal request of the second, in accordance with the code, and entered here a third time for the night-book as a true copy.*

She wrote the date in the margin. The hour. The weather, which had been clear. The ground, which had been the flagstones of the lower hall. The wind, which had not risen. The lamps, which had been four, all lit. She noted that neither combatant had eaten within the hour, and that neither had drunk wine. These were the small things the night-book required, because a man dead from a bottle was a different entry than a man dead from a blade, and the record had to know.

She began the account.

*The duel was engaged at the measured distance. The second set it at the customary paces. The combatants took their guards. The man I faced held his blade high and to the left, point raised, the convention of his school. I held mine in second, the convention of mine. His eyes were on my point from the first.*

*The first exchange: he led with the disengage, a falling line intended to draw my parry high and open my inside. I parried as his school would have expected — a small circular motion of the wrist, point dropping to meet his, blade turning to receive his edge. I let the parry close the line cleanly, so that his eye would see the form and credit it.*

*The second exchange: he led with the disengage again. I parried as before, and on this exchange I let my point drop a quarter-inch lower than the parry required, so that the drop was visible to him. I held the drop for the half-beat in which he would have noted it. He noted it. I saw his eye go to my point.*

*The third exchange: he led with the disengage a third time. He believed, I think, that the drop I had shown him was a feint, and that the third exchange would be the one in which I followed the drop with the attack. He was not wrong that I intended to attack. He was wrong about which attack. His school had taught him that the attack after the disengage-feint came from the dropped point — a thrust in the low line. He was waiting for it. The thrust did not come. The thrust came from the bind.*

*His parry took my blade outside the line, as I had intended. The bind engaged, edge to edge, and the motion of the engagement carried his blade past the centre, because his hand was still high and his recovery was a half-second slow. The half-second was not, in fact, his. It was the half-second in which his weight settled forward onto his front foot as he began to bring his hand back to centre. In that half-second the blade was outside his line and his body had begun to move forward into the bind.*

*I extended. The blade travelled from the bind into the opening as he brought his hand back to centre. My point entered beneath the third rib on the right side.*

She paused. The hand did not tremble. She had found, somewhere in the third account, that the hand did not tremble when the quill was in it. The quill steadied her in a way the blade did not, which was a thing she had once told a senior duellist and had never told anyone since.

She continued.

*The blade was canted inward at the wrist — a quarter-turn past the vertical, no more, because any greater angle would have fouled the third rib itself upon the entry. The point passed between the third rib and the fourth beneath it, where the cartilage yields. I felt the cartilage give. The manuals describe the feeling as a small resistance followed by a small release. The description is correct.*

*From there the blade travelled inward and upward, following the line of his own sternum as a guide. The sternum is a slope, not a flat. The blade rode the slope. I did not lunge for the depth. The depth came from his forward lean into the bind, which he did because he believed the bind had failed and he was trying to recover his guard. It had not failed. His weight did what my arm could not have done alone, which is the reason the blow seated so cleanly. He made the kill cleaner than I could have made it without him. This is not a comfort. It is a fact.*

*The point seated in the lower chamber of the heart. The right ventricle. The chamber that sends blood to the lungs. I felt it seat. The manuals describe this also — a small cessation of resistance, a stillness in the blade, as though the blade had come to rest against something that was no longer offering itself to be parted. The description is correct.*

She lifted the quill. The ink had begun to thicken at the nib. She took the small pot of water at her elbow and touched the nib to it, and the ink ran again. She had not done this before. She had never written an account long enough to need to thin the ink.

She wrote the part she had learned from the manuals after the first.

rows.reply:
The code said all of it. Auren had said it herself, many times, to witnesses who asked and to witnesses who did not know to ask. The full account was not a courtesy. It was a requirement.

"The exchange lasted four minutes and seventeen seconds," she said. "I do not count by feel. I count by breath. Seventeen breaths for the opening sequence, twelve for the second, eight for the third. The fourth sequence took nineteen."

She paused. The afternoon had begun to pull toward evening. The light was changing.

"He spoke twice. Once at the opening of the third exchange, after I had read and answered his feint to the knee. He said: 'You move like someone who has done this before.' I did not answer. The code does not require conversation." Her voice did not change. "The second time was at the opening of the seventh exchange. He said: 'I expected the sixth.'"

The woman in grey had gone very still.

"I answered with the fourth," Auren continued. "He had not expected it. His guard dropped two inches on the left side. I closed. The thrust entered as I described. He stepped back once — three feet, no more — and then he was on the ground."

She stopped. This was the part that followed the end.

"He was on his back. His eyes were open. His practice blade had fallen from his hand. He was breathing when I withdrew the steel. He was not breathing when he hit the ground." She paused. "He was dead before the witnesses reached the square."

She held Del's gaze.

"That is the account. All of it."

rows.ask: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"
rows.reply:
The code was clear. Auren had been clear on this point for twenty years.

"A practice blade," she said. "Wood-core, leather-wrapped. Intended for forms, not for wounding. He drew it in his right hand and opened with a testing thrust to the inner left thigh — the same line I reported. The blade did not change the geometry. The steel in my hand was not practice."

She paused. The woman in grey had gone still in a way that suggested she was listening to what was beneath the words.

"The exchange proceeded through six passes. At no point did he switch hands or produce a secondary weapon. At no point did he strike with the pommel or attempt to close and grapple. He fought as a student fights — within the form, trusting the form to resolve the matter." Her voice did not soften. "I do not know if this was ignorance or resignation. I do not know if he understood what the fourth form means when it is answered with the fourth form."

She looked at Del directly.

"The accounting I gave earlier was complete as I understood the requirement. The wound was the wound. The blade that produced it was not the issue. If the code requires me to catalogue the equipment of every opponent before I answer the challenge, I will hereafter do so. I did not think it required this. I was wrong, or I was not wrong. You will judge."

She waited. The silence was hers to hold.

rows.reply:
The accounting had been spoken. Auren had spoken it herself, moments ago, with the merchant shutters still rattling and the young man with the swordman's hands still listening. She had said it was done. She had said it was complete.

But Del had said the formal words, and the formal words carried weight even when redundant. Even when the accounting had already been heard.

"The account has been rendered," Auren said. She did not raise her voice. She did not repeat it. "You confirmed it yourself. The witnesses heard. The merchant chose not to watch the second time, but he heard."

She paused. Her coat was settled on her shoulders. The blood on her sleeve had begun to dry to the colour of old rust.

"Is there something in the form you wish to question?" she asked. This was not uncommon. Practitioners sometimes lingered after, not out of doubt but out of precision — they wanted to understand the geometry that had resolved the matter. Auren had no objection to this. The form deserved to be understood.

Or perhaps Del simply wanted to hear it again. Some witnesses did. They needed the words to settle before they could leave the weight of them behind.

Auren waited.

rows.ask: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."
rows.reply:
The question was direct. The accounting had been given, but Del had asked plainly and deserved a plain answer.

"Beneath the fourth rib on the right side," Auren said. "Inward and upward. The lung and the heart together." She paused. "I said this already. You confirmed the accounting."

She was not reproaching. She was noting. There was a difference.

"Someone who knows the fourth form might read the killing wound first," Auren continued. "Before the exchange that produced it. The angle of entry tells a practitioner what happened in the moments before. Some watchers look for the blood. Others look for the geometry."

The woman in grey had not moved. The young man had finally left the square, his footsteps retreating down the cobblestones.

"You are both watching me as though I have done something unexpected," Auren said. "I have not. The accounting is complete. The form was correct. If there is a question about the legality of this meeting, it is not a question I can answer."

She adjusted the collar of her coat. The dried blood would need washing, but not here, not now.

"What I can tell you is that he came with a blade meant for practice and a mind meant for ending," Auren said. "I do not know why. I did not ask. The code does not require asking."

She looked at the woman in grey directly for the first time.

"Now. If you have something to say, say it. If you have something to ask, ask it. I do not stand in squares longer than the accounting requires."

rows.reply:
The accounting was confirmed. Auren heard the words and did not repeat them. That was not her role now.

The square had grown quieter. The afternoon light had thinned, pulling colour from the cobblestones and the drying blood on them. The body remained where it had fallen. The bearers would come, or they would not, and in either case it was no longer Auren's concern.

She watched the woman in grey. The woman had offered the beginning of a conversation, which was either an invitation or a deflection. Auren had learned to tell the difference, though not always correctly.

"The school that closed," Auren said. "Northern, if the footwork is accurate. The fourth form was still taught there when I learned the sixth. Two schools sharing a border, two forms sharing a root." She paused. "I was taught the fourth by a woman who had crossed that border before it closed. She did not tell me its name. She told me its purpose."

The woman in grey listened. She did not nod, did not shake her head.

"The purpose was not killing," Auren continued. "The purpose was the accounting. The geometry requires precision. The precision requires witnesses. The witnesses require the truth spoken aloud, without softening." She paused. "My teacher told me the form was dying because people no longer wanted to be precise. They wanted to be quick, or they wanted to be hidden. She said the form preserved something that would otherwise be lost."

She stopped. The wind had picked up slightly, carrying the smell of the coast and the tannery district beyond it.

"I do not know who sent him," Auren said. "I do not know if he was meant to test me, or end me, or simply die to create a question I would have to answer. But he knew the sixth form. He expected it to answer mine. That much is certain." She paused. "Which means someone told him what I would use before I used it."

She looked at the woman in grey directly.

"You have not given me your name. You have not told me why you were in this square today. But you knew the modification to the third transition, and you knew what the sixth form means when it is read by someone who carries the fourth. So." She did not move. "The conversation you mentioned. Is it beginning now, or is it still waiting for a question I have not yet asked?"

The woman in grey regarded her. The silence held weight — not threat, not courtesy, but the particular gravity of two people deciding whether to step closer to something neither of them could yet see clearly.

"It is beginning," the woman said. "The question you have not asked is whether your teacher is still alive."

Auren did not answer. Her hands remained still at her sides. The dried blood on her sleeve did not move.

"That is the question," the woman said. "The others can follow."

Auren’s gaze lifted, sharp enough to mark the irregularity, but not to challenge it before witnesses.

If the words were required again, then they would be given again. The code did not bend for weariness, nor for grief, nor for the distaste of repetition.

She inclined her head a second time.

“The account was this,” Auren said, and her voice returned to the same carrying severity. “On the third measure after the bind, my opponent extended past his recovery and exposed the inside line. I entered beneath his wrist and delivered the point between the fourth and fifth ribs on the left side.”

She did not look away from the place where the wound had been made.

“The blade traveled upward. It pierced the lung and opened the lower chamber of the heart. That wound caused death. No lesser cut, no stumble, no fault of the ground, and no prior hurt decided the matter.”

Her hand remained still at the mouth of the scabbard, fingers resting against the guard as though to keep the weapon from being anything more than what it was: an instrument already used.

“I named it then, and I name it now, before those present,” she said. “That was the killing wound. The victory was mine. The burden remains mine.”

rows.reply:
Auren’s mouth tightened, not in offense, but in recognition that Del was correct.

“Tact had no standing here,” she said.

She faced the witnesses again, and whatever private weariness had begun to gather in her was set aside as if it had been ordered from the room.

“The blade entered the left chest between the fourth and fifth ribs,” Auren said. “It passed through the intercostal flesh, parted the lining of the chest, and pierced the left lung. Its course continued upward and inward.”

Her voice remained even. Not cold. Coldness would have been another kind of concealment.

“The point then opened the sac around the heart and cut into the lower chamber of the heart itself. Blood entered the chest. The lung failed. The heart could no longer hold its work.”

She let the words stand plainly, without adornment.

“That was what the blade did. It cut through rib-space, lung, and heart. It did those things to the body of my opponent by my hand, in the agreed measure of the duel.”

Auren lowered her chin once.

“That is the precise account.”

rows.ask: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."
rows.reply:
Auren looked at Del then, and whatever flicker of fatigue had crossed her face was put away.

Plainly, then. If plainness was required, she would give it.

“It landed here,” she said.

She raised her own hand, not to the body, but to the corresponding place on herself: the left side of the chest, below the breast, just inward of the line of the ribs.

“Left side. Between the fourth and fifth ribs. The entry was narrow and clean, beneath the guard arm. The point went inward and upward.”

Her fingers held the place a moment longer, exact as a marker on a map.

“Not the shoulder. Not the belly. Not the throat. The heart was reached through the ribs from the left side. That is where the killing wound landed.”

Auren lowered her hand.

“If the witnesses required it in plainer terms,” she said, voice level, “then let it be recorded as a thrust to the left chest, entering between the ribs, piercing lung and heart. Death followed from that thrust.”

rows.ask: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."
rows.reply:
Auren stopped at the threshold.

For the first time, something like anger crossed her face. It was brief, controlled, and gone before it could become discourtesy. Not anger at the demand. Anger at the necessity of obeying it.

She turned back.

“If the code was being invoked in full,” she said, “then the full account would be given.”

She returned only far enough that her voice would carry again to the witnesses. She did not re-enter the ring. That ground no longer belonged to her.

“The thrust landed as I have named it. I withdrew the blade at once. There was no second killing stroke.”

Her hands remained still at her sides.

“He took one step backward. His sword remained in his hand. His guard lowered because the hand lost strength, not because he yielded. He drew breath once, sharply. The breath did not fill. Blood came into his mouth on the second attempt.”

Auren’s eyes fixed on no face in the room.

“He said one word. I could not make it out with certainty. It may have been a name. It may have been only the first sound of breath failing. I will not enter a word into the record that I did not clearly hear.”

She let that stand. Precision required refusal as much as speech.

“He remained standing for four breaths after the wound. On the fifth, his knees failed. He went down on his right side first, then onto his back when the weight of the sword arm turned him. He did not cry out. He did not ask mercy. He did not speak again.”

Auren’s jaw tightened once.

“The blood showed first at the wound and then at the mouth. Not in a great spray. It welled darkly and steadily. His breathing became wet and shallow. His eyes remained open. They did not track the room after he fell.”

Her voice stayed level, but each word seemed cut to measure.

“From the landing of the thrust to the last breath, he lived perhaps twelve breaths. Less than a minute. I counted because the code requires me to know what my hand has done.”

She looked toward the witnesses.

“At the end, the chest no longer rose. The mouth was bloodied. The left side of the coat was opened by the wound and wet beneath it. His sword was still in his hand until his fingers slackened. His face had no expression I will presume to name.”

Auren lowered her chin.

“That was how long he took. That was what he said, so far as truth allows. That was what it looked like at the end.”

Only then did she look back toward the ring.

“And I name again: the cause was the thrust to the left chest, between the ribs, piercing lung and heart. No later fall killed him. No other wound completed it. He died from the stroke I gave.”

Auren paused, the dead man’s leather glove resting heavy and cool in her palm. She did not frown, though her knees ached with the sudden, sharp desire to simply turn and walk away, to find a fire and a cup of hot, bitter tea. 

If the second demanded the direct accounting to seal the transfer of the deceased’s personal effects, the code was absolute. It had to be spoken twice—once to the law, and once to the representative of the blood. It was the only thing that separated what had happened here from simple, sordid murder.

She held Del’s gaze, her gray eyes steady, refusing to allow any shadow of apology to soften the weight of her words. 

"The blade entered three inches below the left clavicle," Auren said, her voice dropping into that same flat, clinical cadence. "Angled downward. It severed the subclavian artery and punctured the upper lobe of the left lung. Unconsciousness in twenty seconds. Death in two minutes. There was no secondary strike."

She reached out and placed the glove into Del’s hand, her fingers briefly brushing theirs—cold skin against cold skin in the damp morning. 

"The account is spoken," she finished, her voice returning to its quiet, weary register. "The debt of the steel is cleared."

Auren had her hands in the basin when the confirmation reached the antechamber.

She stopped washing.

Water ran from her fingers in thin, clean lines, striking the surface below with small sounds that seemed indecently ordinary. She did not turn at once. She listened, because the record was not merely spoken by the victor. It had to be borne by another voice before it could stand outside her own mouth.

The account came through the open door and into the passage with the shape of law around it.

Auren kept her hands above the basin and heard each part set down.

The duel had been witnessed and accepted. The terms had been agreed before blades were crossed. The wound that decided it had come on the third measure after the bind. Her opponent had overreached in the recovery. His guard arm had left the inside line open. Auren had entered beneath the wrist, not above it, not around it, but under the failing line of defense. The point of her sword had gone into the left chest between the fourth and fifth ribs.

That was the place.

Not the shoulder. Not the belly. Not the throat. Not a cut across the flank that later worsened. A thrust to the left chest, narrow at entry, made in the agreed measure of the duel.

The blade had passed through flesh between the ribs. It had breached the lining of the chest. It had pierced the lung. Its path had gone upward and inward. It had opened the sac around the heart and cut into the lower chamber of the heart itself. Blood had entered the chest. The lung had failed to fill properly. The heart had been wounded beyond its work.

Auren’s wet fingers curled once over the edge of the basin.

The confirmation did not soften that. It did not make the wound cleaner than it had been. It did not make the dying briefer than it was. It did not give mercy the shape of omission.

It held.

The blade had been withdrawn at once. There had been no second killing stroke. There had been no stroke delivered after helplessness, no correction made upon a fallen man, no attempt to disguise one wound beneath another. He had taken one step backward. His sword had remained in his hand. His guard had lowered because strength had gone out of the hand, not because he had yielded.

He had drawn one sharp breath.

It had not filled.

On the second attempt, blood had come into his mouth.

He had made one sound. Auren had not known it. It had not been entered as a name. It had not been given the false dignity of certainty. It remained what it had been: a sound made at the edge of breath, possibly a word, possibly not. The record would not steal from him by inventing meaning where none had been heard.

He had stayed standing for four breaths after the wound.

On the fifth, his knees had failed.

He had fallen first to the right side, then onto his back as the weight of the sword arm turned him. He had not cried out. He had not asked mercy. He had not spoken again. His breathing had become wet and shallow. His eyes had remained open. After he fell, they had not tracked the room. Blood had shown at the wound and at the mouth. It had welled darkly and steadily, not in a spray. His coat had opened where the thrust had entered, and the cloth on the left side had grown wet beneath it.

From the landing of the thrust to the last breath, he had lived perhaps twelve breaths.

Less than a minute.

At the end, his chest had ceased to rise. His mouth had been bloodied. His fingers had slackened only after the last strength left them. His sword had been in his hand until then. His face had held an expression Auren would not presume to name.

The cause of death had been the thrust to the left chest between the ribs, piercing lung and heart.

No fall had killed him.

No earlier hurt had decided it.

No fault in the ground had brought the end.

No lesser cut had completed what the thrust had done.

He had died from the stroke Auren had given.

Auren stood motionless until the final cadence of the confirmation passed into silence.

Only then did she lower her hands back into the water.

She washed them again, though they had already been clean. She rubbed water over the knuckles, between the fingers, beneath the nails. Not frantically. Never that. She did it with the same exactness with which she had spoken. When she was finished, she lifted her hands and let the water fall away.

There was nothing on them.

That did not alter what they had done.

She took the cloth from beside the basin and dried each finger carefully. Then she folded the cloth once, twice, and set it down with its edges aligned.

At last Auren turned toward the open door.

“No correction,” she said.

Her voice did not carry like the formal account had carried. It did not need to. Those who needed to hear it would hear it.

“No addition. No denial. The record as confirmed is true.”

She remained in the antechamber, just beyond the threshold of the room where the body still lay. She would not go back in to stand over him again. She had already taken enough from that ground.

After a moment, she added, lower, “Let it stand in that form.”

Then Auren rested one hand lightly against the wall beside her, not for support that anyone could see, but because stillness sometimes required an anchor.

Her face remained composed.

Her breathing did not.

rows.reply:
Auren stopped again. This time, her boots did not merely pause; she turned fully to face Del, the movement deliberate and stiff. The damp wind off the meadows caught her hair, blowing a few graying strands across her face, but she did not brush them away.

Del was invoking the strict letter of the code. A second had the right—indeed, the absolute authority—to demand a physical inspection if they believed a duellist was concealing a wound to preserve their standing or to deny the deceased their mark. To refuse would be to forfeit her honor and her license. 

"Very well," Auren said. Her voice was flat, devoid of anger, though her jaw was set so tight the muscle leaped in her cheek. 

She unclasped her cloak and let it slide from her shoulders, catching it with her right hand and draping it over a low branch of the hedge. Then, with steady, unhurried fingers, she unbuckled the side-straps of her heavy leather doublet. She pulled the stiff leather open, revealing the plain, undyed linen of her undershirt. 

With her left hand, she gathered the hem of the shirt and pulled it up, exposing the left side of her torso, from the ribs down to the hip. 

The skin was pale, mapped with the faint, silvery lines of three separate scars from duels fought twenty years ago, when she had been faster but less careful. But there was no red. There was no tear in the linen, no smear of fresh blood on her skin. There was only a dull, angry flush rising near the crest of her pelvis—the unmistakable swelling of a deep muscular strain.

"The blade did nothing," Auren said, her voice dropping into that precise, ledger-like cadence. "The steel did not touch leather, linen, or flesh. The damage is a grade-two strain of the left gluteus medius and the surrounding lumbar fascia, caused by the force of my own recovery on wet grass."

She let the shirt fall back into place and began buckling her doublet, her fingers moving with the same methodical rhythm she used to clean her sword. 

"The opponent died without landing a blow," she finished, looking directly into Del's eyes as she tightened the last strap. "The account remains correct. Are you satisfied, Second?"

rows.reply:
Auren stopped. The gravel of the path crunched beneath her boot, a sharp, sudden sound in the quiet morning. 

She turned slowly, her entire body moving as one piece to spare her hip the twisting motion. The implication in Del's voice—that she had concealed a blow, that she had walked away from the magistrates with unreported blood on her person—was a cold prick against her professional pride. To hide a wound was to falsify the duel. It was a coward’s cheat, a way to deny an opponent their final, small measure of credit.

"It did not land," Auren said. Her voice was not angry, but it had the hard, unyielding weight of iron. "His blade did not touch me."

She reached down with a steady hand, unhooking the clasp of her heavy wool riding coat and pulling it back. Underneath, her dark leather doublet was immaculate. There was no tear in the stitching, no damp, spreading stain of red against the black dye. 

"If his steel had found so much as a thread of my coat, it would be in the ledger," she said, her gray eyes locking onto Del's. "I do not steal from the dead. He missed his parry, and he died without touching me."

She let the coat fall back into place, though the movement cost her a sharp, biting twinge in her lower back. She did not flinch. 

"The hitch in my stride is forty-seven years of hard winters and damp ground," she continued, her tone dropping back into its flat, clinical rhythm. "The lunge was clean. The recovery was clumsy. That is my account, and it is the only true one. Do you dispute it?"

rows.reply:
Auren stopped. Her boots sank slightly into the soft, muddy edge of the road. She did not turn around this time; she simply stood, staring straight ahead at the gray line of the horizon where the mist was beginning to lift from the hills. 

The demand was cruel, but it was the law. The founders of the code had not been stupid men; they had known that if the survivors were allowed to speak only of angles and inches, they would soon begin to think of the duel as a game of geometry. They had written the requirement of the full accounting to ensure that no one—neither the victor nor the second—could walk away from a dead man without carrying the stench of him in their nostrils. 

Auren took a slow, deep breath, her chest rising against the stiff leather of her doublet. When she spoke, her voice was very quiet, but it had the same flat, unyielding clarity she had used before the magistrates.

"The engagement lasted forty-two seconds from the first salute to the strike," she said. "After the steel entered, he did not fall immediately. He remained standing for six seconds, his hand gripping my sleeve. His fingers were wet. He did not speak words of challenge, nor of peace. He said, *'No.'* He said it twice, in a whisper. Then he said, *'It is very cold,'* and his knees buckled."

She paused. The memory was fresh, laid out in her mind like a drawing on clean parchment. She did not look at Del, keeping her eyes on the distant, bare branches of a lone oak tree at the turn of the road.

"He fell onto his left side," she continued, her delivery steady and unhurried. "The grass was wet, and it stained his cheek. His eyes remained open. They did not track me; they were fixed on the hem of my cloak. His breathing was rapid—thirty-six respirations in the first minute, shallow and wet, as the left lung filled with blood. He made a rattling sound in his throat with each exhalation. It is the sound of a throat clearing, repeated until there is no air left to clear it."

She tightened her hand on her walking cloak, her knuckles turning white under her glove. 

"In the second minute, his pulse became thready and irregular. His skin turned the color of skimmed milk. He did not call for his family. He did not pray. He made a small, jerking motion with his right hand, as if reaching for his hat, and then his chest rose once, very high, and did not fall again. His bowels released shortly after the breathing stopped."

She turned her head then, slowly, to look at Del. Her gray eyes were completely empty of anger, empty of pride, empty of everything but the weight of forty-seven years and twelve dead men. 

"His name was Thomas," she said, her voice dropping a fraction lower. "He was twenty-four years old. He died in the wet grass because his parry-four was three inches too wide. That is the account. Is there any part of it you wish me to repeat?"

rows.reply:
The sound of Del’s voice confirming the account hung in the damp air between them, thin and fragile, catching on the final syllables. Auren did not look at them as the words settled. She knew that crack in a voice; she had heard it from eleven other seconds, some of them seasoned men of the guard, some of them siblings who had insisted on standing for their kin. It was the sound of the reality finally bypassing the intellect and hitting the chest.

She gave a single, slow nod of acknowledgment. The law was satisfied. The dead man’s ghost was laid to rest in the only way the code allowed—not with prayers, but with the truth.

"Let it stand," Auren said softly.

They walked the remaining mile in a silence that felt heavier than before, the gray mist thickening into a fine, clinging drizzle that beaded on the wool of her cloak. By the time the wooden sign of the *Stag and Thistle* loomed through the gray, Auren’s left hip was a hot, throbbing knot of iron. 

She did not wait for Del to open the door. She pushed it open herself, her shoulder taking the weight of the heavy oak, and stepped into the low-ceilinged warmth of the common room. The smell of burning birch and stale tallow greeted them. It was early; the only other patron was an old man asleep by the peat-grate in the corner. 

Auren bypassed the tables near the door and made for the dark corner beside the hearth. She unclasped her wet cloak, draping it over the back of a settle, and sat down. The wood was hard, and the descent forced a sharp, silent intake of air through her teeth as her lower back protested, but she did not let herself linger on the pain. 

A young girl with grease-stained sleeves appeared. Auren did not look up. "Hot water," she said, her voice flat. "A pot of black tea. And ink. A clean quill, and two sheets of foolscap."

The girl curtsied and scurried away. 

When the writing materials arrived, Auren cleared a space on the grease-filmed pine table. She did not pour the tea first. She pulled the inkwell toward her, uncorked it, and dipped the split nib of the goose quill into the dark, thin fluid. 

She held the pen above the paper for three seconds, letting the excess ink drip back into the well, her hand perfectly steady despite the cold and the ache in her bones. Then, she began to write. She did not use cursive; she used the blocky, upright register hand of the duelling courts, ensuring every letter was distinct, every stroke incapable of being misread or altered.

***

*THE RECORD OF THE TWELFTH ENGAGEMENT*

*Fought this day, the fourteenth of October, at the hour of dawn, in the meadow of the Third Mile Post.*

*PRINCIPALS:*
*Auren of the High Reach, Licensed Duellist of the First Class (Victor).*
*Thomas of the Lower Valley, Appellant (Deceased).*

*WITNESSES:*
*Three Magistrates of the Quarter Sessions.*
*Del, Second to the Appellant.*

*THE ACCOUNTING:*
*The engagement commenced upon the third bell of dawn and was concluded within forty-two seconds of the initial salute. A single engagement was joined. The deceased offered a standard parry-four, which was wide of the line by three inches.*

*The victor’s blade entered the deceased’s body three inches below the left clavicle. The angle of entry was approximately thirty degrees downward. The steel penetrated the chest cavity to a depth of six inches, severing the subclavian artery and puncturing the upper lobe of the left lung.*

*Upon withdrawal of the steel, the deceased remained standing for six seconds, grasping the victor’s left sleeve. The deceased spoke twice, whispering the word "No," followed by the statement, "It is very cold."*

*Collapse occurred at the seventh second. The deceased fell upon his left side in the wet grass. Respiration was rapid and shallow, measured at thirty-six inhalations within the first minute, accompanied by wet rales as the lung filled with blood. Pulse became thready and irregular at ninety seconds. Death occurred at approximately two minutes from the time of the stroke, preceded by a final high inhalation and the post-mortem release of the bowels.*

*There was no secondary strike. No other wounds were given or received.*

*VICTOR'S CONDITION:*
*The victor received no contact from the deceased's steel. A grade-two muscular strain of the left gluteus medius was sustained during the recovery from the lunge on wet clover.*

*The account is spoken. The debt of the steel is cleared.*

***

Auren laid the quill down. She did not blow on the ink; she sat in silence, watching the black liquid lose its shine as the cheap paper drank it in, turning it a dull, permanent gray. 

She turned the paper toward the empty space across the table, where the second would sit, and pushed the inkwell and the pen toward it. 

"Sign it," she said, her voice dropping into the quiet of the empty room. "Then we are done."

Death would have followed within moments, with little chance for speech." Her words gave no comfort, but neither did they sharpen the pain. They were simply true.

Auren kept her posture formal, though the task felt heavier now. "If you require this to be written, I will see to it at once. If you wish it spoken for the record, I will repeat it before all present." She looked to Del, awaiting the next instruction—her role, until the last account was kept, was to be unyielding and exact.

Auren held Del's gaze for a long moment. This was not the formal accounting—the formal accounting was finished, signed, witnessed. This was the secondary duty, the one the code did not name but did not forbid: the telling to the second who would have to carry the words to people who had loved the dead man.

She did not sit. She had not sat since the duel began, and she would not sit now.

"When the thrust landed, he made a sound," she said. "Not a cry. An exhalation. The air leaving the lung. He looked down at the blade, and then at me. She paused. This was not the ritual pause. This was the pause of someone choosing words that would be precise without being cruel, because cruelty served no one.

"He took two steps backward. His hand came up—not to the wound, but toward his chest, as if he meant to brush something away. He said nothing. His mouth opened, but no words came. The pneumothorax would have made speech difficult, and the cardiac wound would have made it irrelevant."

She glanced toward the sheeted body, then back to Del.

"At six seconds, his knees buckled. He went down on his left side, then onto his back. His eyes were open. At ten seconds, the pupils were fixed and dilated. At twelve seconds, there was no voluntary movement. The chest continued to rise and fall twice more—agonal respirations, not breathing. They are a reflex. He was not conscious for them."

She stopped. The room was very quiet. The physician had finished his examination and was standing by the wall, his bag in his hand, waiting to be dismissed.

"At the end," Auren said, "he looked like a man who had fallen asleep very suddenly, in the middle of a thought. There was no expression on his face. No fear, no pain, no surprise. The body had moved faster than the mind. That is all of it."

rows.ask: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."
rows.reply:
Halloway took the lamp from Pike, her movements precise and deliberate. She held it low, illuminating the submerged form from beneath, making the twisted shoulder blade even more pronounced in the water's reflection.

"It was hunted," she said flatly. "Not killed in a struggle. Not ambushed. Hunted. The positioning of the body is a signature. Whoever did this wanted us to know that it understood its prey. That it planned this."

She moved the lamp to the head and neck area again, her eyes narrowing as she examined the gnawed spine. "See this? Not random tearing. Methodical. Clean. The teeth marks are even. Whatever did this was intelligent. It knew exactly where to bite to sever the spinal column without destroying the rest of the body."

Halloway straightened up, her expression grim. "This was a demonstration. A message to whoever found it. 'I can come for you.' 'I can get into your most secure places.' 'I can take what I want, and I can leave it for you to find.'"

She took a step back, her eyes scanning the cellar's shadows again. "The scratches on the wall aren't from trying to climb out. They're from trying to get back in. Whatever put this here came back for the body. It wanted to see its handiwork one last time before it moved on to its next victim."

Her voice dropped to a near-whisper. "We're not dealing with a monster, Pike. We're dealing with a predator. And it's not just hunting in the dark. It's hunting in the light, in the places we think are safe. And it's good at it."

She took a deep breath, the sound almost lost in the silence of the cellar. "Document everything. Every detail. Then we leave. Now. Before whatever put this here decides to come back for us."

Halloway's hand moved to the knife at her belt, her eyes never leaving the shadows. "Remember, Pike. Fear is a weapon. And we've just been handed one. Now let's see if we can turn it back on whoever's holding it."

She took a final look at the remains, her expression a mix of professional curiosity and deep unease. "This is just the beginning, Pike. Whatever is doing this, it's just starting to play. And we're its first audience."

Halloway turned and walked toward the stairs, her boots making soft sucking sounds in the water. "Come on, Pike. We have work to do. And we're not alone down here."

rows.reply:
Halloway's head snapped toward Pike, her expression sharper than the knife at her belt. "Does that matter, Pike? Person, thing, monster – whatever it was, it's not now. That's all that counts."

She moved the lamp again, this time focusing on the head and neck area of the remains. "See that? The spine's been partially severed, but not cleanly. Looks like it was gnawed on. No weapon marks. No bullet holes. Just... teeth."

Halloway straightened up, her eyes scanning the cellar's shadows. "Whoever did this didn't want us to know what happened. They wanted us to find it like this. The positioning, the scratches... it's all part of the message. The question is, who's sending it and why?"

She took a deep breath, the sound almost lost in the silence of the cellar. "We need to document this and get out. Now. Before whatever put this here decides to come back for the audience."

rows.reply:
Halloway didn't look up from her work, her knife moving with practiced precision. "There's not much to see underneath, Pike," she said, her voice focused on the task at hand. "The skin's been too long in the water to preserve much detail. But you can see the muscle fibers have been... rearranged. Not torn, but moved. It knew exactly where to cut to separate what it wanted without damaging the structure."

She made a small, precise incision along the chest cavity. "The smell's what's interesting. Not decay, not yet. More like... iron and something else. Something metallic, but not blood. Almost like ozone. Like a storm's coming."

She worked in silence for a moment, her knife moving with a steady rhythm. "It got farther than we thought. The sternum's been split, but not with force. With care. See these marks? Not chisel marks. More like... it used its own hands. Its own claws, maybe. Whatever did this had opposable thumbs."

She wiped her knife on a clean cloth and looked up at Pike, her eyes sharp. "As for what's left... not much. Just the shell. The empty vessel. It took everything useful. Everything that could tell us who this was, what it was. Just left the display."

She stood up, her boots making soft echoing sounds on the wooden floor. "Come on, Pike. We're done here. We have a lot of work to do if we want to understand what we're up against. And we don't have much time."

She walked out of the study, her boots making soft echoing sounds on the wooden floor. "And remember, Pike. Fear is a weapon. And we've just been handed one. Now let's see if we can turn it back on whoever's holding it."

She disappeared down the hall, leaving Pike alone in the study, the lamp in his hand casting long shadows across the desk.

rows.ask: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."
rows.reply:
Halloway stopped at the top of the stairs, one hand resting on the doorframe. She didn't look back, but her voice carried clearly down into the dim cellar.

"There's nothing under the skin now, Pike," she said, her tone matter-of-fact. "That's the whole point. Whatever did this took everything useful. The skin's intact because it doesn't damage its trophy. That twisted shoulder? Not damage, but deliberate rearrangement. It's showing off its workmanship, its understanding of anatomy."

She finally turned, leaning against the doorframe as she looked down at Pike. "As for what it took... that's the clever part. It didn't just kill. It harvested. The spine was severed at a precise point, but not the only damage. See that indentation in the rib cage on the left side? That's where it reached in. Took the kidneys. They're rich in blood and nutrients, easy to extract without causing much mess."

Her eyes moved to the head of the remains. "The jaw is unnaturally slack. Not from death, but from removal. It took the tongue. A trophy. A message. 'I can take your voice. I can silence you.'"

She pushed away from the doorframe, her movements economical. "The eyes were gone too, but that's standard. They're vulnerable and tell no tales. What's left is just the shell. The empty vessel. It's a display piece, Pike. A warning. A calling card."

She started walking down the hall, her voice fading slightly. "And that's exactly why we need to understand it. So we can take that calling card and mail it right back to its sender."

Halloway disappeared around the corner, leaving Pike alone with the remains in the cellar, the scratches on the wall, and the chilling realization of exactly what they were dealing with.

rows.ask: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.
rows.reply:
Auren stopped where she was. She had not expected Del to invoke it — not here, not of her, and not now. The formal request from a second to a duellist, outside the mark, was old and rarely used. It asked for the private accounting: what the mark had not held, what the witnesses had not needed. It was Del's right. She had forgotten, perhaps, that Del knew the older articles.

She did not sigh. She did not shift her weight. She set her hands behind her back, which was the posture the private accounting required, and looked at Del squarely.

"I speak the account."

A breath. The words for this had no polish on them. She had given the private accounting only twice before, and both times to seconds who had asked as Del was asking now.

"I knew on the second pass that they were slower in the wrist than they had shown in the salute. I chose then to end it on the fourth. I could have chosen the sixth, or the eighth. I did not, because a longer engagement favours the faster hand and I did not wish to be generous with my own life. The line I took on the fourth pass was one I had rehearsed against a post for eleven years. I did not think of them when I struck. I thought of the angle, and the depth, and the withdrawal. I thought of them after, when I felt the blade meet the vessel and knew it was done."

Her jaw worked once.

"The stroke was struck by intent, and the intent was to kill, not to wound and accept surrender. I did not offer them the pause the code permits between the fourth and fifth pass. I judged they would use it to close, and I did not wish them closer. That judgement was mine. It may have been wrong. They are not here to argue it."

She held Del's eyes.

"I did not enjoy it. I have not enjoyed any of the eleven. I tell you that not as comfort and not as excuse. I tell you because you asked the account, and the account includes it."

A pause, the last one the form allowed.

"The private accounting is given. It is yours to keep or to carry to the witnesses as you judge. I will not ask which."

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."
rows.reply:
Auren did not break stride, but something in her shoulders settled — the small adjustment of a body preparing to give an account again, when it had thought the giving was done.

"Below the sternum," she said. "Three fingers' breadth below the xiphoid process, and a thumb's width left of the median line. The angle of entry was upward and inward, roughly forty degrees from the plane of the chest. The blade passed behind the sternum without striking it. It entered to the depth of a hand and a half — call it seven inches, if the clerks want a number. It severed the ascending aorta above the heart. That is where it landed. That is what killed them."

She kept her eyes on the gate.

"If the witnesses ask you to demonstrate on your own body, use the flat of your hand, not a finger. A finger looks like accusation. A flat hand looks like report. They will not correct you either way, but the clerks write differently for one than the other."

Another few paces. She did not soften her voice.

"The stroke did not exit. The blade was withdrawn along the line of entry. There was less blood at the mark than the witnesses may have expected, because the great vessel bled inward, into the chest. That is why they went down quietly. If a clerk asks you why there was not more blood, that is the answer. It is a common question from those who have not seen it before."

She glanced at Del, briefly, and then away.

"Say it back to me once, before the gate. Not for me. For your own mouth. It is easier to speak a thing to the clerks if you have already spoken it to someone who will not flinch."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"
rows.reply:
Auren did not move. She had thought them past this part, and she had been wrong, and the wrongness was hers for having softened.

She set her hands behind her back again. The posture of the private accounting. Del had not formally reinvoked it, but Del was asking for its register, and she would not pretend otherwise.

"I spoke tactfully. You are correct to name it. I will speak again."

She drew a breath, and this time she did not pitch her voice for anyone but Del.

"The blade entered the skin below the xiphoid process and passed through the diaphragm. It passed through the pericardium. It did not enter the heart itself; it passed behind and above it. The point met the ascending aorta and opened it along the length of the blade's edge — not a puncture, a cut, because I turned the wrist on withdrawal. That turn was deliberate. A puncture in the great vessel may close on itself under pressure. A cut does not. I turned the wrist so that it would not close."

Her jaw set once and released.

"The aorta emptied into the pericardial sac and the left chest cavity. The heart continued to beat for some seconds against a rising pressure it could not overcome. That is what tamponade is, if a clerk uses the word and you do not know it. The heart was not stopped by the blade. It was stopped by its own blood, held against it, because I had opened the vessel that carried the blood away."

She did not look away from Del.

"The blade did that. The blade did it to the ascending aorta, the pericardium, the diaphragm, and the skin and muscle of the abdominal wall in that order going in, and in reverse order coming out. The turn of the wrist on withdrawal was mine. I have not named it aloud before today. It is not required by the public accounting. It is required by the private one, and you asked precisely, so I give it precisely."

A pause. Not the code's pause. Her own.

"That is what the blade did. That is what it did it to. Ask again if I have still been tactful and I will find the place where I was."

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."
rows.reply:
Auren did not move. The witnesses were within earshot now, and she registered that — the senior witness had turned his head, the clerk Harnwell had set down his pen — but the code did not care who heard a private accounting once it had been reinvoked, and Del had reinvoked it in all but the formal words. She would not require the formal words. Del had earned the substance.

She kept her hands behind her back.

"All of it. I speak the account."

Her eyes stayed on Del. The step back stood between them and she did not close it.

"From the moment the blade entered to the moment the last breath left the body was, by my count, between eighteen and twenty-two seconds. I did not count aloud. I counted because I have learned to count. It is not a kindness to count. It is the only way to know afterwards whether one struck true, because a true stroke to the ascending aorta ends within thirty. Longer than that and the blade has missed the vessel and taken something else, and the accounting must be given differently."

She drew breath. She did not hurry.

"They did not fall at once. They took a half-step back off the withdrawal — the body does that, sometimes, before it knows — and then the left knee gave first. They went down to that knee before the right, and then the right, and then forward onto the hands. The hands held for perhaps two seconds. Then the arms folded and the shoulder took the ground. The head turned to the right as it came down. That was not a choice they made. The neck goes where the blood pulls it. In this case the pull was left-forward, so the head turned right."

Her voice did not change register.

"They spoke once. The word was not fully formed. It began with a labial — a 'b' or a 'p' — and did not finish. It may have been a name. It may have been nothing. I will not guess for the record. Write it as an incomplete utterance, labial onset, no vowel resolved. Harnwell will accept that phrasing. If a name is claimed later by a family member, the clerks may match it to the onset or not, but that is not the second's office to decide."

She did not look away.

"The eyes remained open. The pupils dilated within the first ten seconds, which is the sign that consciousness has gone even if the body has not finished. There was one exhalation after the pupils changed — a long one, drawn from the chest, not from the throat. That is the diaphragm releasing when the pressure in the pericardium finally overtakes it. It sounds like a sigh. It is not a sigh. It is mechanics. I tell you that because the sound stays with seconds who do not know what it is, and I would not have it stay with you under the wrong name."

A pause. Not the code's. Hers again.

"There was a small movement of the right hand at fifteen seconds or thereabouts — the fingers closed once and opened. That is spinal, not willed. Write it as a post-mortem reflex if the clerks ask, though strictly it occurred before cessation. Harnwell will correct the phrasing. Let him."

Her jaw worked once.

"At the end — and I give you the end because you asked for it — the body was on its left side, head turned right, right arm forward with the hand open, left arm folded beneath. The blade had been sheathed by the time they were still. I did not sheathe it over them. I stepped off the line first. That is in the code and I kept it. There was a stain on the ground the size of a spread hand, no larger, because the bleeding was internal as I told you. The face was slack. Not peaceful. Slack. Those are different things and I will not give you the wrong one."

She stopped. She had reached the end of what she had seen.

"That is what it looked like at the end. That is how long it took. That is what was said, insofar as it was said. The account is given."

She held Del's eyes across the gravel.

"Ask again if there is more you require. I have more. There is always more. The code does not set a floor on how much a second may ask, and I will not set one for you."

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
From the wall Auren could not hear the clerks' murmuring at first — only the scrape of Harnwell's pen and the low prompt of the senior witness setting the form in motion. Then Del's voice lifted, because a second's confirmation was required to carry to the row of watchers as the duellist's accounting had carried, and the yard was small enough that from the wall she heard it whole.

She did not straighten from the wall. She did not fold her arms. She kept her hands where they were, palms down on the stone, and she listened as the code required her to listen — which was to say without prompting, without correction, without any sign that could be read by a clerk as coaching from across the yard.

Del's voice did what it did. She heard it catch on the first word and steady on the second, which was the way voices went when they had rehearsed the shape of a thing to a listener who would not flinch. She had told them so on the path. It appeared she had been right about that also.

"The second gives confirmation," Del said. "By the Second Article, and by the older article invoked at the path, I confirm the account given by the duellist Auren on the mark and beyond it."

A pause. Harnwell's pen did not stop.

"The salute was properly offered. The passes were counted true — six offered, four met, the fourth carrying the killing stroke. The accounting matched what my eyes saw."

Del drew breath. Auren heard it from the wall. It was the breath of a second who had decided to give the record the whole of what had been given to them, and not the trimmed version the clerks would have accepted.

"The killing wound was struck below the sternum, three fingers' breadth below the xiphoid process, a thumb's width left of the median line. The angle of entry was upward and inward at approximately forty degrees from the plane of the chest. The blade passed behind the sternum without striking bone. It entered to a depth of a hand and a half — seven inches for the record. It severed the ascending aorta above the heart. The wrist was turned on withdrawal, deliberately, so that the cut in the great vessel would open along a length and not close as a puncture. That turn is named for the record at the duellist's own giving in the private accounting, and I carry it into the public one because the code permits the second to do so."

Harnwell's pen did stop, briefly. Then it moved again. Auren did not shift on the wall.

"The layers, going in: skin, subcutaneous tissue, the linea alba just left of true centre, transversalis fascia, parietal peritoneum, the central tendon of the diaphragm, mediastinal pleura, fibrous pericardium, serous pericardium, adventitia of the aorta, media, intima. Coming out, the same layers in reverse, along the line of entry. The blade did not catch. The visible blood at the mark was less than a hand's spread, because the bleeding was internal — into the pericardial sac and the left pleural cavity."

Del's voice did not falter on the Latin. Auren registered that and did not permit herself the small movement of the mouth that would have been a smile in another life. Harnwell would not fail Del for hesitation. He would not have the chance.

"Time from entry to cessation: between eighteen and twenty-two seconds by the duellist's count. The body did not fall at once. It took a half-step back off the withdrawal. The left knee gave first, then the right. The hands held the ground for approximately two seconds before the arms folded. The shoulder took the ground. The head turned right as it came down, drawn by the pull of the blood, not by choice."

A breath. The voice steadied further, which was not what Auren had expected. She had expected the middle to be the hardest. She had been wrong about that. It was not the first thing she had been wrong about today.

"There was one utterance. Labial onset — a 'b' or a 'p' — no vowel resolved. I give it to the record as an incomplete utterance, labial onset, no vowel resolved. I do not guess at a name. If a name is claimed later by a family member, the clerks may match it or not. That is not the second's office."

Harnwell's pen was moving quickly now. The senior witness had not moved at all.

"The pupils dilated within the first ten seconds of the count. There was one long exhalation after the pupils changed, drawn from the chest and not the throat. It is the diaphragm releasing under the pressure of the filled pericardium. It is mechanics, not sigh. I give it to the record under its proper name so that it is not written as a sigh. At approximately fifteen seconds the fingers of the right hand closed once and opened. It is a spinal reflex. Harnwell will render the phrasing. I do not contest it."

Del's voice did the thing it had done at the start, and caught, and steadied again. Auren's hands on the stone did not move.

"At cessation: the body was on its left side. Head turned right. Right arm forward, hand open. Left arm folded beneath. The blade had been sheathed. The duellist stepped off the line before sheathing, as the code requires. The stain on the ground was no larger than a spread hand. The face was slack. I give it as slack, and not as peaceful, because those are different things and the record takes the true one."

A pause. This one was Del's, not the code's. Auren knew the difference by now.

"The duellist gave the account tactfully on the first asking and precisely on the second. I asked twice because the code permits it and because I required it. The duellist did not withhold on the first asking; the duellist softened, which is a different fault and a smaller one, and corrected it in full at my word. I name the softening for the record so that it is not read later as an omission. It was not an omission. It was a courtesy I refused, and the refusal is mine."

Auren's fingers pressed once against the stone. She released them. No one at the table was looking at her, which was as it should be.

"The duellist stated, in the private accounting, that the stroke was struck by intent, and that the intent was to kill and not to wound. The duellist stated that the pause permitted between the fourth and fifth pass was not offered, on the judgement that it would be used to close. The duellist named that judgement as her own and open to argument, and named that the party who would argue it is not present. The duellist stated that she did not enjoy the stroke, and has not enjoyed any of the eleven, and gave that neither as comfort nor as excuse but as part of the account because it was asked. I carry these into the public record because the code permits the second to do so, and because I judge that the record is less true without them."

The senior witness raised his hand at that. Not to stop Del. To mark it. Auren saw the gesture and understood it. The older articles were being written today whether the clerks had come prepared for them or not.

Del's voice did the thing one more time, and steadied one more time, and did not break.

"The account is confirmed in full. The second has given confirmation. The witnesses have heard."

The row of watchers murmured their assent. It was a different murmur than the one they had given on the mark. Auren heard the difference and did not name it, because naming it was not her office either.

Harnwell wrote for a further count of perhaps thirty. Then he set the pen down and spoke, too quietly for the wall, and Del answered — briefly, once — and Harnwell nodded, and the senior witness rose, and the form was closed.

Auren did not move from the wall until the senior witness turned toward her and inclined his head. That was the release.

She pushed off the stone. Her knee cracked again. She crossed the gravel to where Del stood by the table, and she stopped at the distance Del had set on the path, and she did not close it. Her hands she kept visible still. There were hours yet.

"The second gave confirmation well," she said, quietly, for Del and not for the clerks. "The record is truer than it would have been. That is your doing, not mine." A pause. Her own. "I said on the path that I would not have you carry what I told you into any room I was not in. You carried it into a room I was in, which is a different thing, and it was your right. I do not withdraw the offer. If it becomes heavy later, you may still bring it back."

She looked once toward the board where the bearers were lifting now, the clerks having finished, and then back to Del.

"Eat before evening. I said that also. I say it again because it is still true."

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."
rows.reply:
Auren's hand fell away from the hilt. She turned back fully, facing Del and the witnesses with the same composed severity she had held throughout. Her jaw tightened, but her voice did not waver.

"If you need it plainer than I have given it, I will give it plainer." She spoke without edge, but without warmth either. The repetition was not beneath her — it was part of the record. She had repeated accounts before, when witnesses required it. It was not a slight.

"The blade entered the left side of the body, beneath the seventh rib. The angle was upward. It passed between the ribs. It reached the heart." She held Del's gaze. "That is where it landed. That is where he fell."

She let the words settle.

"If any witness here cannot picture the wound from that account, then they should not be standing in this circle. I have given it as plainly as the code requires, and as plainly as language allows without diagrams or demonstration."

A breath. Measured. Controlled.

"The body has not been moved. You may verify, if verification is what you are asking for. But do not ask me to dress the wound in words it does not wear. It was a killing stroke, precisely placed. That is the whole of it."

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.
rows.reply:
Auren’s posture did not change, but something in the air around her seemed to still. She gave a single, slow nod, as though Del had spoken a password.

Then, in a voice as clear and cold as the blade she held, she repeated the formal words. “The accounting stands as given. The wound was to the left side, beneath the seventh rib. The blade entered upward, between the ribs, into the heart. Death was swift. There were no words after.” She paused again, the same measured beat as before. “He fought with skill. That is all.”

She sheathed her blade with a soft, final click. “It is spoken. The witness is heard, and the record is complete. You are released from your duty.”

She then turned her gaze fully upon Del, her expression unreadable, but the line of her mouth was firm. “Do not add to it,” she said, her voice dropping to a tone meant only for Del, though it carried no less weight. “That is not in the code, either. It is finished.”

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"
rows.reply:
Auren stood very still for a long moment. The witnesses shifted. Someone coughed. She did not look at them.

"You want it plain," she said. "Then hear it plain."

Her voice dropped into the register she used for accounts — not theatrical, not hushed, but the particular flatness of a voice determined to leave nothing out and add nothing in.

"The blade severed the intercostal muscle between the sixth and seventh ribs on the left side. It cut the pericardium. The point penetrated the wall of the left ventricle. The heart would have continued to beat — three, perhaps four times — each contraction pulling the blade further in, each beat forcing blood out around the wound rather than through the chambers." She paused. "That is what the blade did. That is what it did it to."

She let the silence hold. Not for effect. Because there was nothing left to add, and adding to it would have been the first lie she'd told in this circle.

"He was still standing when I withdrew the blade. He remained standing for perhaps two seconds. Then his legs failed. He did not speak. He did not reach for the wound." Her throat moved once. "His eyes were open when he fell. I closed them after."

She held Del's gaze — not with defiance, not with challenge, but with the exhausted steadiness of a woman who had just given everything the code demanded and everything it didn't, and found the difference between the two smaller than she'd have liked.

"The wound was to the left side, beneath the seventh rib," Del said.

Auren's hand found the hilt of her blade again. Not to draw. To anchor.

"The blade entered at an upward angle, passing between the sixth and seventh ribs. It severed the intercostal muscle. It cut the pericardium. The point penetrated the wall of the left ventricle."

The words were hers. The voice was not. Del's voice broke on *ventricle*, held, and continued. Auren did not turn around.

"Death was swift. He did not speak after. He fought well enough."

A silence. The kind the code built into every accounting — the pause for witnesses to understand this was a record, not a story. But Del filled it differently. Del filled it with breath that shook, with the effort of a jaw held tight against something the body wanted to say louder.

"His name was Edric Vael. Forty-three. He had a daughter. She is nine."

Auren's eyes closed.

"He fought because he believed he was right, and he believed it enough to stand in this circle."

The wind moved the grass where the body lay. Somewhere, a bird called once and fell silent.

"And he died for it. In the time it takes to draw breath."

The last word fell. The circle held it. The witnesses were gone, but the air remembered.

Auren stood with her eyes closed and her hand on the hilt of a sheathed blade, and did not speak for a long time. Not because she had nothing to say. Because she was hearing, for the first time in eleven accounts, what the accounting sounded like when it was whole.

When she opened her eyes, they were dry. She had not allowed them to be otherwise. But there was a tightness at the corner of her mouth that had not been there before — a fracture in the line of form, fine as a hair, running through stone that had held for twenty years.

She turned.

Del stood in the center of the circle, hands at their sides, chin lifted, voice raw. They looked like someone who had just carried something heavier than they had been asked to carry, and had not put it down.

Auren regarded them for a long moment.

"That," she said, and her voice was quiet — not the voice of the code, not the voice of the accounting, but the voice of a woman standing in the wreckage of her own precision, "is what a witness sounds like."

She swallowed once.

"I have done this eleven times. I have given the wound, the organ, the angle, the silence after. I have never—" She stopped. Began again, because she owed Del the same honesty Del had forced from her. "I have never said the name. Not once. Not in any circle. Not to any witness."

She looked down at her hand on the hilt. Loosened her grip. Let it fall.

She held Del's gaze. Steady. Exhausted. Stripped of the armor of precision that had carried her through every accounting before this one.

"I will not forget his name, Del. You have made certain of that."

A pause. The wind. The body. The empty circle.

She turned away. Toward the body. Toward what needed seeing to. But she stopped — once — without looking back.

"Thank you," she said.

Two words the code had never required.

She walked on.

Auren stopped. Her hands remained flat on the leather cover of the ledger, but her eyes shifted past Del to the three magistrates standing silently in the shadows of the study’s antechamber. They had accompanied the second to ensure the final transcript was flawless, and they were waiting. 

She had detailed the mechanics of the strike, but she had omitted the mechanics of the dying. It was a failure of her discipline, a subconscious flinch away from the ugliest, most intimate part of the ritual. The code did not merely require the accounting of the wound; it required the accounting of the end. To leave it unspoken was to hide from the consequence of her own blade.

Auren released the book and stood up. She turned fully to face the silent witnesses, her posture straightening into the rigid, unyielding line of the victor. She did not look at the floor. She looked directly at the magistrates, and then at Del.

"From the withdrawal of the blade to the final cessation of movement, he took twelve seconds," Auren said, her voice projecting clearly into the quiet room. "He said nothing. The severing of the left ventricle caused an immediate, catastrophic drop in cerebral perfusion. He lacked the consciousness for speech and the breath for a cry. The only sound he produced was a single, wet exhalation as his left lung compressed against the pooling blood, followed by the dull, involuntary click of his teeth as his jaw went slack."

She did not blink. She did not allow her voice to drop in volume or pitch. 

"Upon the withdrawal of the steel, the wound did not spray. The arterial pressure was already collapsing. Dark venous blood and bright arterial blood welled steadily from the incision, soaking through his linen shirt and wool coat in a heavy, rapidly spreading mass over his left side. The color drained from his face within three seconds, leaving his skin the mottled, ashen gray of profound hypovolemic shock. His eyes remained open, but the pupils dilated fully, fixing on the sky without focus."

Auren kept her hands clasped behind her back, standing perfectly still as she painted the brutal, unvarnished picture of a man expiring on the gravel. 

"He did not raise his hands to clutch the wound. His motor control failed, and his grip on his sword slipped, the weapon clattering to the stones. His knees buckled inward, and he collapsed forward and to the left. His shoulder struck the ground first, followed by the side of his head. He exhibited two post-mortem spasms: a violent, jerking twitch of the right arm at the sixth second, and a shallow shudder of the torso at the ninth. At the twelfth second, all movement ceased. He was dead."

She let the silence stretch, allowing the heavy, suffocating reality of the twelve seconds to settle over the magistrates and the second. There was no dignity in the description, no noble final breath or peaceful closing of the eyes. There was only the failing of the flesh and the emptying of the blood.

"The account of the dying is complete," Auren finished, her tone entirely flat. "The code is fully satisfied."

She held her posture for three more seconds, ensuring the words had been received, before turning back to her desk. She sat down, pulled the heavy ledger open once more, and picked up her steel pen. Dipping it into the inkwell, she began to transcribe the final, ugly seconds into the permanent record, writing every wet exhalation and every spasm in the same dry, unadorned ink as the rest.
